meta.title: Conflicts and peacemaking
meta.lede: This page records wars, conflicts between religious communities, and the settlements that ended or eased them, in which religion was among the causes that anyone involved gave or that a historian names. It is not a ranking, not a count of which religion has caused most wars, and not a verdict on who was right: each entry says what each side said the matter was, how well each statement is documented, and where its numbers for the dead come from.
meta.scope_note: Religion is rarely the only cause of a war. An entry is here when a party gave religion as a reason, or when historians name it among the causes; whether it mattered most is, for many wars, what historians dispute, and the tool takes no side. The entries are a selection made by the author across the regions and centuries, not a ranking of what mattered most, and many conflicts are not written up yet.
rules: Each side is called by the name it uses for itself; the names others give it are shown beside.
What each side said the matter was is given in its own words where a source records them, and the source is named. A side’s account is a statement about what it said, not a finding.

Causes are graded religious, political, economic or mixed, each with how well it is documented and the sources for it. Historians seldom agree on one cause of a war, and none of these gradings is the tool’s own verdict.

The dead are given as a range, with what is counted, who gives each end and how sure that is. Where no source gives a figure the entry says “Not recorded”; where fewer people died than a word like war suggests, it says what the sources do record.
Where a source belongs to one side or is written by one, the entry says whose it is.
Anything that runs past 1945 is within living memory: it is marked, and every statement in it is labelled documented, reported or claimed, or disputed.

war: Armed conflict between states, peoples or organised forces.
sect: A dispute or open conflict between religious communities, or between a state and one of them, that is mainly a schism, a persecution or a quarrel over belief or rule, with or without fighting. An armed rising or war is listed under War.
peace: A treaty, edict, agreement or effort that ended or limited a conflict, or sought to reconcile those who had been in one.

treaty: The parties signed or agreed terms.
settlement: One authority set the terms, whether or not the others accepted them.
victory: The fighting ended when the forces of one side held the field, or the place, or the argument.
ceasefire: The fighting stopped without the matter being settled.
exhaustion: No treaty or decisive result; the parties stopped or could not go on.
collapse: A party’s state or organisation ended
A government, army or movement came to an end for other reasons than defeat in one battle.
continuing: Fighting, or the dispute, goes on in the sources’ latest accounts.
other: None of the above; the entry says how.

documented: A record anyone can check supports it: a treaty, an inscription, an official or court record, a party’s own published words, a census, a measured date.
reported: Said by someone, a party, a chronicler or a later historian, and not fixed by a record. The entry says whose claim it is.
disputed: Sources or scholars disagree. The entry shows each view and does not choose between them.

meta.living: Within living memory: this entry runs past 1945. Each statement carries its own label, so that people who remember it, and people who were on either side, can see what rests on a record and what does not.
meta.grades_note: Sources are graded A (a record from the time), B (a scholarly work or database) and C (a reference summary). Each was opened and read by the author on the day shown. A source that belongs to one side says whose it is.
meta.review_note: Each source named was opened and read by the author on the day shown. Found a mistake? Setup, then Tell the maker what to change.
meta.strand_blurb: Wars, conflicts between religious communities, and the settlements that ended them. Each entry gives its parties in their own words, its causes (religious, political, economic or mixed, each graded), the dead as a sourced range, and how it ended. The full entries are on the Conflicts page.

entries.label: The Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty (the “Treaty of Kadesh”)
entries.summary: About 1259 BCE Ramesses II of Egypt and Ḫattušili III of the Hittites swear a treaty of peace and alliance, after years of conflict over Syria. It is the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives in both parties’ versions. Both kings call on the gods of Egypt and Hatti to witness the oath and to curse whoever breaks it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
sources.note: it quotes the Egyptian version (Karnak, Ramesseum) and the Hittite one (cuneiform tablets from Hattusa); neither text was opened

parties.name: Ramesses II, king of Egypt
parties.said: The Egyptian version, the article says, states straightforwardly that the two states had been at war. It ends with an oath before “a thousand gods, male gods and female gods” of Egypt and Hatti, with the mountains, rivers, sky, earth, sea, winds and clouds as witnesses; whoever breaks the oath is to be cursed by the gods, who “shall destroy his house, his land and his servants”.

parties.name: Ḫattušili III, king of the Hittites
parties.said: The Hittite version opens more evasively, the article says: “as for the relationship between land of Egypt and the Hatti land, since eternity the god does not permit the making of hostility between them because of a treaty valid forever.” Each side promises that it will not invade the other’s land, will help the other against enemies and rebels, and will hand back political refugees.

causes.note: The treaty settled the rival claims to Syria by a pledge of no invasion, set the division of the disputed holdings, and bound each king to help the other against outside enemies and rebels; the article says the Hittite king also wanted Ramesses’s recognition of his rule against a rival claimant, and feared Assyria.

The oath is sworn before the gods of both lands, who are called on to guarantee it and to curse the breaker; the article says appeal to the gods was a common feature of major international agreements, because only the gods could enforce them.

Scholars argue, the article says, that Ramesses would accept the loss of Syria if the Hittites kept the division of it, gave Egypt access to ports in Hittite territory and opened trade as far north as Ugarit; what he hoped to gain is not known.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the Battle of Kadesh, about 1274 BCE, is given in its own entry, and the sources read give no figure for the dead; the article on the battle says its casualties are unknown.

outcome.note: A treaty of peace and alliance, which, the article says, was copied from silver tablets given to each side; the Egyptian version was cut on the walls of the temple at Karnak and the Ramesseum, and the Hittite one survives in cuneiform tablets.

after.note: The article’s opening says the treaty did not bring an enduring peace, quoting a scholar that “an atmosphere of enmity between Hatti and Egypt lasted many years” until a treaty of alliance was signed; its section on the aftermath says peaceful dealings continued through the rest of Ramesses’s reign, with his marriage to a Hittite princess in his thirty-fourth year, until Hatti fell to Assyria nearly a century later.

entries.label: The Cyrus Cylinder and the Persian conquest of Babylon
entries.summary: After the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, an inscription in the name of Cyrus the Great is buried as a foundation deposit. It says the god Marduk chose Cyrus, that he entered Babylon in peace, restored temples and sanctuaries and returned displaced people and the images of the gods. Scholars dispute what it shows: a general policy of tolerance, a conventional Mesopotamian royal inscription, or propaganda, and whether it concerns the Jews.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cyrus Cylinder
sources.note: it reports the scholars and the British Museum statements it names; the text of the cylinder was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Fall of Babylon
sources.note: the opening only was read

parties.name: Cyrus the Great, king of Persia, as the inscription presents him
parties.said: The article says the text portrays Cyrus as chosen by Marduk to restore peace and order, welcomed by the people of Babylon, and as a benefactor who repatriated displaced people and restored temples and sanctuaries across Mesopotamia and elsewhere in the region. It reports the British Museum’s description of the cylinder as an instrument of ancient Mesopotamian propaganda, in a long tradition of royal declarations at the start of a reign.

parties.name: Nabonidus, the last Babylonian king, and the Babylonian priesthood
parties.said: No statement of Nabonidus about Cyrus is quoted in the sources read. The article says the cylinder denounces him as impious, while a stela he commissioned shows that he favoured the moon god Sin over Marduk, which the article says the Babylonian priestly elite found unacceptable, and it adds that other evidence shows his reign was largely peaceful and that he was recognised as a legitimate king.

causes.note: The text says Marduk chose Cyrus and that Nabonidus neglected Marduk; the article agrees that Nabonidus’s greater devotion to Sin was a problem for the priests. It reports Amélie Kuhrt’s view that the restoration of sanctuaries was a literary device underlining the piety of Cyrus, and Lester Grabbe’s that the Persians’ religious policy was not very different from that of the Assyrians and Babylonians, who tolerated but did not promote local religious practice.

How far the cylinder shows a general policy toward conquered peoples is argued. The article reports Peter Bedford’s view that it is not a manifesto for a general policy toward local religions throughout the empire, and Kuhrt’s suggestion that Cyrus adopted an Assyrian practice of giving privileges to cities in strategic or sensitive regions.

Biblical scholars have traditionally read a passage of the cylinder as supporting the Book of Ezra’s account that Cyrus let the Jews return, but the article says the text names only Mesopotamian sanctuaries and does not mention Jews, Jerusalem or Judea. It says the two biblical edicts differ and that their authenticity is unresolved, though they are widely believed to reflect some Persian royal policy.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article on the fall of Babylon gives the conquest as an Achaemenid victory in 540 and 539 BCE, with the Battle of Opis in late 539, and the sources read give no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: The cylinder was found in the ruins of Babylon in 1879 and is now in the British Museum. The text says Cyrus entered the city in peace. In 2010 the museum announced that two cuneiform tablets carry the same text, which it said shows that the text was probably a proclamation widely distributed across the Persian empire.

after.note: In the late 1960s the last Shah of Iran promoted the cylinder as “the world’s first charter of human rights”, and in 2010 the Iranian president called it the “First Charter of Human Rights”. The article says historians have called that reading anachronistic; C. B. F. Walker of the British Museum wrote that it is a building inscription in the Babylonian and Assyrian tradition and not a general declaration of human rights or religious toleration, and Neil MacGregor cautioned against narrowing its meaning to one political agenda.

entries.label: Ashoka’s edicts on the honour of all religions
entries.summary: After conquering Kalinga, King Ashoka of the Maurya empire has fourteen Rock Edicts cut in stone across his lands. One honours the followers of every religion and asks that none praise its own while condemning others; another records his remorse at the dead and deported of the Kalinga war.

sources.title: The Edicts of King Ashoka: an English rendering by S. Dhammika (Buddhist Publication Society, 1993), Rock Edicts V, XII and XIII
sources.note: a translation of the inscriptions; some translators render the word Dhammika gives as “religions” as “sects”

sources.title: S. Dhammika, introduction to The Edicts of King Ashoka (1993)
sources.note: the translator’s account of the king and the war; the same page

parties.name: King Ashoka, who calls himself “Beloved-of-the-Gods, King Piyadasi”
parties.said: Rock Edict XII: he “honors both ascetics and the householders of all religions”, but values more “that there should be growth in the essentials of all religions”, whose root is “restraint in speech, that is, not praising one’s own religion, or condemning the religion of others without good cause”. Rock Edict XIII: he feels “deep remorse for having conquered the Kalingas”.

parties.name: The religious communities of the empire and of the conquered country: Brahmans, ascetics and householders of different religions
parties.said: No statement of theirs survives in the sources read. Rock Edict XIII says they were among those hurt when Kalinga was conquered: “Brahmans, ascetics, and householders of different religions” who were “injured, killed or separated from their loved ones”.

causes.note: Rivalry and mutual condemnation among religions: Edict XII warns that whoever praises his own religion out of devotion and condemns others “only harms his own religion”.
The conquest of Kalinga, eight years after the king’s coronation, which Rock Edict XIII names as the cause of his remorse and of his turn to the Dhamma.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: Rock Edict XIII gives the toll of the Kalinga war itself as “one hundred and fifty thousand” deported, “one hundred thousand” killed “and many more died (from other causes)”.

outcome.note: The king ordered the edicts cut at sites across his lands. Edict V says he appointed Dhamma Mahamatras, officers who worked “among all religions” for the welfare of those devoted to Dhamma; Edict XII says many officers worked for growth in the essentials of all religions.

after.note: Dhammika’s introduction says that after the war Ashoka devoted the rest of his life to applying Buddhist principles to government, that the protection of all religions was seen as a duty of the state, that his edicts stand in more than thirty places across India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan, and that he died in 232 BCE. How far the edicts were obeyed is not recorded in the sources read.

entries.label: The Maccabean Revolt in Judea
entries.summary: In 167 BCE a Jewish rebellion led by Mattathias and his sons, the Maccabees, begins in Judea against the Seleucid Empire after King Antiochus IV bans Jewish practices. The Temple is retaken and rededicated in 164 BCE, the origin of Hanukkah. Historians dispute how far the cause was religious repression, a civil war between traditionalist and Hellenized Jews, or taxation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maccabean Revolt
sources.note: it reports the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees, Josephus and the modern historians it names; none was opened

parties.name: The Maccabees, Mattathias and his sons, above all Judas Maccabeus, with their followers in the Judean countryside
parties.said: The article says the books of 1 and 2 Maccabees, written after the revolt, describe it as a collective response to cultural oppression and national resistance to a foreign power, urge unity among the Jews and call the Hellenizing faction lawless and corrupt. It gives the festival of Hanukkah as the remembrance of the cleansing of the Temple and the rededication of the altar on 25 Kislev.

parties.name: The Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes and the high priests he appointed, Jason and Menelaus
parties.said: The article says Antiochus launched a campaign of repression against the Jewish religion in 168 BCE and that the reason is not entirely clear. It says Josephus blames Menelaus for persuading him to issue his decrees, and that the Seleucids eventually relented and lifted the ban on Judaism. The article on Antiochus calls the rebellion of the Maccabees one of the notable events of his reign.

parties.name: Hellenized Jews, among them the Tobiad clan and the supporters of Menelaus
parties.said: No statement of theirs is preserved in the sources read; the books of the Maccabees describe them only as lawless and corrupt. The article says that in the revisionist view a majority of the Jews cautiously supported Menelaus, and that the revolt was best understood as a civil war between traditionalist Jews in the countryside and Hellenized Jews in the cities.

causes.note: The article says Jewish practices were banned and the Temple was made the site of a worship mixing Greek and Jewish elements, but that Antiochus’s reason is not entirely clear. It says Sylvie Honigman argues that the accounts of religious oppression are misleading and probably false, and that the struggle was fundamentally economic and was read as religious only in retrospect; the article says this has attracted partial support but has not become a consensus.

The article says the conflict between Jason and Menelaus, each of whom bought the high priesthood from Antiochus, was largely political rather than cultural, all sides being Hellenized and divided over Menelaus’s alleged corruption. It says Daniel Schwartz argues that Antiochus put down a real rebellion that was later lost to history, and that defenders of the direct reading of the sources call the evidence for such a rebellion thin to nonexistent.

The article says Honigman holds that the loss of civil rights in 168 BCE was an administrative punishment after local unrest over increased taxes, and that the claim that Menelaus sold Temple vessels to pay for his bribe was meant to discredit him and Antiochus.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the revolt.

outcome.note: The Maccabees captured Jerusalem in 164 BCE and the Seleucids eventually lifted the ban on Judaism. The main phase ended in 160 BCE when Judas Maccabeus died at the Battle of Elasa and the Seleucids regained direct control for a time; the article says conflict continued until 134 BCE, when the Maccabees eventually attained independence.

after.note: The Hasmonean dynasty, descended from the Maccabees, lasted until 37 BCE, when Herod, with Roman support, defeated its last ruler. The article says it kept a blend of Jewish and Greek traditions while restoring Judaism to primacy in Judea; it also reports John Ma’s argument that the Temple was restored in 164 BCE on Menelaus’s petition to Antiochus, not liberated by the Maccabees.

entries.label: The First Jewish–Roman War (the Great Jewish Revolt)
entries.summary: In 66 CE unrest in the Roman province of Judaea grows into a revolt against Rome. The Romans under Vespasian and then his son Titus retake the country, and in 70 they destroy Jerusalem and its Temple; the last strongholds fall by 73 or 74. Historians weigh nationalism, religious zeal and economic grievance differently, and the figures for the dead are disputed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Jewish–Roman War
sources.note: it reports Josephus, Tacitus and the historians named; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bar Kokhba revolt, its account of the evidence and of the period between the two revolts

parties.name: The Judean rebels: the provisional government and the factions called Zealots, Sicarii and others
parties.said: The article says the rebels minted coins inscribed “Israel” and adopted a new era, “the freedom of Israel”. It reports Josephus, who commanded the defence of Galilee and wrote after his capture by the Romans, as saying that the Jews preferred to die in battle rather than bear a long suffering under the governor Florus.

parties.name: The Roman Empire: the governors of Judaea, then Vespasian and Titus
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says ancient sources name the governor Gessius Florus’s looting of the temple treasury and his killing of Jerusalem’s residents as the spark, and that Tacitus blamed Roman misgovernment rather than Jewish defiance, writing that the Jews showed restraint under harsh governors until Florus’s actions.

causes.note: Most scholars, the article says, see the revolt as a clear case of ancient Jewish nationalism, aiming at freedom from Roman control and an independent Jewish state; David Goodblatt compares the rebels’ aims to those of modern national liberation movements.

Zeal for God’s sole rule and law, which Martin Hengel and Philip Alexander see as driving the rebel factions, and apocalyptic hopes, which Jonathan Price stresses; Tessa Rajak finds no evidence that the rebels were moved by messianic or end-of-days hopes.

Heinz Kreißig read the revolt as a class struggle, citing the burning of debt records; Jonathan Price and Guy Rogers find little evidence of economic grievances and read that act as a tactic to win popular support.

casualties.unit: deaths in Jerusalem, in the siege of 70 and its fall
casualties.basis: People who died in Jerusalem, from battle, famine and the sack of the city; deaths elsewhere in Judaea are not counted in this range.
casualties.note: Josephus, who wrote under Roman protection, gives 1.1 million, which the article says is widely considered exaggerated; Guy Rogers reads it as meant to flatter the Romans and suggests 20,000 to 30,000; Charles Murison thinks it may mean the total losses of the war. Tacitus gives 600,000 as the number besieged. Moshe David Herr estimates that a quarter of Judaea’s Jews were killed and a tenth taken captive; Josephus’s 97,000 captives is accepted by several scholars.

outcome.note: Roman forces took Galilee in 67 and Jerusalem in 70, where the Temple was burned; the last strongholds fell by 73 or 74.

after.note: The article says the war ended the Jewish polity in Judaea and brought displacement, enslavement and the loss of land, but that Jewish life recovered and Jews stayed the largest group in the region until they rose again in the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–136.

entries.label: The Bar Kokhba revolt
entries.summary: Led by Simon bar Kokhba, Jewish rebels set up an independent state in Judaea in about 132 against the Roman Empire under Hadrian, which had planned to rebuild Jerusalem as a Roman colony. Rome crushes the revolt by about 135 or 136. Our only long account is by Cassius Dio, and the scale of the losses is argued about.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bar Kokhba revolt
sources.note: it reports Cassius Dio, Eusebius, the rabbinic sources and the scholars named; none was opened

parties.name: Simon bar Kokhba and the Jewish state he led
parties.said: No writing of his own is quoted in the sources read. The article says rabbinic literature describes him explicitly as a messianic figure, with both sympathetic and critical views of his leadership and of the revolt’s outcome, and that Cassius Dio’s account does not name him.

parties.name: The Roman Empire under the emperor Hadrian
parties.said: No statement of his is quoted in the sources read. The article says Cassius Dio names Hadrian’s plan to rebuild Jerusalem as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, dedicated to Jupiter, as the trigger, and that the Historia Augusta, a fourth-century collection, names a ban on circumcision; recent scholarship increasingly rejects that second source.

causes.note: The plan for Aelia Capitolina, which ended hopes of rebuilding the Temple, is now generally seen as the main cause; whether a ban on circumcision came before the revolt or followed it as a punishment is a matter on which scholars differ.
Resentment of Roman rule and national hopes stayed high in Judaea after the first revolt, the article says.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range. The main ancient figure is Cassius Dio’s 580,000 “slain in the various raids and battles”, besides those who died of famine, disease and fire, “past finding out”. Peter Schäfer thinks the figures may be inflated; Hannah Cotton (2003) finds them highly plausible by Roman census declarations; Dvir Raviv and Chaim Ben David (2021) find them consistent with the archaeology of depopulation; Shimon Applebaum estimated that about two-thirds of Judaea’s Jewish population died.

outcome.note: The main phase ran from autumn 132 to summer 135, and Rome’s suppression ended with the siege and fall of Betar, which Eusebius names as the site of the last stand.

after.note: The article says Judaea proper was nearly emptied of its Jewish population by killing, enslavement and displacement. Hadrian then banned Torah study and the Hebrew calendar, executed sages and burned sacred texts, and put statues of Jupiter and himself on the Temple ruins; the measures lasted until his death in 138.

entries.label: The Great Persecution of Christians in the Roman Empire
entries.summary: In 303 the emperors Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius and Constantius begin a series of edicts that take away the legal rights of Christians and order the clergy and then everyone to sacrifice to the Roman gods. The persecution is hardest in the eastern provinces and ends there with an edict of toleration in 311.

sources.title: Lactantius, On the Manner in Which the Persecutors Died, chapters 34 and 35 (the edict of Galerius), in the Church Fathers collection of New Advent
sources.partisan: Lactantius, a Christian writer who preserves the edict and writes against its authors
sources.note: an English translation of the nineteenth century

parties.name: The emperors Diocletian, Maximian, Galerius and Constantius
parties.said: In the edict of 311 that ended the persecution in the East, Galerius says the emperors had “studied to reduce all things to a conformity with the ancient laws and public discipline of the Romans”, and had aimed that the Christians, who had abandoned the religion of their forefathers, “should return to right opinions”. The article says Diocletian styled himself a restorer of traditional Roman values and wished to inspire a religious revival, with unity in worship at its centre.

parties.name: The Christian communities of the empire
parties.said: No statement of theirs from the time is quoted in the sources read. The article records that many Christians evaded the edicts, some by bribery and many by flight, and that Lactantius and Bishop Peter of Alexandria held that flight was permitted, citing the saying “when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another”.

causes.note: The emperors’ wish to restore traditional Roman worship and unity of worship, which, in Galerius’s own edict, Christians had abandoned.

The article ties the persecution to Diocletian’s traditionalist programme of renewal, the Tetrarchy, and to the long-standing Roman suspicion of independent societies; it says the removal of religious minorities was one step in a reform of the empire’s moral fabric.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a count: the article says the persecution varied in intensity, weakest in Gaul and Britain, where only the first edict was applied, and strongest in the eastern provinces, and that the Liber Pontificalis alleges that 17,000 Christians were killed in a single thirty-day period; it gives no counted figure.

outcome.note: Galerius ended the persecution in the East by an edict issued in 311, preserved by Lactantius; the agreement of 313 between Constantine and Licinius is usually named as the end of persecution across the empire.

after.note: The article says the persecution did not succeed: Christians were never purged systematically in any part of the empire. Some Christian communities were split between those who had complied with the authorities and those who had refused; in Africa the Donatists went on resisting the central church until after 411. By 324 Constantine ruled the whole empire, and under Theodosius I (378–395) Christianity became the state religion.

entries.label: The Donatist schism in North Africa
entries.summary: From 311 a dispute over whether the sacraments of clergy who had handed over scriptures under persecution were valid divides the Christians of North Africa. The Donatists hold that the church must be faultless; the Catholic church, backed by the Roman emperors, condemns them. A conference at Carthage in 411 rules against them, and force is then used to bring them back.

sources.title: Augustine of Hippo, Letter 185 (to Boniface), in the Church Fathers collection of New Advent
sources.partisan: Augustine, a bishop on the Catholic side of the dispute
sources.note: an English translation of the nineteenth century

sources.title: Wikipedia: Councils of Carthage, the section on the Conference of 411

parties.name: The Donatists, the followers of Donatus Magnus
parties.said: The article says they held that Christian clergy must be faultless for their ministry to be effective and their sacraments valid, that a church must be a church of “saints”, and that they were themselves the church with valid sacraments. No text of their own was read.

parties.name: The Catholic church of Africa and Rome, with the Roman authorities, and Augustine of Hippo
parties.said: Augustine writes in Letter 185 that when emperors make good laws for the truth against falsehood, “those who rage against them are put in fear, and those who understand are reformed”, and likens the correction of the Donatists to a shepherd’s or a physician’s care, which it would be “mistaken kindness” to withhold. The article says he cited the parable of the great banquet, “compel them to come in”, to justify force, but rejected the death penalty.

causes.note: Whether sacraments given by clergy who had handed over scriptures in the persecution under Diocletian (traditores) were valid, which began with a disputed consecration of the bishop of Carthage in 311; Augustine’s letters and the article both set the dispute out this way.

The Roman authorities took the Catholic side: the article records a commission under Pope Miltiades that condemned the Donatists two years after 311, repression because of their link with the violent Circumcellions, and an imperial decree requiring them to give up their churches.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure. The article speaks of the violent Circumcellions on one side and of persecution by the Roman authorities on the other, and says Augustine himself protested at the treatment of the Donatists.

outcome.note: A conference at Carthage in 411, ordered by Emperor Honorius and presided over by Marcellinus, found for the Catholic party, which, the article says, led to the violent suppression of the Donatists.

after.note: The article says Donatists remained a force in Augustine’s lifetime and disappeared only after the Muslim conquest of the seventh and eighth centuries.

entries.label: The edicts of toleration of 311 and 313
entries.summary: In 311 the emperor Galerius, near death, lets Christians exist again and rebuild their meeting places. In 313 Constantine and Licinius agree at Milan to treat Christians kindly and to give back their property. Scholars now doubt that a formal “Edict of Milan” was ever issued, though the texts survive.

sources.title: Lactantius, On the Manner in Which the Persecutors Died, chapters 34 and 35 (the edict of Galerius), in the Church Fathers collection of New Advent
sources.partisan: Lactantius, a Christian writer who preserves the edict

sources.title: Wikipedia: Diocletianic Persecution, the section on the Peace of Galerius and the Edict of Milan

parties.name: The emperor Galerius (311)
parties.said: His edict, as Lactantius gives it, says that because many Christians persisted in their opinions and neither honoured the gods nor worshipped their own God, “from our wonted clemency” he had “judged it fit to extend our indulgence to those men, and to permit them again to be Christians, and to establish the places of their religious assemblies; yet so as that they offend not against good order”, and that they should pray to their God for the emperor and the commonwealth.

parties.name: The emperors Constantine and Licinius (313)
parties.said: The article says they agreed at Milan to treat Christians kindly and allow religious freedom more broadly; the version Lactantius preserves is a letter from Licinius to the governors of the eastern provinces, which orders meeting places and other property to be returned “without payment or any claim of recompense and without any kind of fraud or deception”, so that divine favour may “preserve and prosper our successes together with the good of the state”.

causes.note: The persecution of Christians and the failure of the emperors’ aim of bringing them back to the old worship: Galerius’s own edict says that many persisted and that the persecution had not won them over.
Whether the agreement at Milan was an act of Constantine’s faith or a political calculation is disputed; the article says the majority of historians think his adoption of Christianity was genuine.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the persecution it ended are not counted in the sources read (see the entry for the Great Persecution).

outcome.note: Galerius’s edict gave Christians the right to exist and to assemble in peace, but, the article notes, did not restore their confiscated property and admitted no wrong. The text of 313 ordered that property be restored. Neither made Christianity the state church: that came in 380 with the Edict of Thessalonica.

after.note: The article says scholars no longer much debate that there was no formal “Edict of Milan”: the text in Lactantius is a letter of Licinius, and Eusebius’s version differs markedly from it. The edict of Galerius seems to have been promulgated only in his own provinces.

entries.label: The Conference of Carthage (411)
entries.summary: On the order of Emperor Honorius, Catholic and Donatist bishops meet at Carthage in 411 to end the Donatist schism. The imperial official who presides, Marcellinus, finds for the Catholic party. The ruling is followed by the suppression of the Donatists.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Councils of Carthage, the section on the Conference of 411
Augustine of Hippo, Letter 185 (to Boniface), in the Church Fathers collection of New Advent
sources.partisan: Augustine, a bishop on the Catholic side of the dispute

parties.name: Emperor Honorius, who ordered the conference, and Marcellinus, who presided
parties.said: The article says the conference was held by command of the emperor “with a view to terminating the Donatist schism”, and that Marcellinus found in favour of the orthodox party.

parties.name: The Catholic bishops, with Augustine of Hippo
parties.said: Augustine’s Letter 185 argues that imperial laws made for the truth against falsehood are good because they put those who resist them in fear and reform those who understand; he holds that to leave the Donatists in error would be a mistaken kindness.

parties.name: The Donatist bishops
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read.

causes.note: The Donatist schism, a dispute about the validity of sacraments given by clergy who had handed over scriptures under persecution.
The emperor ordered the conference, and its president was an imperial official: the schism was treated as a matter for the state.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article says its ruling led to the violent suppression of the Donatists, and gives no figure.

outcome.note: Marcellinus ruled for the orthodox party; the ruling was the basis for the suppression of the Donatists.

after.note: The Donatist church did not disappear at once: the other source says Donatists were still a force in Augustine’s lifetime; the article on Donatism says they lasted until the Muslim conquest.

entries.label: The persecution at Najran and the Aksumite war in Himyar
entries.summary: Yūsuf As’ar Yath’ar, a king of Himyar in Arabia who had turned to Judaism, attacks the Christians of Najran and Zafar. Kaleb, the Christian king of Aksum across the Red Sea, sends an army that ends his rule. Sources date the invasion from about 520 to 525, and historians disagree about why the king acted as he did.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dhu Nuwas
sources.note: it reports the Sabaean inscriptions and the Syriac accounts; neither was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Kaleb of Axum
sources.note: it reports Procopius and John of Ephesus; neither was opened

parties.name: Yūsuf As’ar Yath’ar, king of Himyar, and his army
parties.also: Called Dhu Nuwas in Arab tradition, Masruq in Syriac sources and Dounaas in Greek
parties.said: An inscription calls him “king of all nations”, and Himyarite inscriptions record his campaigns against the Aksumites at Zafar and the fighters at Najran, with 12,500 trophies, 11,000 captives and 290,000 camels, cattle and sheep taken. The Arab historians, the article says, tell that he wrote to the Lakhmid king and to the Persian king urging them to do the same to the Christians under their rule.

parties.name: Kaleb, king of Aksum, with the Byzantine emperor Justin I
parties.also: Also called Ella Asbeha and, in Greek, Elesbaas
parties.said: No statement of his own is quoted in the sources read. The articles say that refugees from Najran begged Justin I to avenge the Christians, that Kaleb sent troops to depose the king and end the persecution of Christians, and that Procopius has the Aksumites invading at Justin’s request.

causes.note: The Christian sources tell of an attack on the Christians of Najran and Zafar by a king who had adopted Judaism, and of an Aksumite army sent in answer; the Quran, the article notes, mentions the persecution without naming the king.

Many modern historians, the article says, take the king’s turn to Judaism as tactical: a counterweight to Christian Aksum and a way to win favour with Sasanian Persia, in a struggle between Byzantium and Persia for influence in Arabia; one historian, Christopher Haas, differs.

casualties.basis: The dead at the siege and burning of Najran in 523–524 only; the dead of the wider war are not given.
casualties.note: The Sabaean inscriptions, as the article reports them, record “1000 killed, 1500 prisoners” at Najran; the Syriac accounts, as ’Irfan Shahid summarises them, put the dead at about 2,000. The article adds that Dhu Nuwas killed Arethas, the Miaphysite Christian leader, with 340 of his followers in 523.

outcome.note: Kaleb’s soldiers routed the Himyarite army and killed the king, and Kaleb set up a Christian viceroy, Sumyafa Ashwa.

after.note: About 525 Abraha deposed the viceroy and made himself king; Procopius, the article says, has Kaleb making several unsuccessful attempts to recover Yemen, and his successor negotiating a peace with Abraha, who acknowledged Aksum’s authority and paid tribute. Stuart Munro-Hay calls the Aksumite expedition the end of Aksum as a great power in the region.

entries.label: The Soga–Mononobe conflict over Buddhism in Japan
entries.summary: In 587, after the death of Emperor Yōmei, two great clans of the Yamato court, the Soga, who backed the adoption of Buddhism, and the Mononobe, who opposed it, fight over the succession. The Soga win at the Battle of Shigisan, and Buddhism spreads under their rule.

parties.name: The Soga clan, led by Soga no Umako
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Umako went to great lengths to promote Buddhism and was instrumental in its acceptance, and that in 593 relics of the Buddha were set in the foundation stone of a pagoda at Asuka-dera, the temple built under his lead.

parties.name: The Mononobe clan, led by Mononobe no Moriya, with Nakatomi no Katsumi
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Moriya, like his father, was a devoted opponent of Buddhism, which had recently come to Japan from the continent, and that he worked with Nakatomi no Katsumi to counter Umako’s efforts; he is credited with burning the first Buddhist temples in Japan.

causes.note: Whether the court should adopt Buddhism, the religion newly brought from the continent: the Mononobe opposed it and the Soga supported it, and the articles tie the fortunes of each clan to the emperors’ own attitude, Bidatsu’s to the Mononobe’s advantage and Yōmei’s, who became Buddhist, to the Soga’s.
After Yōmei’s death in 587 each clan tried to influence the succession, and the dispute became open battle.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: Soga no Umako defeated Mononobe no Moriya at the Battle of Shigisan in 587, which secured the Soga’s dominance at court.

after.note: The article says Umako carried out political reforms with Prince Shōtoku, strengthened his clan’s hold on government by marrying his daughters into the imperial family, and promoted Buddhism, whose acceptance in Japan he was instrumental in.

entries.label: The Constitution of Medina
entries.summary: About 622 or soon after, according to most historians who accept the document, a text known as the Constitution of Medina sets out the rights and duties of the Muslims who had left Mecca, the clans of Medina and the Jewish groups there, with Muhammad as chief arbiter. It declares them one community while each keeps its own religion. Its date, whether it is one document or several, and which Jewish groups it included are all disputed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Constitution of Medina
sources.note: it reports the scholars it names (Serjeant, Watt, Grimme, Caetani and others); none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Islamic state
sources.note: a long article that follows the traditional account of the sirah; only the opening and the sections on Medina and the Jewish clans were read

parties.name: Muhammad and the Muslims: the Muhajirun, who came from Mecca, and the Ansar, the helpers of Medina
parties.said: The article says the document redefined ties among the “Believers”, setting faith above blood, and that Jonathan Berkey finds it notable for treating the Jewish tribes as “one community with the believers” who also “have their religion and the Muslims have theirs”. It quotes Welch that the constitution shows Muhammad’s diplomatic skill, letting the ideal of a community based on religion sink temporarily into the background.

parties.name: The Jewish groups of Medina named in the document, but not, the article notes, the three major tribes, Qaynuqa, Nadir and Qurayza
parties.said: No statement of theirs is recorded in the sources read. The article says it is unclear with which Jews the agreement was made: only smaller groups that had lost their tribal structure, Judaized Arabs, or also the three major clans. The article on the first Islamic state says that in the traditional account the Jewish clans did not keep to the treaties.

parties.name: The Arab clans of Medina, among them the Aws and Khazraj, polytheist and Muslim
parties.said: No statement of theirs is recorded in the sources read. The article says that, according to traditional Islamic belief, delegates of the twelve important clans invited Muhammad as a neutral outsider to be chief arbitrator after about a hundred years of fighting, and that the document named him Chief Magistrate.

causes.note: According to the traditional account in both articles, fighting among the clans of Medina, mainly its polytheist and Jewish inhabitants, had gone on for about a hundred years before 620, and after the Battle of Bu’ath, in which all the clans were involved, blood feud was no longer workable without one authority to decide disputes. The document named Muhammad chief magistrate and united the clans and the emigrants.

The article says faith became the main binding tie of the new community, in contrast to the tribal norms of pre-Islamic Arabia, while the Jewish groups kept their own religion. It reports Watt’s likening of the community to a tribe based on religion rather than kinship, and Serjeant’s view that earlier theocratic communities existed.

The date is argued: Watt puts it in 622 or soon after, Grimme after the battle of Badr in 624, Caetani before it. Serjeant held it to be eight documents issued over some seven years; others call it a municipal charter or a unilateral proclamation rather than a treaty, and a few historians remain sceptical. One suggestion in the article is that, if it existed, it was made after the three major Jewish clans had been removed from Medina.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the fighting among the clans of Medina that came before it.

outcome.note: A text of about 47 clauses, known only from excerpts in early Muslim sources, mainly Ibn Hisham, and without a chain of narrators, though most historians accept it as authentic. The article says it has been called the world’s first constitution to establish pluralism, religious freedom and collective defence.

after.note: The article on the first Islamic state says Muhammad’s attitude toward the Jewish scholars of Medina turned negative after contradiction, ridicule and rejection, that the Banu Qaynuqa were expelled, and that the Banu Qurayza, charged with treachery in the siege of Medina in 627, were besieged and their fighting men put to death. It says Muslims and Western historians differ on whether Muhammad ordered it and on how many were put to death.

entries.label: The early Muslim conquests

places.name: The Iberian Peninsula, the western end of the expansion

entries.summary: From 622 to 750 the Muslim community founded by Muhammad at Medina, and then the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates, expand out of Arabia in a series of wars, and Muslim rule is set up over most of the Middle East and North Africa and parts of Central and South Asia and southern Europe. Explanations of the speed of the conquests differ: historians point to the exhaustion of the Byzantine and Sasanian empires and to the unity of the new state, and the sources give religious as well as other reasons.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Early Muslim conquests
sources.note: a very long article; its opening and the sections on the armies, the campaigns in Syria, Egypt and Persia, the explanations and the aftermath were read

parties.name: The Muslim armies of the Rashidun and Umayyad caliphates, from the time of Muhammad’s successors Abu Bakr and Umar
parties.said: The article says early Muslim historians viewed the conquests as a reflection of the religious zeal of the conquerors and evidence of divine favour, while the modern historian Fred Donner suggests that the first Islamic state, with its ideological coherence and mobilisation, was the main factor. It says that on the surrender of Jerusalem Caliph Umar promised to tolerate its Christians and not to turn churches into mosques.

parties.name: The Byzantine and Sasanian empires and the peoples under them: Greeks, Persians, Copts, Berbers, Visigoths and others
parties.said: The article says contemporary Christian writers saw the conquests as God’s punishment of their fellow Christians for their sins, and that the Byzantine emperor Heraclius had portrayed his war against Zoroastrian Persia as a holy war. It says Jews and some Christians in both empires may have been dissatisfied and either welcomed the Muslim troops or been indifferent, while Arab Christian confederations such as the Ghassanids first allied themselves with the Byzantines.

parties.name: The Christian kingdom of Makuria in Nubia
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the Baqt says an Arab expedition south against the Christian kingdoms of Nubia in 651 or 652 ended in a treaty, not a conquest, and that the treaty largely blocked the spread of Islam and the Arabs there for half a millennium.

causes.note: The role of religion is explained differently in the article: early Muslim historians saw religious zeal and divine favour; contemporary Christian writers saw a divine punishment; Donner stresses the ideological coherence of the new state. The article says the theory that the conquests were an economic migration was popular early in the twentieth century but has largely fallen out of favour among historians, and that detailed explanations are hard because only fragmentary sources survive.

Most historians cited agree that the Sasanian and Byzantine empires had been left exhausted militarily and economically by decades of war against each other and by plague, and that a Sasanian civil war of 628 to 632 hastened political collapse.

After the conquests the new rulers generally left old elites with local political, religious and financial authority, while peasants paid taxes that often reached half their produce; the article says scholars differ in their accounts of the taxation and of how conversion followed. It does not give the conquests an economic cause that is generally accepted.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sections read give no overall figure for the dead of the conquests, only accounts of single battles and sieges.

outcome.note: The article’s infobox gives a Muslim victory. By about 750 Muslim rule stretched from Sind to the Iberian Peninsula over an area it estimates at 13,000,000 square kilometres, and the Byzantines were left with part of Anatolia and southeastern Europe. In Nubia the advance ended in the treaty of 652 that the second article describes.

after.note: The article says there is no evidence of mass conversion to Islam in the immediate aftermath: the first to convert were Christian Arab tribes, then former Sasanian elites. It says Umar settled Arab armies in garrison towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat, and that the old elites kept much of their authority in return for taxes.

entries.label: The Treaty of al-Hudaybiya between Medina and the Quraysh of Mecca
entries.summary: In March 628 Muhammad, leading followers from Medina who had set out on a pilgrimage, and representatives of the Quraysh of Mecca make a ten-year truce at al-Hudaybiya, after the Quraysh had refused to let the pilgrims enter the city. The Muslims were to make the pilgrimage the following year. About two years later the truce ended after an attack involving allies of both sides, and Mecca fell to Muhammad.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Treaty of al-Hudaybiya
sources.note: it relies on early Muslim accounts and on historians it names; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Conquest of Mecca
sources.note: the opening only was read

parties.name: Muhammad and the Muslims of Medina, with Ali, who wrote the agreement
parties.said: The article says Muhammad stated that his aim was to perform the pilgrimage rather than fight. According to the traditional accounts he accepted the Quraysh envoy’s changes to the wording: the document began “In your name, O God” in place of “In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate”, and named him “Muhammad, son of Abdullah” in place of “Messenger of God”. The article reports that some followers, among them Umar, objected to the terms.

parties.name: The Quraysh of Mecca, represented by Suhayl ibn Amr
parties.said: The article reports the Quraysh as saying that even if Muhammad had come not wanting to fight, he would never enter by force against their will, and that they regarded letting him in unconditionally as weakness and a declaration of defeat. It says Suhayl objected to the title “Messenger of God” because the Quraysh did not recognise Muhammad’s claim to be one.

causes.note: The pilgrimage to the Kaaba, a pilgrimage centre since before Islam, was at stake. The article says Islamic tradition makes the obligation of pilgrimage to Mecca date from the Medinan period; the truce let the Muslims return the following year and stay three days while the Quraysh left the city.

Historians cited in the article differ on what each side gained. Fred Donner suggests the pilgrimage was a way to obtain a truce, since Medina lay between hostile Khaybar and Mecca; Montgomery Watt reads the terms as an effort to improve relations with the Quraysh and encourage them to accept Islam. The article says that by signing, the Quraysh implicitly acknowledged Muhammad as a political equal.
The article says Watt held that the treaty helped to remove restrictions on Medinan access to the Meccan trade routes to Syria, and that it included concessions to the Quraysh.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the armed conflicts between Medina and Mecca that came before it.

outcome.note: A truce of ten years. A person of the Quraysh who fled to Muhammad without the permission of a guardian was to be returned, and one who went the other way was not; anyone could choose to make a covenant with either side; the Muslims were to go back to Medina that year, and make the pilgrimage the next carrying only sheathed swords.

after.note: The article says the treaty held for about two years, until the Banu Bakr, an ally of the Quraysh, attacked the Banu Khuza‘ah, an ally of Muhammad, with some help from the Quraysh according to the accounts. Muhammad offered the Quraysh three alternatives, they did not agree, and he prepared an expedition against Mecca; the article on its conquest, in December 629 or January 630, says it formally ended the conflict between his followers and the Quraysh.

entries.label: The Baqt: the treaty between Makuria and Muslim Egypt

places.name: Fustat, the seat of Muslim rule in Egypt

entries.summary: About 652 the Christian kingdom of Makuria in Nubia and the new Muslim rulers of Egypt make a treaty, called the Baqt, after an Arab army has pushed south. It lets the people of the two lands trade and travel, and it sets a yearly delivery of enslaved people from Nubia in return for foodstuffs. Known mostly from later Muslim writers, it is said to have lasted nearly seven hundred years.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Baqt
sources.note: the article says almost all that is known comes from Muslim sources and that no early copy of the treaty survives; none was opened

parties.name: Makuria, a Christian kingdom of Nubia, under a king whom the Arabic sources call Qalidurut
parties.said: No statement of theirs is recorded in the sources read. The article says the agreement is known only in its Arabic form, that almost all information about the Baqt comes from Muslim sources, and that the Makurian king appears there only as Qalidurut.

parties.name: The Muslim rulers of Egypt, whose governor Abd Allah ibn Sa’d led the expedition and negotiated the treaty
parties.said: The article says later Islamic historians state that Nubia was not worth conquering and that the expedition was meant to subordinate the region to Egypt, while earlier sources suggest the Arab armies suffered a rare defeat at the second battle of Dongola and agreed to the Baqt when they saw that conquest would be hard. The two accounts differ.

causes.note: Why the Arab army made terms is not settled in the sources read: later Islamic historians say the region was not worth conquering, earlier sources suggest a defeat, and the article on the second battle of Dongola, dated 652, gives the result as a Makurian victory followed by the Baqt.

The Nubians were to maintain a mosque for Muslim visitors and residents, and Muslims had no duty to protect Nubia from third parties. The article says the treaty caused controversy among Islamic theologians, who disagreed over whether it broke the duty to expand the dar al-Islam, and that it largely blocked the spread of Islam and the Arabs into Nubia for half a millennium.

The main provision was a yearly delivery from Nubia of 360 enslaved people, of stated quality and a mix of men and women, in exchange for cargoes of wheat and lentils; in some reports forty more were due. The article says a tribute of 400 a year was sent from the 7th century to the 14th, and that trade and travel between the two states were to be free.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the fighting before it, and the article on the second battle of Dongola gives the casualties on both sides as unknown.

outcome.note: A treaty negotiated between Abd Allah and the Makurian king. The article says no copy survives, that the earliest copies date from several centuries later and differ widely, and that it may have been an oral agreement. The terms it counts as clear: no attack by either side, free trade and safe passage, no settlement in the other’s land, and the return of fugitives and escaped enslaved people.

after.note: The article says payment was halted in the 830s, during unrest in Egypt, by King Zacharias III; the Abbasids demanded it and the arrears, and his son Georgios went to Baghdad in 835, where the arrears were cancelled and payment was changed to every three years. It describes relations as closest under the Fatimids, worse under the Ayyubids and very poor under the Mamluks, with open war, and says the Baqt ended in the mid-fourteenth century with the collapse of organised government in the region.

entries.label: The First Fitna: the first civil war of the Islamic community
entries.summary: After the killing of the third caliph, Uthman, in 656, the Muslim community divides. Ali, the fourth caliph, fights Aisha’s party at the Battle of the Camel and Mu’awiya of Syria at Siffin, and a third group, the Kharijites, breaks away from him. It ends with Ali’s assassination in 661 and the founding of the Umayyad caliphate.

parties.name: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the fourth caliph, and his supporters
parties.said: No statement of his own is quoted in the sources read. The article says he was elected caliph after Uthman’s killing, that his accession was clouded by the unresolved murder, and that he agreed to arbitration at Siffin reluctantly, under pressure from most of his troops.

parties.name: Mu’awiya, governor of Syria, and the Uthmaniyya (partisans of the slain caliph Uthman)
parties.said: As the article tells it, Mu’awiya, a kinsman of Uthman, refused to recognise Ali as caliph and declared war on the basis of his right to seek blood-revenge for his cousin.

parties.name: Aisha, Talha and Zubayr
parties.said: They argued that Ali had failed to give priority to prosecuting Uthman’s killers, and rose to demand a new elective council. They fought Ali at the Battle of the Camel in December 656.

parties.name: The Kharijites
parties.said: They seceded from Ali’s camp after the arbitration at Siffin and, the article says, declared Ali, Mu’awiya and their followers to be unbelievers. The article records Kharijite violence against civilians and the Battle of Nahrawan, where Ali’s forces crushed them.

causes.note: Who should be caliph after Uthman’s death, and whether justice for his killers came first: the article names these as the quarrel between Ali and his opponents.
The dispute was within one religious community, over its leadership; the Kharijites turned it into a religious judgement on both sides after the arbitration at Siffin.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded for the war as a whole. For one battle, Siffin in July 657, the article’s infobox gives 25,000 killed on Ali’s side and 45,000 on Mu’awiya’s, without naming who counted them.

outcome.note: Siffin ended inconclusively in an arbitration (657–658). Ali was assassinated in 661 by a Kharijite; his son Hasan then made a treaty acknowledging Mu’awiya’s rule, and Mu’awiya founded the Umayyad caliphate.

after.note: The Rashidun caliphate gave way to the Umayyad caliphate. A second civil war followed after 680 and the Battle of Karbala. The articles treat the division between Ali’s supporters and the others as a root of the later Shia and Sunni communities, a reading each community states in its own terms.

entries.label: The Battle of Karbala
entries.summary: Husayn, a grandson of Muhammad, refuses to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and travels towards Kufa after its people invite him. His small party is stopped at Karbala by the caliph’s army, and on 10 October 680 Husayn is killed with most of his companions. Its yearly remembrance, Ashura, is central to Shia observance.

parties.name: Husayn ibn Ali and his companions and family (about 72 men, the article says)
parties.said: The article gives Husayn’s reply to the vanguard that stopped him, as the classical accounts record it: he had come because the people of Kufa had written, “Come to us, for we have no Imām”; if they kept their pledges he would come, and if not he would leave. He refused the demand for allegiance to Yazid.

parties.name: The Umayyad caliph Yazid I and his governors
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Yazid demanded allegiance from Husayn and other dissidents when he succeeded his father Mu’awiya, and that the governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad would give Husayn safe passage only if he submitted to his authority.

causes.note: Mu’awiya had named his son Yazid as successor, making the caliphate hereditary; Husayn and others contested it, and Kufa, which resented Umayyad rule, invited Husayn to lead.

Modern historians read Husayn’s aim differently: Wellhausen saw an ill-prepared bid by an ambitious man; Halm a struggle for political leadership; Madelung a religious man moved by the conviction that Muhammad’s family had a right and duty to lead the community; Jafri a man who did not seek leadership for himself but meant to rouse the community’s conscience by his death.

casualties.basis: The men with Husayn who died at Karbala on 10 October 680, as the classical accounts count them; the article says about twenty were descendants of Abu Talib.
casualties.note: The article gives “seventy or seventy-two”. For the other side it gives eighty-eight dead in Ibn Sa’d’s army, buried before he left; its infobox says more than 100.

outcome.note: Husayn was killed and most of his companions with him; the women and children of his family were taken first to Kufa and then to Damascus.

after.note: The killing led to the Second Fitna, in which the people of Kufa organised two campaigns of vengeance, the Tawwabin and then Mukhtar al-Thaqafi. The article says the day, Ashura, is commemorated in Shia Islam each year; other Muslim communities remember it in their own ways.

entries.label: The Byzantine Iconoclasm: the dispute over religious images
entries.summary: In about 726 the Byzantine emperor Leo III is said to begin a ban on religious images, and for much of the next century emperors, bishops and monks quarrel, with some civil strife and persecution, over whether images of Christ and the saints may be venerated. Church councils decide opposite ways in 754 and 787, and veneration is restored for good in 843. The dispute is one of the threads in the later split between the Eastern and Western Churches.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Byzantine Iconoclasm
sources.note: it says the iconoclast case is known mostly from the writings of its opponents; none of those was opened

parties.name: The iconoclast emperors, beginning with Leo III and Constantine V, and the bishops of the Council of Hieria of 754
parties.said: The article says the Council of Hieria, with 338 bishops, declared that “the unlawful art of painting living creatures blasphemed the fundamental doctrine of our salvation, namely the Incarnation of Christ”. Leo III is said to have called image veneration “a craft of idolatry”. The article adds that the council’s claim to be an ecumenical council is now disregarded by both the Orthodox and the Catholic traditions.

parties.name: The defenders of images, among them Patriarch Germanos I, John of Damascus, Theodore the Studite, the empresses Irene and Theodora, and the Second Council of Nicaea of 787
parties.said: The article says John of Damascus declared that he did not worship matter “but rather the creator of matter”. The Second Council of Nicaea decreed in 787 that images are to receive “the veneration of honor, not indeed the true worship paid to the divine nature alone”; the other article says it held that the honor given to an image passes to its subject and is therefore not idolatrous.

parties.name: The Papacy and the Frankish court
parties.said: The article says the Papacy firmly supported the use of images throughout the period. The article on the council says the Frankish clergy rejected the Second Council of Nicaea at a synod in 794, and that Charlemagne supported the Libri Carolini, written to rebut its decrees; some scholars judge the Latin translation of the council’s acts that the Franks used to have been very poor.

causes.note: The question was whether images of Christ and the saints may be made and venerated. The article says the iconoclasts held that no lifeless image could be a true likeness and that depicting Christ would either separate or confuse his divine and human natures; the defenders held that the Incarnation allowed him to be depicted as he appeared in the flesh, and that veneration of an image differs from worship. It notes that the iconoclast case survives mostly in quotations by its opponents.

The article says a volcanic eruption in 726 and military reversals against the Muslims may have led Leo III to see image veneration as an offence that had brought God’s anger on the empire, and that Leo V’s revival of iconoclasm in 815 followed defeats by the Bulgarians. It also says the classic account that makes Leo III the first iconoclast is now in doubt, that the debate may have begun in the provinces, and that defenders argued that an emperor could not decide such a question without the Church.

The surviving sources, which are those of the defenders of images, accuse Constantine V of attacking monasteries, secularising large ones in Constantinople and having relics thrown into the sea. The article says the view that monasteries were secret bastions of support for images is controversial, and that many monks followed church and imperial policy.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure for the dead. The article records several civil wars during the strife, and, in the sources of the defenders of images, persecution of monks and the killing of Stephen the Younger in 765.

outcome.note: Veneration of images was restored twice: at Nicaea in 787, in a council called by the empress Irene, and for good in 843 by the regent Theodora, on condition that her late husband Theophilus not be condemned. The first Sunday of Great Lent is kept in the Orthodox Church and Byzantine-rite Catholic churches as the “Triumph of Orthodoxy”.

after.note: The article says the episode widened the divergence between the Byzantine and Carolingian traditions of what was still one Church, and helped to reduce Byzantine political control over parts of Italy. The other article says that many Protestants who follow Calvin reject the canons of the council of 787 as promoting idolatry, and that the Papacy did not formally confirm its decrees until 880.

entries.label: The East–West Schism between the Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Churches
entries.summary: In 1054 a legate of the pope and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other, and the break of communion between the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church is dated from then by convention, though scholars propose other dates from 1009 to 1484. Disputes over papal authority, the Filioque clause of the creed and the bread of the Eucharist lay behind it. In 1965 Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras I withdrew the mutual excommunications, without restoring communion.

sources.title: Wikipedia: East–West Schism
sources.note: a long article; only the opening and the sections on 1054, the Fourth Crusade, Lyon and 1965 were read

sources.title: Wikipedia: Catholic–Orthodox Joint Declaration of 1965
sources.note: a short article; the text of the declaration was not opened

parties.name: The Church of Rome, through the legates of Pope Leo IX led by Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida
parties.said: The article says the legation went to Constantinople in 1054 to deny Cerularius the title of “ecumenical patriarch”, to insist that he recognise the pope’s claim to be head of all the churches and to seek the emperor’s help against the Normans, and that when Cerularius refused, Humbert excommunicated him. It adds that the validity of the legates’ act is doubtful, because Pope Leo had died.

parties.name: The Church of Constantinople, under Patriarch Michael I Cerularius
parties.said: The article says Cerularius ordered the closing of all Latin churches in Constantinople in 1053, the first action that led to a formal schism, that he supported Leo of Ohrid’s attacks on Western customs such as unleavened bread, and that he excommunicated Humbert and the other legates in reply, an act that applied to the legates personally. It says each side has occasionally accused the other of heresy and of having begun the schism.

causes.note: The article names the Filioque clause of the Nicene Creed, leavened or unleavened bread in the Eucharist, the pope’s claim to universal jurisdiction, the place of the See of Constantinople among the five patriarchates, the coronation of Charlemagne as emperor in 800 and the iconoclasm dispute among the matters on which East and West differed.

The article names geopolitical tensions between the Greek East and the Latin West, among them the Norman conquest of southern Italy, which led the pope to ask the Byzantine emperor for help. It says the Church split along doctrinal, theological, linguistic, political and geographical lines.

Which event made the break is argued: the article says 1054 has become conventional but scholars have proposed 1009, 1204, 1277 and 1484, and it counts the Fourth Crusade of 1204 and later attempts at union, such as the Second Council of Lyon of 1272, as part of how the division was fixed.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the schism was a break of communion rather than a war. The article names the Fourth Crusade of 1204 and other military conflicts as deepening it, and gives no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: Communion has not been restored. The Catholic–Orthodox Joint Declaration of 7 December 1965 was read out at the Second Vatican Council in Rome and at a ceremony in Istanbul; it withdrew the exchange of excommunications between the Holy See and the Ecumenical Patriarchate, and the article says it did not end the schism.

after.note: The article on the declaration says it showed a desire for greater reconciliation between Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I, and that Metropolitan Philaret of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia challenged the Patriarch’s efforts in a 1965 epistle, claiming they would lead to heresy. The article on the schism calls the nullifying of the anathemas a gesture of goodwill and not a reunion.

entries.label: The First Crusade
entries.summary: In 1095 Pope Urban II calls at Clermont for an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem, after the Byzantine emperor asks the West for help against the Seljuk Turks. The crusading armies take Antioch in 1098 and Jerusalem in 1099 and found Latin states in the Levant. On the way, bands of crusaders attack Jewish communities in the Rhineland.

sources.title: Wikipedia: First Crusade
sources.note: it reports the chroniclers and the historians named; none was opened

sources.title: Urban II: Speech at the Council of Clermont, 1095, according to Fulcher of Chartres, in the Internet Medieval Sourcebook, Fordham University
sources.partisan: Fulcher of Chartres, a chronicler on the crusading side; the acts of the council were not preserved

parties.name: Pope Urban II and the armies of the First Crusade
parties.also: Called Franks in Arabic sources and Latins in Byzantine ones
parties.said: In Fulcher’s version of the speech at Clermont, Urban says: “your brethren who live in the east are in urgent need of your help”, that Turks and Arabs have conquered the lands of the Greek empire as far as the Mediterranean, and that those who have waged private war should now fight in a proper cause: “Let those who for a long time, have been robbers, now become knights.” The article says the aim was to return the Holy Land to Christian rule.

parties.name: The Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos
parties.said: In 1095 he sent ambassadors to the Council of Piacenza to ask for military help against the Seljuk Turks, who, the Fordham note says, had taken nearly all of Asia Minor from him.

parties.name: The Seljuk Turks and other Muslim rulers of Anatolia and the Levant, and the Fatimid caliphate of Cairo
parties.said: No statement of theirs about the war is quoted in the sources read. The article says there is little written evidence of the Islamic reaction before about 1160, that what there is suggests the crusade was barely noticed, and that the Turks and Arabs may have taken the crusaders for the latest of the Byzantines’ mercenaries.

causes.note: A call to an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Historians Jonathan Riley-Smith and Rodney Stark hold, the article says, that Muslim authorities in the Holy Land often enforced harsh rules against open expressions of the Christian faith; the article adds that Latin Christendom afterwards saw the success of the crusade as the work of divine providence.

The Byzantine emperor’s request for military help against the Seljuk Turks, who had taken most of Asia Minor, and the article’s statement that the practices of the Seljuk rulers began to threaten local Christians, pilgrimage from the West and the Byzantine Empire itself.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the article’s infobox says only “moderate or heavy” for the crusaders and “very heavy” for the Muslim side. For the killing after the capture of Jerusalem it says the crusaders’ own eyewitness accounts leave little doubt that very many were killed, and that some historians think later medieval sources exaggerate its scale.

outcome.note: The crusading armies took Antioch in 1098 and Jerusalem in 1099. The article says Muslims were killed without distinction after the capture of Jerusalem, and that Jews who had taken refuge in their synagogue died when it was burnt; some Muslims and Jews survived or were ransomed.

after.note: Most crusaders went home; only about 300 knights and 2,000 foot soldiers stayed, and Baldwin became the first Latin king of Jerusalem. The Muslim counter-attacks of the 1110s failed; lasting success came later under Zengi and Saladin, and the last crusader states fell by 1302. Earlier, the preaching of the crusade had been followed in 1095–96 by attacks on Jewish communities in France and Germany, at Speyer, Worms and Mainz among other places.

entries.label: The Great Law of Peace of the Haudenosaunee
entries.summary: According to Haudenosaunee tradition, the Peacemaker, Dekanawidah, and his spokesman Hiawatha end a cycle of war among five nations, the Mohawk, Onondaga, Oneida, Cayuga and Seneca, and bind them in a confederacy under the Great Law of Peace. The date is not known, and the sources read give different ones.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Great Law of Peace
sources.note: it gives the date as about 1102 and, a few lines later, as the late twelfth century

sources.title: “Who We Are”, the Haudenosaunee Confederacy’s own page
sources.partisan: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy’s own account of itself

parties.name: The Peacemaker, Dekanawidah, and Hiawatha (Aionwatha)
parties.said: The Confederacy’s own page says it was “founded by the prophet known as the Peacemaker with the help of Aionwatha”, and “intended as a way to unite the nations and create a peaceful means of decision making”, its nations “united by a common goal to live in harmony”. The Wikipedia article reports the tradition that the Great Law “ended the ancient cycle of enmity and continuous conflict between the separate tribes”.

parties.name: The five nations: Mohawk, Onondaga, Oneida, Cayuga and Seneca
parties.also: Called the Iroquois by the French and the League of Five Nations by the English
parties.said: The Wikipedia article says the original five nations ratified the constitution near modern Victor, New York, and that the Tuscarora joined in 1722. The Confederacy’s page says each nation keeps its own council, with chiefs chosen by the clan mothers, and leaves matters that touch all the nations to the Grand Council.

causes.note: A long cycle of enmity among the nations, which the tradition says the Law ended; the Confederacy’s page says its aim was a peaceful way of deciding together.
The Peacemaker is called a prophet on the Confederacy’s page, and the Law is told with laws and ceremonies to be performed at set times, so that peace and ceremony are joined in the tradition.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the wars it is said to have ended.

outcome.note: The Law, told in 117 articles and first recorded on wampum belts, joined the five nations in a confederacy with a Grand Council; the Tuscarora joined in 1722. The Confederacy’s page says the date of the joining of the nations is unknown and “time immemorial”.

after.note: In the nineteenth century the Law was written down in English and other languages. Of how the Haudenosaunee came to dominate the region, the article reports Lewis Morgan’s view that it was their superior organisation, and George Hunt’s that economic forces, the need for furs for the European trade and their position on the trade routes, were at work.

entries.label: The Treaty of Jaffa (1192), which ended the Third Crusade
entries.summary: In September 1192 Saladin, sultan of Egypt, and Richard the Lionheart, king of England, agree a three-year truce that ends the Third Crusade. Jerusalem stays under Muslim rule and is open to Christian pilgrims; the Christians keep a coastal strip from Tyre to Jaffa. Neither side was content with the terms.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Third Crusade, the sections on negotiations, outcome and aftermath
sources.note: it quotes Saladin’s biographer Baha al-Din; his book was not opened

parties.name: Saladin, sultan of Egypt
parties.also: The treaty is also called the Treaty of Ramla
parties.said: His biographer Baha al-Din reports his distress at the terms: “I fear to make peace, not knowing what may become of me. Our enemy will grow strong, now that they have retained these lands.” The article says Saladin had been weakened by the trials and expense of the war.

parties.name: Richard I, king of England, who led the crusade, with the Kingdom of Jerusalem
parties.said: No statement of his is quoted in the sources read. The article says Richard had too few men and too few supplies to take Jerusalem, and that each ruler had to deal with threats to his kingdom at home; it adds that neither man liked the overall accord but had little other choice. The truce was negotiated with the help of Balian of Ibelin.

causes.note: The treaty mainly addressed the status of Jerusalem and the rights of Christian pilgrims; the Third Crusade’s religious focus, the article says, was the recovery of Jerusalem, which it did not achieve.
Both leaders were worn down by the war and pressed by troubles at home, and the crusading army had split over whether to attack Jerusalem or Egypt.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the war it ended; the Third Crusade’s infobox says only that crusader losses were greater than Muslim ones and cites a Muslim estimate of more than 50,000 Frankish dead.
