outcome.note: A three-year truce, signed on 1 or 2 September 1192. Jerusalem stayed under Muslim control and was open to pilgrimage by Christians and Muslims, with safe passage through Palestine; the Christians held the coast from Tyre to Jaffa; the fortifications of Ascalon were to be demolished and the town returned to Saladin.

after.note: The article says neither side was fully satisfied: many Christians in the West were disappointed that Richard had not tried to retake Jerusalem, and many in the Islamic world that Saladin had not driven the Christians out. Trade flourished along the coast.

entries.label: The Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars
entries.summary: Pope Innocent III calls a crusade in 1209 against the Cathars of Languedoc, a Christian movement the Church condemns as heresy and whom many local nobles protect. The French crown takes the lead and the campaign becomes a war for Toulouse as well. It ends in 1229 with the Treaty of Paris, and the Inquisition follows. Few Cathar texts survive, so most of what is known comes from their opponents.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Albigensian Crusade
sources.note: it reports the chroniclers and historians named; none was opened

parties.name: Pope Innocent III, his legates, and the crusaders, with the French crown
parties.said: The article says that after Raymond VI of Toulouse was excommunicated again in 1209, Innocent called a crusade against the Albigensians in the view that a Europe free of heresy could better defend its borders against Muslims. The legates Arnaud Amalric and Milo wrote to the Pope that at Béziers the crusaders “put to the sword almost 20,000 people”; it was later alleged that Amalric said “Kill them all! God will know his own”, which the historian Joseph Strayer doubts he said.

parties.name: The Cathars of Languedoc and the nobles who protected them, among them the counts of Toulouse and Foix and the viscounts of Béziers and Carcassonne
parties.said: No Cathar text about the war is quoted in the sources read. The article on Catharism says few Cathar texts survive and that most present understanding comes from Catholic denunciations. The article on the crusade says many powerful nobles protected Cathar leaders, with an interest in independence from the French king, and that Raymond VI did not openly embrace Cathar belief but sympathised with it.

causes.note: The campaign was begun by Innocent III to eliminate Catharism in Languedoc, whose dualist beliefs, the article says, conflicted with the doctrine of the Incarnation and the Catholic sacraments; the Cathars were condemned as heretics.

The article says the Crusade was carried on mainly by the French crown and took on a political aspect: it brought the county of Toulouse under the crown and weakened the region’s distinct culture, and the nobles’ protection of the Cathars was partly a matter of independence from the king.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox says at least 200,000 Cathars were killed, without a basis; for the fall of Béziers in July 1209 the legates’ letter claims almost 20,000, which Strayer thinks too high though he holds that nearly every man, woman and child in the town was killed.

outcome.note: Ended by the Treaty of Paris in 1229: Raymond VII was recognised as ruler of Toulouse in return for fighting the Cathars, returning church property, handing over castles and destroying the defences of Toulouse, and his daughter was to marry the brother of the French king.

after.note: The Inquisition was set up under Pope Gregory IX in 1234 and worked in Toulouse, Albi and Carcassonne through the thirteenth century and much of the fourteenth to end what was left of Catharism. The article records a scholarly disagreement over whether the crusade amounts to the deliberate destruction of a people: Raphael Lemkin and Mark Pegg say it does, while Robert Lerner and Laurence Marvin dispute it.

entries.label: The Treaty of Jaffa (1229) and the return of Jerusalem
entries.summary: On 18 February 1229 the emperor Frederick II and the Ayyubid sultan al-Kāmil, who never meet, agree by envoys that ends the Sixth Crusade without a battle: Jerusalem is returned to the Christian kingdom, while the Muslim holy places on the Temple Mount stay in Muslim hands. The reaction in both the Christian and the Muslim worlds was largely hostile.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Treaty of Jaffa (1229)
sources.note: the text of the treaty is not preserved; the article reconstructs it from Christian and Muslim writers it names, none of which was opened

parties.name: Frederick II, Holy Roman emperor, who led the Sixth Crusade
parties.said: In his letter to Henry III of England, the article says, Frederick claimed that he was allowed to rebuild Jerusalem “in as good a state as it had ever been”; the Muslim sources report that he was not to rebuild its walls, and the article notes that the largest difference between the Christian and Muslim accounts is over this point.

parties.name: Al-Kāmil, Ayyubid sultan of Egypt
parties.said: He defended the treaty, the article says, with these words: “We have only conceded to them some churches and some ruined houses. The sacred precincts, the venerated Rock and all the other sanctuaries to which we make our pilgrimages remain ours as they were; Muslim rites continue to flourish as they did before.” To him, the article says, Jerusalem was both militarily insignificant and indefensible.

causes.note: The status of Jerusalem and of its holy places for both faiths was the centre of the bargain: the article says the Haram al-Sharif stayed in Muslim hands, with Christians and Muslims both allowed to pray there.
Al-Kāmil was at the same time negotiating with his brother al-Ashraf over the redistribution of Ayyubid lands in Asia; the earlier truce of 1192 had left Jerusalem under Muslim rule.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead, and the article says the Sixth Crusade ended without a major battle.

outcome.note: Jerusalem, with a corridor to the coast, went to the emperor; the Haram al-Sharif stayed under a Muslim garrison and judge, with access for pilgrims of both faiths; other Muslims, and Jews, were to leave the city. The treaty recognised Christian possession of Acre, Jaffa, Nazareth, Sidon and Toron, and set a truce of ten years, five months and forty days.

after.note: The article says the reaction in both the Christian and the Muslim worlds was largely negative; in besieged Damascus a sermon was preached in the Umayyad Mosque denouncing the treaty and praising the sanctity of Jerusalem. Jerusalem was not refortified during the ten years of the truce.

entries.label: The Hussite Wars in Bohemia
entries.summary: After the execution of the reformer Jan Hus in 1415, civil wars are fought in Bohemia from 1419 between Hussites and the Catholic forces of the Emperor Sigismund and the Papacy, who launch several crusades against them. The Hussites divide into moderate Utraquists, who held that all should receive communion in both bread and wine, and radical Taborites. The wars end in 1434 and a compromise, the Compacts, follows.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Hussite Wars
sources.note: it reports the historians it names; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Compacts of Basel
sources.note: a very short article

parties.name: The Hussites: the moderate Utraquists (Calixtines) and the radical Taborites and Orphans, under leaders such as Jan Žižka and Jan Želivský
parties.said: The article says that on 2 September 1415 the knights and nobles of Bohemia and Moravia sent the protestatio Bohemorum to the Council of Constance, condemning the execution of Hus in the strongest language. It says that shortly before his death Hus accepted communion in both kinds, which became the watchword of the Utraquists, and that the Compacts, which the moderates drew up, asked that the sacrament be given freely in both kinds to all in Bohemia and Moravia.

parties.name: The Catholic side: Sigismund, king and later Emperor, the Papacy and the monarchs loyal to Rome, with the Bohemian Catholic nobility
parties.said: The article says Sigismund, persuaded by the Council that Hus was a heretic, sent threatening letters declaring that he would shortly drown all Wycliffites and Hussites, and obtained the pope’s permission to launch a crusade against them. It counts five anti-Hussite crusades.

causes.note: From about 1402 Hus denounced what he judged the corruption of the Church and the papacy and promoted ideas of John Wycliffe that the Church had declared heretical; in 1411 he spoke against indulgences proclaimed in Bohemia. He was imprisoned, tried and executed on 6 July 1415, despite a safe-conduct from Sigismund.

The article says Sigismund, who planned to be crowned Holy Roman Emperor, which required the pope, suppressed the Hussites. It records the first Defenestration of Prague on 30 July 1419, in which a procession led by the priest Jan Želivský threw the king’s representatives from the New Town Hall, the death of King Wenceslaus IV that August, and the forcing out of the Catholic Germans from Prague and other places in Bohemia.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article gives no figure for the dead. It says that, by some estimates, the population of the Czech lands, about 2.80 to 3.37 million around 1400, was 1.50 to 1.85 million by 1526, and that the lands were left totally ravaged.

outcome.note: The article dates the end of the fighting to 30 May 1434, after the Utraquists, who changed sides in 1432, and Catholic forces defeated the Taborites at Lipany. The Compacts, accepted at Jihlava on 5 July 1436 by Sigismund, the Hussite delegates and the Catholic Church, allowed communion in both kinds in Bohemia and Moravia; the Church refused to recognise John of Rokycan as archbishop of Prague.

after.note: The article says the Utraquist creed stayed the established church of Bohemia until all non-Catholic services were banned shortly after the Battle of White Mountain in 1620, that the Moravian Brethren carried on some Taborite traditions, that Pope Paul II excommunicated the Hussite king George of Poděbrady in 1466, and that the religious peace of Kutná Hora of 1485 is counted as the definitive end of the wars.

entries.label: The Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire and the Requerimiento
entries.summary: Between 1519 and 1521 Hernán Cortés and a small Spanish force, with large armies of Native allies led by Tlaxcala, overthrow the Aztec Empire and take Tenochtitlan. Spain had justified its claims in the Americas in a declaration, the Requerimiento, that spoke of a God-given right to rule. Whether the Aztec ruler took the Spaniards for gods is disputed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire
sources.note: it reports Hugh Thomas and the ethnohistorians named; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish Requirement of 1513
sources.note: the text of the Requerimiento was not opened

parties.name: Hernán Cortés and the Spanish, with their Native allies from Tlaxcala, Tetzcoco, Totonacapan and elsewhere
parties.said: The Requerimiento, the article says, declared Castile’s divinely ordained right to take possession of the New World; read to Native peoples, it demanded that they accept Spanish rule and allow Catholic preaching on pain of war, slavery or death, and said that any deaths that followed rejection were their own fault. The article notes it did not demand conversion, and that Cortés in his own letters never claimed that he was taken for a god.

parties.name: The Aztec Triple Alliance under Moctezuma II: Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan
parties.said: No statement of Moctezuma’s own is quoted in the sources read. The article reports Hugh Thomas’s account that Moctezuma debated whether Cortés was a god or the envoy of a great king, since 1519 was the year the god Quetzalcoatl was promised to return; other ethnohistorians hold that the Aztec leaders did not see the Spaniards as supernatural, and the article notes that the idea appears only in European writings of the 1540s.

causes.note: Spain’s stated ground was that its Christian faith gave it the right, and the duty, to take possession of the lands and peoples of the New World in the name of God and the Crown, and that Catholic doctrine put the salvation of souls before civil concerns; the second article says the conversion of Native peoples was the rationale that legitimised the conquests.

The article says the Aztecs ruled through local rulers on the perception of unbeatable military strength, a system open to loss of prestige under challenge, and that the Spanish won with allied armies of Native peoples as well as with their weapons.
The second article says the Requerimiento was not generally questioned until the Crown abolished its use in 1556 because of its potential to enrich the royal treasury.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives 200,000 Aztecs dead, including civilians, 1,800 Spaniards dead and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan and other Native allies, without saying who counted them; epidemics are treated separately.

outcome.note: Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521 to the Spanish and their Native allies, and the Aztec Empire came to an end.

after.note: The second article says critics such as Bartolomé de las Casas were appalled at the Requerimiento, and that the Crown abolished it in 1556; it was sometimes read to empty villages or to people who could not understand it.

entries.label: The German Peasants’ War
entries.summary: In 1524 and 1525 peasants and townspeople across southern and central Germany rise against landlords and church dues. Their Twelve Articles ask that congregations choose their own pastors, as well as an end to serfdom. Armies of the princes and the Swabian League crush the risings, and many thousands die. Historians disagree about how far religion or economic hardship drove it.

sources.title: Wikipedia: German Peasants’ War
sources.note: it reports Roland Bainton, Luther and the other writers named; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Twelve Articles
sources.note: the text of the Articles was not opened

parties.name: The peasant armies, including the Christian Association of Upper Swabia, with preachers such as Thomas Müntzer
parties.said: The Twelve Articles, adopted at Memmingen in March 1525 and printed some 25,000 times in two months, demanded, the article says, that communities be able to choose and dismiss their clergy, that the great tithe be used for public purposes after a reasonable salary for the pastor, that the small tithe and serfdom be abolished, that forests and pastures taken from the villages be restored, and that arbitrary justice end.

parties.name: The princes, nobles and the Swabian League, with Hesse, Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel and Saxony
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the aristocracy’s opposition was intense, that the Swabian League’s army and the princes’ forces defeated the peasant bands, and that survivors were fined and executed.

parties.name: Martin Luther, who opposed the rising
parties.said: In his pamphlet Against the Murderous, Thieving Hordes of Peasants Luther wrote, the article says, that “nothing can be more poisonous, hurtful, or devilish than a rebel”. The other article notes that Luther also commented on the Twelve Articles.

causes.note: The article says Luther’s Reformation may have added intensity to the movements but did not create them, and that his teaching of the priesthood of all believers could be read as promising more equality than he meant; the historian Roland Bainton saw a revolt that began in the language of the Reformation and was driven far beyond it by economic tensions.
The article names rising rents, tightening serfdom and the loss of access to common land as causes.

A demand for an end to arbitrary justice and administration and for rights of communities; the other article says the Twelve Articles are considered a first draft of human rights and civil liberties in continental Europe.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article says the aristocracy killed up to 100,000 of about 300,000 poorly armed peasants, and its infobox says more than 100,000 killed on the peasants’ side and minimal losses on the other.

outcome.note: The risings were put down by the forces of the princes and the Swabian League during 1525, with a decisive battle at Frankenhausen on 15 May; the survivors were fined and some executed, and few of the peasants’ aims were achieved.

after.note: The article lists a major influence on the Anabaptist movement among the results, and says the revolt was Europe’s largest and most widespread popular rising before the French Revolution of 1789.

entries.label: The Ethiopian–Adal War
entries.summary: A war between the Christian Ethiopian Empire and the Muslim Adal Sultanate, led by Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, that overran much of the Ethiopian highlands and ended when Portuguese musketeers helped the Ethiopians defeat and kill the Imam in 1543. The main Arabic chronicle does not say why he went to war, and historians offer several reasons.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ethiopian–Adal War
sources.note: it reports the Futūḥ al-Ḥabaša, the Arabic chronicle, and the historians named; none was opened

parties.name: The Adal Sultanate under Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi
parties.said: The Futūḥ al-Ḥabaša, the Arabic chronicle written on his side, calls him “Imam of the End of Time”, but, the article says, does not explain his reasons for invading. The two main Arabic accounts report prophecies that a righteous leader would rise from his homeland to conquer Ethiopia.

parties.name: The Ethiopian Empire (Emperor Lebna Dengel, then Galawdewos), with about 400 Portuguese musketeers
parties.said: No statement of theirs about the cause of the war is quoted in the sources read. After the war, the article says, Galawdewos refused Portuguese hopes that he would accept Catholicism and wrote his own Confession of Faith defending Ethiopian religious practice against the friars’ arguments.

causes.note: Asa J. Davis argues that Ahmad’s turn to conquest reflected Muslim resentment at paying tribute (jizyah) to a non-Muslim state; B. G. Martin sets the war in a wider pattern of sixteenth-century mahdist and messianic movements, while warning against any single cause.
J. Spencer Trimingham holds that the war began once Ahmad had consolidated power and “refused tribute”, which made war “inevitable”.

Berhanou Abebe points to demographic, climatic and economic pressures and to the highlands’ wealth in slaves, ivory and gold; Chekroun and Hirsch caution that no contemporary source documents a drought or a population crisis.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure for the dead. The article says the war was devastating for the Harari, whose population fell, and weakened both sides.

outcome.note: With Portuguese help the Ethiopian forces defeated Ahmad, who was killed in February 1543. His army split, and in October 1544 Galawdewos defeated and killed the vizier Abbas, who had tried to hold the border provinces.

after.note: The article says relations between the Emperor and the Portuguese soured and the Portuguese were sent to the provinces, that the war weakened both states and opened a way for the Oromo to move into lands north of the Blue Nile and towards Harar, and that the province of Fatagar was permanently lost. Ahmad’s war, the other article says, drew in a wider struggle between the Portuguese and Ottoman empires.

entries.label: The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
entries.summary: In 1532 Francisco Pizarro and 168 Spanish soldiers, with Indigenous allies, capture the Inca ruler Atahualpa at Cajamarca after a reading of the Requerimiento, a Spanish demand that Native peoples accept the Church and the Crown. A campaign of some forty years follows, ending in 1572 with the Viceroyalty of Peru. Disease, an Inca civil war and Native allies of the Spanish are all named among the causes of the empire’s fall.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire
sources.note: it reports the speeches at Cajamarca; the Spanish chroniclers behind them were not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Spanish Requirement of 1513
sources.note: the opening only was read here

parties.name: Spain, under Francisco Pizarro and later the Viceroyalty of Peru, with Indigenous allies such as the Cañari, Chachapoya, Huanca and Chanka
parties.said: The article quotes the speech read to Atahualpa at Cajamarca for the Spaniards: that they came as servants of God to teach the truth about God’s word and to “lay the foundation of concord, brotherhood, and perpetual peace”. The Requerimiento article says such a declaration was read to Native peoples to inform them of Spain’s right to conquest, and that those who resisted were regarded as defying God’s plan.

parties.name: The Inca state, under Atahualpa and then Manco Inca, and the Neo-Inca State at Vilcabamba
parties.said: The article quotes Atahualpa’s answer at Cajamarca: “I will be no man’s tributary.” It says he had heard from scouts that the Spanish had been killing and enslaving people on the coast, and that his advisers had debated whether the newcomers were gods or men.

causes.note: Friar Vicente de Valverde, with an interpreter, set out the doctrines of the faith and offered a Bible as authority before the battle of 16 November 1532; the article says the interpreter was unskilled, which probably added to the misunderstanding. At Atahualpa’s later trial the charges included idolatry, polygamy and incestuous marriage, and the article says many were forcibly converted afterwards.

An Inca civil war between the princes Huáscar and Atahualpa, after the sudden death of Huayna Capac and his heir in 1528, was under way when the Spanish arrived. The article says Native groups such as the Huanca, Cañari, Chanka and Chachapoya fought with the Spanish against Inca rule, and that the Spanish offered safety to those who accepted vassalage.

The article judges that the Spanish motives for the attack seemed to be loot and impatience, though it says accounts of the circumstances vary. It records Spanish plunder and enslavement of local peoples afterwards and the use of the Inca forced-labour system, the mita, for the silver mines of Potosí.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives 70,000 dead on the Inca side after the first conquest and the outbreak of disease. It says about 2,000 Incas were killed at Cajamarca with one Spanish soldier wounded, and that the population of the Inca realm is roughly estimated to have fallen from 10 to 15 million in 1520 to under 3 million in 1570, with disease named as the greatest single cause.

outcome.note: Atahualpa was put to death by garrotting on 29 August 1533. After rebellions and the retreat of Manco Inca to Vilcabamba, the Neo-Inca State was ended and the Inca Túpac Amaru was killed in 1572, which the article gives as the end of the conquest.

after.note: The Spanish created the Viceroyalty of New Castile in 1542, soon called the Viceroyalty of Peru; under Viceroy Francisco de Toledo Indigenous people were resettled in Spanish-style towns called reductions. The article says Spanish missionary work could then continue unimpeded, and that some historians hold that it took a generation for the continent to come under Christian influence.

entries.label: The Peace of Amasya between the Ottoman Empire and Safavid Iran
entries.summary: On 29 May 1555 the Ottoman sultan Suleiman and the Safavid shah Tahmasp I make peace at Amasya after a war that began in 1532, and fix the border between their empires. The treaty guaranteed Persian pilgrims access to Mecca, Medina and the Shia holy sites in Ottoman Iraq, and required the Safavids to end the ritual cursing of the first three caliphs and other companions of Muhammad, whom Sunnis hold in high esteem.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Peace of Amasya
sources.note: a short article; the text of the treaty was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ottoman–Safavid War (1532–1555)
sources.note: a short article

parties.name: The Ottoman Empire under Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the war says it was triggered by territorial disputes and by the assassination of the governor of Baghdad, a sympathiser of Suleiman, which it says Tahmasp ordered, and the article on the treaty says the Ottomans guaranteed Persian pilgrims access to Mecca and Medina and to the Shia holy sites in Ottoman Iraq.

parties.name: The Safavid Empire under Shah Tahmasp I
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Safavids were required to end the ritual cursing of the first three Rashidun caliphs, Aisha and other companions of Muhammad, a condition it calls common in Ottoman–Safavid treaties and, here, considered humiliating for Tahmasp. The article on the war says the Safavids had also been in talks with the Habsburgs about an alliance against the Ottomans.

causes.note: The treaty’s religious terms: the Safavids to end the ritual cursing of the figures Sunnis hold in high esteem, and Persian pilgrims guaranteed access to Mecca and Medina and to the Shia holy places in Ottoman Iraq.

The treaty fixed the border: Armenia and Georgia were divided equally between the two empires, the Ottomans obtained most of Iraq including Baghdad, and the Persians kept Tabriz and their other north-western territories in the Caucasus. Buffer zones were set up in eastern Anatolia and Kars was declared neutral, its fortress destroyed.
The article says the Ottoman gain of Baghdad gave them access to the Persian Gulf.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article on the war gives, in its infobox, heavy losses on the Safavid side and 30,000 in 1533 to 1536 and 20,000 in 1548 to 1549 on the Ottoman side, without saying who counted them.

outcome.note: The treaty was agreed on 29 May 1555 at Amasya, with both sides exhausted by the war. Suleiman returned Tabriz but kept Baghdad, lower Mesopotamia, western Armenia, western Georgia, the mouths of the Euphrates and Tigris and part of the Persian Gulf coast.

after.note: The article says the treaty was followed by twenty years of peace, and that the decisive parting of the Caucasus and the irrevocable ceding of Mesopotamia to the Ottomans came with the Treaty of Zuhab of 1639.

entries.label: The Peace of Augsburg
entries.summary: In 1555 the Imperial Diet at Augsburg ended the first wave of fighting between Lutheran and Catholic estates of the Holy Roman Empire. Each ruler could choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his territory; subjects who disagreed could emigrate; other confessions, Calvinism among them, were left outside the settlement.

sources.title: Peter H. Wilson, Europe’s Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (2009), as the author summarises it in Rorotoko, 23 April 2010 (“The wide angle”)
sources.note: the author’s own short account; the book itself was not opened

related.note: Historians differ on how far the limits of the Augsburg settlement, which left Calvinists outside it, led to the war; Wilson counts 63 years of internal peace in the Empire after it.

parties.name: The Catholic estates of the Holy Roman Empire, and the emperor Charles V, whose brother Ferdinand negotiated for him
parties.said: The article says Charles V had been unwilling to accept the religious division of Western Christendom as permanent, and had sought to settle it through a general council of the Catholic Church; at Passau in 1552 even the Catholic princes had called for a lasting peace, fearing the controversy would never be settled.

parties.name: The Lutheran estates of the Empire (the Schmalkaldic League and its heirs)
parties.said: The article records that the Peace of Passau of 1552, won after a victory by Protestant armies, had given Lutherans religious freedom until the next Diet, and that the Lutheran estates now sought a lasting legal footing for it. The Peace itself, in Article 24 as the article quotes it, lets subjects who wish to leave sell their estates and go, “hindered neither in the sale of their estates … nor injured in their honor”.

causes.note: The legal standing of Lutheranism beside the Catholic Church in the Empire, after the Augsburg Interim of 1548 and the Protestant revolt of 1552.
The authority of the emperor against the princes’ rights to decide the religion of their own territories.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: it ended the first wave of fighting between Protestants and Catholics in the Empire (the Schmalkaldic War of 1546–47 and the revolt of 1552), for which the sources read give no figure.

outcome.note: Signed on 25 September 1555. Princes could choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for their territories (the phrase later used for this, cuius regio, eius religio, is not in the Peace itself, Wilson notes, but comes from a later commentary); subjects who did not conform could emigrate; church rulers who converted had to resign; and, by Article 17 as the article quotes it, all “who do not belong to the two above named religions shall not be included”.

after.note: Wilson counts 63 years of internal peace in the Empire between 1555 and 1618. The article says the settlement was tested in the Cologne War of 1583–88 and left Calvinists and Anabaptists without legal recognition until 1648, and lists its failure to hold among the reasons the Thirty Years’ War followed.

entries.label: The French Wars of Religion
entries.summary: A series of civil wars between French Catholics and Protestants (Huguenots) from 1562 to 1598, bound up with a struggle for power around the crown. Foreign states backed each side. The article estimates that two to four million people died from violence, famine or disease. The wars ended with the Edict of Nantes.

sources.title: “Nantes, Edict of”, in Encyclopedia of Modern Europe (Gale), via encyclopedia.com

parties.name: The Huguenots (French Calvinist Protestants) and their noble leaders, among them the Prince of Condé, Admiral Coligny and Henry of Navarre
parties.also: Called Protestants, the Reformed, or in royal documents “the R.P.R.”
parties.said: No statement of their own is quoted in the sources read. The article records that they won a limited toleration in the Edict of Saint-Germain of January 1562, lost the freedom to worship in the Edict of Saint-Maur of 1568, and that after an attack on Coligny in August 1572 their nobles demanded justice from the king.

parties.name: The Catholic faction: the Guise family and the Catholic League, with Spain and Savoy
parties.said: No statement of their own is quoted in the sources read. The article records that Catholic confraternities and leagues formed in 1568 in reaction to a peace that gave Huguenots toleration, and that on 12 May 1588 Parisians raised barricades to defend the Duke of Guise “against the alleged hostility of the king”.

parties.name: The Crown: Catherine de’ Medici and her sons Francis II, Charles IX and Henry III, then Henry IV
parties.said: The article says moderates, the Politiques, hoped to keep order by centralising power and making concessions to the Huguenots. When Henry IV settled the matter in 1598, the edict he issued stated as its aim the eventual peaceful reunion of his subjects in one faith and, meanwhile, the coexistence of the two (encyclopedia.com).

causes.note: Tension between Catholics and the growing Calvinist church, which the article dates from the 1530s, over worship, church property and the crown’s policy of repression or toleration.
A prolonged struggle for power after the death of Henry II in 1559 among Catherine de’ Medici and noble houses, in which each side drew help from outside the kingdom.
The article describes religious division as exacerbating existing regional divisions and the nobles’ quests for power; how to weigh them is not settled in the sources read.

casualties.unit: deaths from violence, famine or disease caused by the wars
casualties.basis: The whole period 1562–1598, in France; the article counts deaths from famine and disease that the conflict directly caused.
casualties.note: The article gives the range without naming who proposed each end. It reports separately that Catholic mobs killed between 5,000 and 30,000 Protestants across France after St Bartholomew’s Day, 24 August 1572, and that street fighting at Toulouse in 1562 killed over 3,000, mostly Huguenots.

outcome.note: Ended by the Edict of Nantes in April 1598, issued by Henry of Navarre as Henry IV of France after he converted to Catholicism in 1593.

after.note: Huguenot revolts followed in the 1620s and ended with the Peace of La Rochelle of 1629, which withdrew the Edict’s military clauses. The Edict was revoked in 1685; a Protestant rising in the Cévennes lasted from 1702 to 1710; some civil rights were restored in 1787.

entries.label: The Edict of Torda in Transylvania
entries.summary: On 28 January 1568 the Diet of the Three Nations of Transylvania, meeting at Torda at the request of the Antitrinitarian preacher Ferenc Dávid, confirms earlier edicts and decrees that preachers may preach the Gospel each according to his understanding and that no one may be reviled for his religion. It did not give individuals a right to religious freedom and did not cover Orthodox Romanians, Jews or Muslims, but the article calls it an unprecedented act of religious tolerance.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Edict of Torda
sources.note: it quotes the edict; the original was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ferenc Dávid
sources.note: the opening only was read

related.note: How far the Edict of Torda shaped the Warsaw Confederation of 1573 is argued; the article on the edict says it influenced Polish–Lithuanian legislation.

parties.name: The Diet of the Three Nations of Transylvania, the Hungarian nobles, the Saxons and the Székelys, under King John Sigismund Zápolya
parties.said: The article quotes the edict as providing that preachers shall preach and explain the Gospel each according to his understanding, that if the congregation like it, well, and if not no one shall compel them, and that “no one shall be reviled for his religion by anyone”, since faith is the gift of God. It says the delegates confirmed on 28 January the toleration edicts of 1557 and 1563.

parties.name: Ferenc Dávid, the Antitrinitarian court preacher, and Giorgio Biandrata, the court physician
parties.said: The article says Dávid defended religious freedom by quoting Gamaliel’s advice to the judges of the Sanhedrin about the imprisoned Apostles: if their work is of human origin it will fail, but if it is of God the judges will not be able to stop it. It says he and Biandrata convinced the king of their Antitrinitarian theology by the end of 1567.

parties.name: The Eastern Orthodox Romanians, the Jews and the Muslims of the principality
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the edict did not cover them, that the Orthodox Church was recognised in practice without being counted a received religion, and that later princes exempted Orthodox priests from feudal obligations and gave special privileges to Jews.

causes.note: The edict allowed both Trinitarian and Antitrinitarian teaching to be preached freely and forbade mistreatment on religious grounds. The article says John Sigismund had gone from Catholicism to Lutheranism in 1562 and to Calvinism in 1564 before accepting Antitrinitarian theology.

After the Ottomans occupied the central regions of the Hungarian kingdom in 1541, John Sigismund ruled the lands to the east under his mother’s regency, and the Diets acknowledged the right of the Three Nations to regulate their own affairs. The Saxons treated religion as an internal matter and introduced the Lutheran Reformation in 1544 and 1545.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article gives no figure for the dead. It records that Hungarian Hussites were expelled in the 1430s and that the Diet of 1523 ordered the persecution of Lutherans, a decree largely ignored after 1526.

outcome.note: The edict was adopted at Torda on 28 January 1568. The article says it did not recognise an individual’s right to religious freedom but a local community’s right to choose its pastors, and that it did not cover the Orthodox Romanians, the Jews and the Muslims. It calls it the first law to sanction an Antitrinitarian community in a European state.

after.note: John Sigismund died in 1571. His Catholic successor, Stephen Báthory, urged the Saxon preachers to condemn Calvinist and Antitrinitarian teaching, and the article says they did not obey; Dávid, who went on to reject infant baptism and the adoration of Christ, was imprisoned in 1579 and died that year. The article says the coexistence of four received denominations was not questioned afterwards.

entries.label: The Eighty Years’ War (the Dutch Revolt)

places.name: Münster, where the peace was made

entries.summary: From about 1568 to 1648 rebels in the Habsburg Netherlands fight the Spanish government of Philip II and his successors. The causes include the Reformation, centralisation, taxation and the privileges of the nobility and towns. The northern provinces form the Calvinist-dominated Dutch Republic, and the war ends with Spain’s recognition of its independence in the Peace of Münster in 1648.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Eighty Years’ War
sources.note: a short article; its start is given as 1566 or 1568

parties.name: The rebels of the Netherlands: nobles, towns and provinces, under William the Silent, the Union of Utrecht and then the Dutch Republic
parties.said: The article says that under William the Silent the Catholic and Protestant-dominated provinces sought to establish religious peace through the Pacification of Ghent, but the general rebellion failed to sustain itself. The Union of Utrecht kept up the resistance, proclaimed independence in the Act of Abjuration of 1581 and set up the Calvinist-dominated Dutch Republic in 1588.

parties.name: The Spanish government of the Habsburg Netherlands, under Philip II and his successors, with the Duke of Parma as governor
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Philip II sent his armies and regained control of most rebel-held territory, that widespread mutinies in the Spanish army then caused a general uprising, and that in the Twelve Years’ Truce of 1609 the Spanish granted the United Provinces de facto independence.

causes.note: The article names the Reformation among the causes. The Pacification of Ghent of 1576 aimed at religious peace between the provinces, and the Union of Utrecht allowed complete personal freedom of religion, while letting provinces that wanted to stay Roman Catholic join it.

Centralisation by the Habsburg crown and the rights and privileges of the Dutch nobility and cities, both named in the article as causes. The Union of Utrecht answered the Union of Arras of 1579, in which two southern provinces and a city declared for Catholic Spain.
The article lists excessive taxation among the causes, and says the Dutch colonial empire began with Dutch attacks on Portugal’s overseas territories during the war.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the article read gives no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: After a stalemate and the Twelve Years’ Truce of 1609 to 1621, the war resumed as part of the Thirty Years’ War and ended with the Peace of Münster, whose text of 79 articles was fixed on 30 January 1648 and affirmed on oath on 15 May. Spain kept the Southern Netherlands and recognised the Dutch Republic as independent.

after.note: The article says the Republic also gained formal independence from the Holy Roman Empire in the broader settlements of 1648, which it calls a formalisation of a situation long in existence; France and Spain did not make peace and stayed at war until 1659.

entries.label: The Warsaw Confederation: religious tolerance in Poland–Lithuania
entries.summary: In January 1573, in the first interregnum of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, an assembly of nobles signs the Warsaw Confederation, in which representatives of all the major religions pledge mutual support and tolerance. It guarantees dissenters political equality with Catholics and is regarded as one of the first European acts to grant freedom of religion. The sources say it did not come out of a war and had no means of enforcement.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Warsaw Confederation
sources.note: it quotes the historians it names; the text of the confederation was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Union of Brest
sources.note: read for what came after

parties.name: The Convocation Sejm: about 200 nobles of Poland and Lithuania, Protestant, Orthodox and Catholic, with Mikołaj Sienicki, Jan Firlej and Jan Zborowski most involved in the drafting
parties.said: The article says that on 28 January 1573 representatives of all the major religions pledged mutual support and tolerance, and that the act was not imposed by a government or after a war but came from members of Polish–Lithuanian society. It says the killings in France on St Bartholomew’s Day in 1572 influenced it, leading the nobility to ensure that no monarch could carry out such an act in Poland.

parties.name: Many Catholic bishops, with the primate Jakub Uchański as interrex
parties.said: The article says many dignitaries of the Catholic Church opposed the articles, and that the one bishop who signed, Franciszek Krasiński, was said by a chronicler to have done so under “threat of the sword”. Later acts were signed by bishops “except the article of the confederation”, and Bishop Wawrzyniec Goślicki was excommunicated by the Holy See for agreeing to them in 1587. Cardinal Hosius called the kingdom “a place of shelter for heretics”.

parties.name: The Holy See under Pope Gregory XIII, and Henry of Valois, the king elected under the confederation
parties.said: No statement of theirs about the confederation is quoted in the sources read. The article says Rome followed the royal election closely, that the Pope ordered public prayers and sent Cardinal Commendone, who was told to back the Habsburg candidate, and that Henry of Valois was elected on 11 May 1573 with the Protestants’ agreement, his pacta conventa including the confederation’s provisions at the dissenters’ request.

causes.note: The confederation guaranteed religious tolerance, civil rights and political equality to the dissenters who did not follow the dominant Catholic state religion, in a state of Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox, Armenian, Jewish and Muslim communities. The article says it legalised customs of tolerance older than itself, such as the privileges Casimir III gave to Armenians and the Orthodox in the fourteenth century.

The Sejm met in the first interregnum, 1572 to 1574, to keep the union of Poland and Lithuania and its legal order and to prepare the election of a king; the article says the confederation helped a new political system, the nobles’ democracy, to arise.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the sources read give no figure for the dead of the religious conflicts it was meant to prevent. The article records later violence, among it a Calvinist church in Kraków wrecked by a crowd in October 1574 and anti-Jewish outbreaks in several cities in the 1590s.

outcome.note: The confederation was concluded in Warsaw by the Convocation Sejm and promulgated in Kraków on 28 January 1573, and the pacta conventa that the new king had to swear to included its provisions. The article says its text was added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World Programme in 2003.

after.note: The article says the confederation had no means of enforcement and could not override Polish customary law, which needed the consent of both lay and Church estates, and the Catholic bishops had not given theirs; its provisions bound only the nobility, and with the Counter-Reformation non-Catholic groups were gradually restricted again. After the Union of Brest of 1596 the Crown outlawed the Orthodox Church, and the other article says the Church of Rus’ split into Greek Catholic and Orthodox jurisdictions. Historians are said to differ on whether the freedom was meant for the nobility alone or for all classes.

entries.label: Akbar’s policy of universal peace (sulh-i-kul) and the House of Worship
entries.summary: The Mughal emperor Akbar, who had ended the tax on non-Muslims in 1568, opens a House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 where scholars of many faiths debate, and rules on the principle of sulh-i-kul, “universal peace”. The debates grew bitter, and in 1582 he proclaims a syncretic teaching, the Dīn-i Ilāhī, which many Muslim scholars condemn.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Akbar, the sections on religious policy and relations with Hindus and Jains

parties.name: The emperor Akbar and his court, including his minister Abu’l-Fazl
parties.said: According to Abu’l-Fazl, the article says, the emperor was a universal agent of God, so that his rule was not bound to any one faith, and he was forbidden to discriminate between religions. In a letter to Philip II of Spain Akbar wrote that most people “follow the religion in which [they] were born and educated, thus excluding [themselves] from the possibility of ascertaining the truth, which is the noblest aim of the human intellect.”

parties.name: Muslim scholars and clerics who objected, such as the qadi of Bengal and Shaykh Ahmad Sirhindi
parties.said: The article says many Muslim scholars of the period declared the new teaching blasphemy and called Akbar an apostate, and that the debates at the House of Worship grew more acrimonious and led to greater bitterness among the faiths instead of the understanding they were meant to bring.

causes.note: An empire of many faiths: the article lists Sunni, Shia, Ismaili and Sufi Muslims, Parsis, Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Jews, Jesuits and Materialists among those Akbar invited to debate; he concluded from the discussions that no single religion could claim a monopoly of truth.

Abu’l-Fazl saw the policy as a rational choice to keep harmony in the empire. M. Athar Ali, the article says, holds that sulh-i-kul was a part of general imperial administration and not only a religious aim, and some scholars hold that the view of the Dīn-i Ilāhī as a new religion arose from mistaken translations of Abu’l-Fazl.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: it is a policy of rule, and the sources read name no one killed in connection with it.

outcome.note: Akbar had repealed the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, in 1568; he built the House of Worship in 1575, appointed officials by merit whatever their religion, and from 1584 banned the killing of animals on Jain holy days and lifted the tax at Jain pilgrimage places. In 1582 he and some loyal officials took up the Dīn-i Ilāhī.

after.note: The article says the Dīn-i Ilāhī gained no more than 19 identified followers, was made defunct by Akbar’s son Jahangir, and was abolished by his great-grandson Aurangzeb, who reimposed Islamic law.

entries.label: The Union of Utrecht and religious freedom in the Dutch provinces
entries.summary: On 23 January 1579 several Dutch provinces and cities sign the Union of Utrecht, an alliance against Philip II of Spain that also settles defence, taxation and religion. It allowed complete personal freedom of religion and has been called one of the first unlimited edicts of religious toleration. Provinces and cities that wished to remain Roman Catholic were free to join.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Union of Utrecht
sources.note: the text of the treaty was not opened

parties.name: The provinces and cities that signed: Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht and the province of Groningen, with others joining in 1579 and 1580
parties.said: The article says they made a joint commitment against King Philip II of Spain, hoping to force him to stop his harsh administrative measures, and that the treaty regulated defence, taxation and religion, with complete personal freedom of religion allowed. It says the treaty was seen as a precursor of a later constitution.

parties.name: The southern provinces and cities of the Union of Arras, which declared for Roman Catholic Spain
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Union of Utrecht was a reaction of the Protestant provinces to the Union of Arras of the same year, in which two southern provinces and a city declared their support for Catholic Spain.

parties.name: King Philip II of Spain
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the United Provinces still recognised Spanish rule after the Union of Utrecht, that in 1581 they declared independence in the Act of Abjuration, and that the Spanish accepted their de facto independence only in the Twelve Years’ Truce of 1609.

causes.note: The treaty allowed complete personal freedom of religion, which the article calls one of the first unlimited edicts of religious toleration, and an additional declaration allowed provinces and cities that wished to remain Roman Catholic to join the union.

An alliance of provinces and cities for common defence against the king, completing the General Union of 1576 made by the Pacification of Ghent; the article on the war says that Pacification was an attempt by Catholic and Protestant provinces to establish religious peace while opposing the king together, and that it failed to sustain itself.
Taxation was among the matters the treaty regulated; the article on the war lists excessive taxation among the causes of the Dutch Revolt.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the war it belongs to is given in the entry for the Eighty Years’ War, and the sources read give no figure for its dead.

outcome.note: The treaty was signed on 23 January 1579 by Holland, Zeeland, Utrecht (but not all of it) and the province, not the city, of Groningen; other cities and provinces signed in the following months, and Antwerp was the capital of the union until its fall to the Spanish.

after.note: The article regards the union as the foundation of the Republic of the Seven United Provinces. The article on the war says the union kept up its resistance, proclaimed independence in 1581 and set up the Calvinist-dominated Dutch Republic in 1588.

entries.label: The Edict of Nantes (1598) and its revocation (1685)
entries.summary: In April 1598 Henry IV of France granted his Protestant subjects freedom of conscience and the right to worship in specified places, while keeping Catholicism as the established religion; it ended the French Wars of Religion. In October 1685 Louis XIV revoked it, made Protestantism illegal and ordered its ministers out of the kingdom.

sources.title: “Nantes, Edict of”, in Encyclopedia of Modern Europe (Gale), via encyclopedia.com
Revocation of the Edict of Nantes, 22 October 1685, in the Internet Modern History Sourcebook, Fordham University
sources.note: the king’s own words giving his reasons

parties.name: King Henry IV of France (1598)
parties.said: In the revocation of 1685 his grandson describes his aim as wanting “the peace which he had procured for his subjects” not to be troubled over religion. The encyclopedia entry says the edict’s stated goal was the eventual peaceful reunion of the king’s subjects in one faith, with coexistence of the two confessions meanwhile. The Wikipedia article adds that Pope Clement VIII, on hearing of it, protested “This crucifies me”.

parties.name: The Huguenots (French Calvinist Protestants)
parties.said: No statement of their own is quoted in the sources read. The encyclopedia entry says that after Henry’s conversion in 1593 they worried their precarious freedom to worship might be taken away; the Wikipedia article says they had been fighting for their rights for decades.

parties.name: King Louis XIV of France (1685)
parties.said: The revocation says that “the better and the greater part of our subjects” of the Reformed religion had embraced the Catholic faith, which made the Edict’s execution “nugatory”, and that he had “determined that we can do nothing better, in order wholly to obliterate the memory of the troubles” than to revoke it. It calls the Reformed religion “this false religion”.

causes.note: Whether French Protestants could worship, and where, in a kingdom whose established religion was Catholic; in 1685 the king’s own stated reason was that most had become Catholic.

The wish of both kings to secure the crown’s authority and civil peace: the encyclopedia entry reads the Edict as testimony to the growth of royal authority more than to a willingness to accept religious difference permanently.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the wars it ended are given in the entry for the French Wars of Religion.

outcome.note: Four texts made up the Edict of 1598: 92 general articles, 56 particular articles and two royal writs (brevets) with the military and pastoral clauses. Protestants gained freedom of conscience and public worship in specified places; Catholicism remained the established religion. The revocation of 1685 ordered ministers who would not convert to leave within a fortnight, and forbade private worship.

after.note: The Wikipedia article says as many as 400,000 people fled France after the revocation, most to Britain, Prussia, the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, South Africa and North America, and that rights for non-Catholics were not restored until the Edict of Versailles of 1787.

entries.label: The Thirty Years’ War
entries.summary: A revolt in Bohemia in 1618 grows into a war that draws in most of Europe’s states and is fought mostly across the German lands. It ends with the Peace of Westphalia. Armies, hunger and disease caused heavy losses of life, and some regions lost a large part of their people. Historians disagree about how far religion, rather than power, drove it.

sources.title: Peter H. Wilson, Europe’s Tragedy: A History of the Thirty Years War (2009), as the author summarises it in Rorotoko, 23 April 2010 (“In a nutshell”, “The wide angle”)
sources.note: the author’s own short account; the book itself was not opened

sources.title: The Treaty of Westphalia (Treaty of Münster, 1648), an English translation of the time, Avalon Project, Yale Law School
sources.note: the treaty between the Emperor and France; it confirms the religion agreement made with Sweden

parties.name: The Habsburg emperors (Ferdinand II, then Ferdinand III), the Catholic League and the Spanish Habsburgs
parties.said: Wilson’s reading of their position: they treated the Bohemian rising of 1618 as a rebellion against the emperor, and had acted against Protestantism only where it lacked a firm legal foundation. In 1629 Ferdinand II issued an Edict of Restitution requiring church lands taken since 1555 to be returned; it was withdrawn in the Peace of Prague of 1635.

parties.name: The Bohemian Protestant nobles, the Protestant princes and cities of the Empire, and their allies (Denmark, Sweden, the Dutch Republic and, from 1635, Catholic France)
parties.said: The Bohemian Protestants suspected that Ferdinand, who had reconfirmed their religious freedoms in 1617, was only waiting for a chance to overturn them. Wilson adds that in the appeals for help that followed few on any side appealed on religious grounds: each party stressed its constitutional rights, or “liberties” as they were called.

causes.note: The standing of the Lutheran and Reformed churches in the Empire, after a settlement in 1555 that recognised only Catholics and Lutherans, was at issue from the start, and the treaty that ended the war settled it.
The authority of the Habsburg emperor against the freedoms of the German princes, and the rivalry of France and the Habsburgs, which the article says gave the war its scope and extent.
The article says disputes over money and territory, including rivalry for the Baltic trade, came to outweigh religion in places.

Historians differ on how much religion mattered. Wilson writes that the war “was neither inevitable nor a religious conflict” and that the religious explanation “does not hold up”; the article calls religion an important factor in starting it, and says its scope came from other forces.

casualties.unit: deaths from fighting, hunger and disease
casualties.basis: Soldiers and civilians, from all causes, in the Empire and neighbouring lands; the article says the German lands lost roughly 40 percent of their people, from 18–20 million in 1600 to 11–13 million in 1650.
casualties.note: The range is the one the article gives; it says claims of up to 12 million are no longer considered realistic. Wilson’s own total is about 5 million: around 1.8 million soldiers and at least 3.2 million civilians, within the Empire. Most civilians died of plague and hunger rather than in fighting.

outcome.note: Ended by the Peace of Westphalia, three treaties of 1648 signed at Münster and Osnabrück. They confirmed the autonomy of the states of the Empire, gave Sweden and France territory, and recognised Dutch independence. The terms for religion are in their own entry.

after.note: The article says the German lands did not regain their pre-war population until about 1750. Pope Innocent X denounced the terms. Wilson says the loss of life, in proportion to the Empire’s population, was far higher than in either world war.

entries.label: The Pequot War
entries.summary: The English colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Saybrook and Connecticut, with Narragansett and Mohegan allies, fight the Pequot nation of southern New England and end the war with the Treaty of Hartford, which forbids the Pequot name and language. The colonists’ own accounts speak of the Lord’s judgement; modern accounts stress trade, land and two killings of traders.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pequot War
sources.note: it quotes the accounts of John Mason and John Underhill; neither was opened

sources.title: “Pequot War (1636–1637)”, Connecticut History, a CTHumanities project

parties.name: The Pequot nation and the Western Niantic
parties.said: The article says the Pequot sachem Sassacus sent wampum to atone for the killing of the trader John Stone but refused the colonists’ demand that the warriors responsible be handed over; the Pequots said later that Stone was killed in reprisal for the Dutch killing of their sachem Tatobem, and that they had not known he was English. The article notes that contemporary accounts say they did know.

parties.name: The English colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Saybrook and Connecticut, with the Narragansett and Mohegan
parties.said: The Connecticut Colony formally declared war on the Pequot and their allies on 1 May 1637. Of the attack on the Mystic fort Captain John Mason wrote, as the article quotes him, that God “laughed his Enemies and the Enemies of his People to scorn”, making the fort “as a fiery Oven”.

causes.note: The accounts of Mason and Underhill, written within a year, describe the destruction of the fort as the Lord’s work; Alfred Cave calls them “more polemical than substantive”, and the article’s own list of causes names no religious cause.

Control of the fur trade and of wampum production, the Pequots’ ties to Dutch traders and the Mohegans’ to the English, and, the other article says, years of confrontation over land, trade and livestock.

The killing of the traders John Stone in 1634 and John Oldham in 1636, and the refusal to hand over those responsible. Alden Vaughan writes that the Pequots were not “solely or even primarily responsible” and that the Bay colony’s escalation of violence made all-out war unavoidable.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range for the war. The article says about 700 Pequots were killed or taken captive by its end, and that of an estimated 500 Pequots in the Mystic fort on 26 May 1637 seven were taken prisoner and seven escaped; the figures for the dead alone differ between accounts.

outcome.note: Ended by the Treaty of Hartford of 1638, which, the sources say, forbade the Pequots to return to their lands, to speak their language or to call themselves Pequots, and disbanded the survivors.

after.note: Hundreds of Pequot prisoners were enslaved, most sold to colonists in Bermuda and the West Indies; others were given as captives to the Narragansett and Mohegan; the colonial authorities classed the Pequots as extinct. The other source notes that the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation lives today in southeastern Connecticut.

entries.label: The Shimabara Rebellion
entries.summary: In December 1637 mostly Catholic peasants and masterless samurai in Shimabara and Amakusa, led by Amakusa Shirō, rise against heavy taxes, famine and the suppression of Christianity. The shogunate besieges them at Hara Castle and defeats them in April 1638. Christianity in Japan survives only out of sight.

parties.name: The rebels of Shimabara and Amakusa: peasants, many of them Catholic, and masterless samurai, led by Amakusa Shirō
parties.said: The article says they rose against the policies of the domain lords, who had sharply raised taxes and violently forbidden Christianity, and notes that the picture of a purely peasant uprising is not entirely accurate. Shirō is said to have put up posters in Hara Castle saying: “those who accompany me in being besieged in this castle, will be my friends unto the next world.”

parties.name: The Tokugawa shogunate, the domain lords Matsukura Katsuie and Terasawa Katataka, and the Dutch East India Company
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that the shogunate sent more than 125,000 troops, supported by the Dutch, and that afterwards it expelled the Portuguese traders it suspected of helping the rebels, enforced the ban on Christianity more strictly and promoted Buddhism in the area.

causes.note: The domain of Shimabara had been Christian under the Arima family, and the lords who replaced it forbade Christianity violently; the people of Amakusa suffered the same under the Terasawa family.
A heavy tax burden to pay for a new castle and for the lord’s ambitions with the shogunate, and famine in the 1630s.
Unemployed samurai from extinct local clans joined the rising, and the shogunate suspected European Catholics of helping it.

casualties.unit: rebels and sympathizers killed or executed
casualties.basis: The people on the rebel side who died in the siege of Hara Castle or were executed after it fell.
casualties.note: The article says shogunate forces executed an estimated 37,000 after the castle fell, and its infobox gives 30,000 to 37,000 for the rebels. For the shogunate’s side the infobox gives 10,000 to 70,000, without a basis.

outcome.note: The shogunate’s forces stormed Hara Castle in April 1638 after a siege; Shirō was killed and his head was displayed at Nagasaki.

after.note: Japan’s seclusion policy was made stricter by 1639 and the ban on Christianity enforced harder, so that Christianity survived underground. Matsukura Katsuie was beheaded for misrule; the people of Shimabara were registered with local temples and Buddhism was promoted there.

entries.label: The Peace of Westphalia: the terms for religion
entries.summary: Three treaties signed in 1648 ended the Thirty Years’ War. Those between the Empire, Sweden and France set the terms for religion within the Empire: the Augsburg settlement was confirmed and extended to the Reformed (Calvinist) churches, and 1624 was fixed as the year by which each territory’s religion was to be judged.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Thirty Years’ War, the section on the Peace of Westphalia
The Treaty of Westphalia (Treaty of Münster, 1648), an English translation of the time, Avalon Project, Yale Law School
sources.note: the treaty between the Emperor and France; the Osnabrück treaty with Sweden was not opened

parties.name: The Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III and the Catholic estates of the Empire
parties.said: The treaty text opens by saying that “Discords and Civil Divisions” in the Empire had drawn Germany and its neighbours into “a long and cruel War”. It confirms the agreement on church lands and the exercise of religion made with Sweden, and applies it in the same way to those it calls “the Reformed”.

parties.name: The Lutheran and Reformed estates of the Empire, with Sweden and France
parties.said: The treaty gives the agreement “touching the Differences about Ecclesiastical Lands, and the Liberty of the Exercise of Religion” as made with the Swedish crown, and for one town, Oppenheim, restores churches and church property “as they were in the Year 1624”.

causes.note: Who could hold church lands and worship in the open, and on what footing, after a settlement of 1555 that had recognised only Catholics and Lutherans.
The rights of the states of the Empire against the emperor, which the article says the peace confirmed together with the supremacy of the Imperial Diet.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the war it ended are given in the entry for the Thirty Years’ War.

outcome.note: As the article summarises the treaty with Sweden: Article 5 reconfirmed the Augsburg settlement, took 1624 as the “normal year” for deciding which religion held in a state, and guaranteed freedom of worship for religious minorities; Article 7 recognised Calvinism as a Reformed faith and ended the rule that subjects must follow a ruler who changed religion. The terms did not apply to the Habsburg hereditary lands.

after.note: The article records that Pope Innocent X denounced the terms, and that exiles were disappointed because Catholicism was accepted as the dominant religion in Bohemia and the Austrian lands.

entries.label: The Maryland Toleration Act (An Act Concerning Religion)
entries.summary: In 1649 the assembly of the colony of Maryland, whose proprietors were Catholic, passes a law that no one professing belief in Jesus Christ may be troubled for his religion. The same Act punishes with death anyone who denies the Trinity. It is repealed in 1654, restored in 1657, and ended in 1692.

sources.title: Maryland Toleration Act, 1649, in the Avalon Project, Yale Law School
sources.note: the text of the Act; the page’s title gives the date as 21 September 1649, Wikipedia gives 21 April 1649

parties.name: Cecilius Calvert, Lord Baltimore, the Lord Proprietary, and the General Assembly of Maryland
parties.said: The Act gives its reasons: that “the inforceing of the conscience in matters of Religion hath frequently fallen out to be of dangerous Consequence”, and the wish for “the more quiett and peaceable governement of this Province” and “mutuall Love and amity amongst the Inhabitants”. It then says no person “professing to beleive in Jesus Christ” shall be “troubled, Molested or discountenanced” for his or her religion, nor “compelled to the beleife or exercise of any other Religion”, if they are not unfaithful to the Lord Proprietary.

parties.name: Those who deny the Trinity: Jews, Unitarians and other dissenters from Trinitarian Christianity
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The Act punishes with death and the loss of lands and goods anyone who blasphemes God, denies that Jesus Christ is the son of God, or denies the Trinity or the Godhead of any of its three persons.

causes.note: Catholic and Protestant colonists, and Trinitarian Christians of several kinds, had to live together in one colony; the Wikipedia article says the Calvert family founded it partly as a refuge for English Catholics. The Act itself says it is passed for a quiet and peaceable government and for mutual love among the inhabitants, because enforcing conscience had proved dangerous elsewhere.
The Act’s protection is conditional on loyalty to the proprietor and the civil government.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: no one is recorded as killed under it in the sources read.

outcome.note: A law of the colony. It protected the worship of Trinitarian Christians and barred insults against them (the word “heretic” among them); it set death for denying the Trinity and whipping, prison or fines for insulting the Virgin Mary, the apostles or the evangelists.

after.note: The article says the Act was repealed in 1654 after Protestants took control of the colony, who then barred Catholics from open worship; passed again in 1657; and rescinded after the revolt of 1689, with Catholic worship banned. It calls the Act a significant step though not a guarantee of religious freedom, and says toleration returned to Maryland only in the era of the American Revolution.

entries.label: The Flushing Remonstrance and the end of New Netherland’s ban on other worship
entries.summary: In December 1657 about thirty residents of Flushing in the Dutch colony of New Netherland petition Director-General Peter Stuyvesant for an exemption from his ban on Quaker worship, in a document called the Flushing Remonstrance. Stuyvesant has some of the signers arrested; in 1663 the directors of the Dutch West India Company tell him to end religious persecution in the colony. Historians differ on how far the document foreshadows American freedom of religion.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Flushing Remonstrance
sources.note: it names the historians behind it; the text of the Remonstrance was not shown in the part read

parties.name: The signers: about thirty residents of Flushing, none of them Quakers, with the town clerk Edward Hart, who wrote it, and the sheriff Tobias Feake
parties.said: The article says they asked for an exemption from Stuyvesant’s ban on Quaker worship, being affronted by the persecution of Quakers and by his religious policies. It does not quote the text in the part read; it says the original, probably in Dutch, is lost, and that an official English copy of 1657 survives.

parties.name: Peter Stuyvesant, Director-General of New Netherland, and the Dutch Reformed Church
parties.said: The article says Stuyvesant asserted that he was not violating the signers’ “freedom of conscience”, only their right to worship outside family prayer meetings, and that he proclaimed 13 March 1658 a day of prayer for repenting of “the sin of religious tolerance”. The article on him says he was a member of the Dutch Reformed Church, opposed religious pluralism and was committed to its supremacy in the colony.

parties.name: The directors of the Dutch West India Company, in Amsterdam
parties.said: The article says that in 1663 they advised Stuyvesant by letter to end religious persecution in the colony, after John Bowne petitioned them. The article on Stuyvesant says that in 1657, when he forbade Lutherans to worship in their homes, the directors, three of whom were Lutherans, told him to withdraw the order, and that the Company’s position was that more tolerance led to more trade.

causes.note: In 1656 Stuyvesant issued an ordinance forbidding every congregation other than the Dutch Reformed Church. The article lists penalties under it: the Baptist minister William Wickenden and the sheriff William Hallett jailed, fined and exiled for baptising in Flushing; the Quaker preacher Robert Hodgson sentenced to two years of hard labour; and Henry Townsend and Samuel Spicer fined for Quaker meetings, Townsend banished as well.

The article says Stuyvesant’s policy was not far from the one developing in the Netherlands, official recognition of the Dutch Reformed Church with broad tolerance within it and a habit of looking away from non-conforming practice. It cites Thomas Broderick, who argues that the Remonstrance should be read as a document of the seventeenth-century Dutch experience, whose true legacy is discussion rather than toleration.
The article on Stuyvesant says the Company’s position was that more tolerance led to more trade and benefited everyone.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: no deaths are recorded in the sources read. The penalties recorded are arrests, fines, imprisonment on bread and water, banishment, hard labour and, the article on Stuyvesant says, public torture of Robert Hodgson.

outcome.note: Stuyvesant dismissed the local government and had four signers arrested; two recanted at once, Edward Hart was released on penalty of banishment after his family and friends petitioned, and Tobias Feake recanted weeks later and was fined and barred from public office. After John Bowne was banished in 1662 for hosting Quaker meetings, the Company backed him and in 1663 told Stuyvesant to end religious persecution. In 1664 English forces took the colony, and Stuyvesant obtained freedom of religion in the Articles of Capitulation.

after.note: The article says the Quaker Meeting House in Flushing, built in 1694, is the oldest house of worship in continuous use in New York State, and that some historians consider the Remonstrance a precursor of the freedom-of-religion provision of the United States Bill of Rights, a reading that Broderick cautions against.

entries.label: King Philip’s War in New England
entries.summary: In 1675 a coalition of Algonquian peoples led by Metacom, whom the colonists called King Philip, fights the Puritan colonies of New England and their Native allies, among them Christian Indians. It is among the deadliest wars in colonial American history. Missionary conversion was one of the grievances Metacom is recorded as naming.

sources.title: Wikipedia: King Philip’s War
sources.note: it reports the colonial records and the historians it names; none was opened

parties.name: The Wampanoag confederacy under Metacom, with the Nipmuc, Pocumtuc and Narragansett and others
parties.also: Metacom was called King Philip by the colonists
parties.said: The article says one grievance of many Wampanoags was the attempts of colonial missionaries to convert them, and that Metacom declared that he and other Wampanoag leaders greatly feared that any of their people “should be called or forced to be Christian Indians”. It also names the colonists’ livestock on Wampanoag farms and hunting grounds.

parties.name: The Puritan colonies of Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay and Connecticut, with Mohegan, Pequot and Christian Indian allies
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that court officials, after Metacom was brought before them without proof, warned that they would take Wampanoag land and guns if they had any further report that he was plotting war, and that Plymouth hanged three Wampanoags on 8 June 1675 for the murder of John Sassamon, a Native convert to Christianity and an adviser to Metacom.

causes.note: Missionary attempts to convert the Wampanoags were among their grievances; the other article says praying towns were established by missionaries such as the Puritan John Eliot, and that Native people converted voluntarily or involuntarily.
The intrusion of the settlers’ unfenced livestock, and the colonists’ efforts to buy large tracts of land at Nemasket, where Sassamon’s body was found.
Native diplomacy with the colonies had broken down after Massasoit’s death, and the trial and hanging of three Wampanoags over Sassamon’s death are named as the first shots of the war.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article calls it the greatest calamity in seventeenth-century New England and, to many, the deadliest war in colonial American history, with twelve towns destroyed and Plymouth and Rhode Island losing one tenth of their men fit to serve; its infobox gives more than 5,000 dead on the Native side and more than 2,500 on the colonial side, without a basis.

outcome.note: The article’s infobox gives a victory to the New England Confederation in the south and to the Wabanaki in Maine, and says the war in the far north ended with the Treaty of Casco Bay on 12 April 1678.

after.note: The sections read do not describe the aftermath in detail. The other article says that praying towns, whose people had converted, had already been a source of disputes over land in the 1650s and 1660s, as in the dispute at Dedham that ended with the land at Natick awarded to Eliot’s converts.

entries.label: The Pueblo Revolt
entries.summary: In August 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, led by Popé of Ohkay Owingeh, rise against the Spanish colony and its Franciscan missions, killing many settlers and missionaries and driving the rest out of the province. The Spanish return twelve years later. Both sources name the suppression of Pueblo religion among the main causes.

sources.title: “1680: The Pueblo Revolt”, Library of Congress Law Library blog (2013)
sources.note: a library’s short account

parties.name: The Pueblo peoples of New Mexico, led by Popé (Po’pay) of Ohkay Owingeh and by leaders of Taos, Picuris, Santo Domingo and other pueblos
parties.said: The article says Popé promised that, once the Spanish were killed or expelled, the ancient Pueblo gods would reward the people with health and prosperity, and that he and his lieutenants went from town to town ordering a return “to the state of their antiquity”, with all crosses, churches and Christian images to be destroyed.

parties.name: The Spanish colonial government and the Franciscan missions of Santa Fe de Nuevo México
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Spaniards were resolved to replace Pueblo worship with Christianity; that in 1608 the Franciscans baptized seven thousand Pueblos to persuade the Crown not to abandon the province; and that Fray Alonso de Posada outlawed Kachina dances and ordered the masks, prayer sticks and effigies burned.

causes.note: The Library of Congress account calls forcible conversion and the suppression of native religious practice the greatest source of tension, and tells of local religious leaders rounded up and tried in Santa Fe in the 1670s, some hanged and the others whipped; the article calls the persecution of Pueblo religious practice the most inflammatory cause and says scholars see the revolt as the first Native American religious traditionalist revitalization movement.
Tribute and labour were demanded under the encomienda and repartimiento systems; drought and famine in the 1660s and 1670s, and Apache raids the colony could not stop, added to the strain.
The aim was to be rid of Spanish rule: the revolt united the Rio Grande pueblos, who spoke six languages, using Spanish as a common language.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range. The article gives 400 people killed on the Spanish side, among them 21 of the 33 Franciscan missionaries in New Mexico; it gives no figure for the Pueblo dead in its text (its infobox says over 600, without a basis).

outcome.note: The Pueblos rose on 10 August 1680, a day earlier than planned because the Spanish had learned of the plan, closed the roads to Santa Fe and drove the Spanish settlers out of the province, which they did not re-enter for about twelve years.

after.note: The article says the Spanish returned to New Mexico twelve years later. The Library of Congress account says little is known of Popé himself, who is first heard of in the 1670s trial of Pueblo religious leaders.

entries.label: The Toleration Act of 1689 in England
