entries.summary: In May 1689, after the revolution of 1688 that brought William and Mary to the throne, the English Parliament passes the Toleration Act, which lets Protestant dissenters who take certain oaths and reject transubstantiation have their own places of worship and teachers. It does not apply to Roman Catholics, Jews, nontrinitarians or atheists, and it keeps political and university restrictions on dissenters.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Toleration Act 1688
sources.note: the statute itself was not opened; the article is also titled the Toleration Act 1689

sources.title: Wikipedia: Penal law (British)
sources.note: the opening only was read

parties.name: Parliament and the government of William and Mary, the act being written by Daniel Finch, 2nd Earl of Nottingham
parties.said: The article says the act received royal assent on 24 May 1689, and that the Whig and Tory parties that had rallied around William and Mary had promised the nonconformists such an act if the revolution succeeded. It quotes the historian Kenneth Pearl calling it “in many ways a compromise bill”.

parties.name: The Protestant nonconformists: Baptists, Congregationalists and English Presbyterians
parties.said: The article says nonconformists believed that James II’s attempts to circumvent Parliament put at risk the religious liberties of his Declarations of Indulgence. Under the act they gained their own places of worship and schoolteachers, if they accepted certain oaths, but remained excluded from political office and the universities, had to register their meeting houses and could not meet in private homes.

parties.name: Roman Catholics, Jews, nontrinitarians and atheists, whom the act intentionally left out
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Catholics and Unitarians were not hunted down after the act but had no right to assemble and pray, and that Unitarians were granted toleration only by an act of 1813.

causes.note: The act allowed freedom of worship to nonconformists who took the oaths of Allegiance and Supremacy and rejected transubstantiation, that is, to Protestants who dissented from the Church of England; the article says the penal laws before it sought to enforce the Church of England’s religious monopoly, and the Clarendon Code is one of the sections of the other article.

The article says James II’s attempt to dispense with the Test Acts through the Declarations of Indulgence of 1687 and 1688 helped to spark the constitutional crisis that led to the revolution of 1688, after which a series of acts, among them the Bill of Rights 1689 and this act, gave a new settlement.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article says that before it dissenters, among them Roman Catholics, were subject to religious persecution and kept from office, and gives no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: The act received royal assent on 24 May 1689. It intentionally did not apply to Roman Catholics, Jews, nontrinitarians or atheists, kept the disabilities of dissenters, required meeting houses to be registered and dissenting preachers to be licensed, and was not repealed in full until the Statute Law (Repeals) Act 1969, in force on 1 January 1970.

after.note: The article says toleration was extended to Unitarians in 1813, that Catholics were allowed to worship under strict conditions by an act of 1791, and that later acts removed the oaths and tests that barred nonconformists and Catholics from office, among them the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and the Jews Relief Act 1858.

entries.label: The Salem witch trials in colonial Massachusetts

places.name: Salem Town, where the courts sat

entries.summary: From February 1692 to May 1693 more than two hundred people are accused of witchcraft in colonial Massachusetts, and nineteen are hanged after trials in courts sitting at Salem. Historians point to the beliefs of the Puritan colonists, a political crisis over the colony’s charter, a frontier war and quarrels within Salem Village. The trials ended when leading clergymen came to doubt the spectral evidence, and the convictions were annulled in 1711.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Salem witch trials
sources.note: it quotes the court records and the historians it names; none was opened

parties.name: The accusers, among them girls of Salem Village, and the magistrates and judges of the special courts
parties.said: The article says that in the years afterwards several of the accusers, mostly teenage girls, admitted that they had fabricated their charges, and that Ann Putnam Jr., one of the most active, asked forgiveness in the Salem Village church in 1706, saying she had not acted out of malice but had been deluded into naming innocent people. It says the court of Oyer and Terminer was set up on 27 May 1692 by the new governor and council.

parties.name: The accused, about 78 per cent of them women, from Salem and at least twenty-five other New England communities
parties.said: The article says more than 200 people were accused, thirty found guilty and nineteen hanged, and that Giles Corey died under torture for refusing to enter a plea. No statement by the accused as a body is quoted in the sources read.

parties.name: Ministers and critics, among them Increase and Cotton Mather, Samuel Parris and the Quaker Thomas Maule
parties.said: The article says the trials ended when leading clergymen began to doubt the spectral evidence, and quotes Thomas Maule, who wrote in 1695 that “it were better that one hundred Witches should live, than that one person be put to death for a witch, which is not a Witch”; he was jailed for a year and then found not guilty. The article on Cotton Mather says he advised the judges against spectral evidence yet defended the court in a book of 1693, and that historians now tend to downplay his part.

causes.note: The article says the Puritan colonists had come to build a society on their religious beliefs, and that the prevailing belief was that women were inherently sinful and more open to damnation, and that Puritans tried to thwart the Devil’s attempts to take their souls. It says the village minister Samuel Parris added to tensions by seeking out “iniquitous behavior” and requiring public penance for small faults.

The colony’s charter of 1629 was vacated in 1684 and the governor Andros ousted in 1689, leaving its leaders without constitutional authority until a new charter arrived in February 1692. The article says King William’s War on the Maine frontier sent refugees into Essex County, thirteen years after King Philip’s War.

The article says Salem Village, whose neighbours thought it quarrelsome, had arguments over property lines, grazing rights and church privileges, and a strained relationship with Salem Town; it says a vote in 1689 to give Parris the deed to the parsonage and land conflicted with a village resolution of 1681.

How far belief, politics or local feud explains the trials is argued. The article describes the episode as a case of mass hysteria and moral panic and as a colonial form of the wider early modern witch trials, and quotes the historian Marion Starkey that in the village’s atmosphere serious conflict may have been inevitable.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article gives 25 deaths, nineteen of the accused hanged, Giles Corey dead under torture and at least five who died in jail, out of more than 200 accused and thirty found guilty.

outcome.note: The court of Oyer and Terminer sat in 1692 and a Superior Court of Judicature in 1693, both at Salem Town; the last trial was in May 1693. In 1702 the General Court declared the trials unlawful and in 1711 the colonial legislature annulled the convictions of 22 people it named.

after.note: The article says a fast day was ordered for 14 January 1697, on which Samuel Sewall had his apology read in Boston’s South Church and a trial juror and eleven others asked forgiveness, and that in 1703 the Salem Village church reversed the excommunication of Martha Corey. In November 2001 the Massachusetts legislature passed an act exonerating all who had been convicted, and the last conviction, that of Elizabeth Johnson, was cleared on 26 May 2022.

entries.label: The Guaraní War over the seven Jesuit missions

places.name: São Miguel das Missões, one of the seven missions

entries.summary: In 1754 the Guaraní of seven Jesuit mission towns refuse to leave land that the Treaty of Madrid of 1750 gave to Portugal, and a joint Spanish and Portuguese force is sent against them. Their leader Sepé Tiaraju is killed in February 1756 and the Guaraní are defeated at Caiboaté days later. Spain and Portugal annul the treaty in 1761.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Guaraní War
sources.note: a short article

parties.name: The Guaraní of the seven missions east of the Uruguay River, led by Sepé Tiaraju
parties.said: The article on Sepé Tiaraju says that after a century and a half of communal life in the missions, most Guaraní saw neither a return to the forests nor a move elsewhere as an option. The cry “This land has owners!” is attributed to him.

parties.name: Spain and Portugal, with a joint army under José de Andonaegui and Gomes Freire de Andrade
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says their Treaty of Madrid of 1750 ended a border conflict by ceding Colonia del Sacramento to Spain and setting the border at the Uruguay River, which gave Portugal land that included seven Jesuit missions, to be dismantled and moved to the Spanish side.

parties.name: The Jesuit priests of the missions
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Jesuits surrendered control of the missions in 1754; the sources do not say what they advised the Guaraní.

causes.note: The Treaty of Madrid moved the border between the Spanish and Portuguese colonies to the Uruguay River, and the Guaraní of the seven missions east of it were ordered to leave. They refused to move or to accept Portuguese rule.

The missions were founded by Spanish Jesuits in the early seventeenth century, and the article on Sepé Tiaraju calls the people in them Christianised Guaraní; it also says they lived a communal life there. The sources read do not say how far belief, rather than home and land, moved them to resist.

The article on Sepé Tiaraju says the mission Guaraní kept what is believed to have been the largest herd of cattle in Latin America, so that European interest in the area went beyond land; the article on the war says the seven missions were among the most populous in South America, with 26,362 people in a Jesuit census.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range for the whole war: the article gives 1,511 Guaraní killed and 152 taken prisoner at Caiboaté on 10 February 1756, against four Spanish and Portuguese killed and about thirty wounded, and an infobox figure of 16,000 Guaraní killed or displaced. A census of 1756 counted 14,284 Guaraní in the seven missions, about 15,000 fewer than in 1750.

outcome.note: The Guaraní were defeated at Caiboaté on 10 February 1756, three days after Sepé Tiaraju was killed in a skirmish, and the missions were occupied by Spanish and Portuguese forces, who made the Guaraní leave them. The article says Spain and Portugal annulled the treaty in the Treaty of El Pardo of 1761.

after.note: The Portuguese held the missions until 1759, when Spain ended the treaty by itself and took back the land, and the border of the La Plata region was fixed by the Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1777. The article on Sepé Tiaraju says he remains a folk saint in Rio Grande do Sul and that in 2018 the Catholic Church began a process of beatification, declaring him a Servant of God.

entries.label: Pontiac’s War in the Great Lakes region
entries.summary: In 1763 Native peoples of the Great Lakes and Ohio country, with the Odawa leader Pontiac among the best known, attack British forts and settlements after Britain takes over the region from France. A religious awakening led by Neolin, a Lenape teacher, is named among the causes. The war ends in negotiated peace by 1766, and the Crown issues the Royal Proclamation of 1763.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Pontiac’s War
sources.note: it reports the historians it names (Dowd, Richter, Middleton, Calloway); none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Neolin
sources.note: the opening only was read

parties.name: A coalition of Native peoples of the Great Lakes and Ohio country, among them the Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi, Seneca (Mingo), Lenape, Shawnee, Wyandot and Miami
parties.also: Pontiac, the Odawa leader after whom the war is named, was the most prominent of many leaders
parties.said: The article says Neolin called on Indians to shun the colonists’ trade goods, alcohol and weapons, and quotes him: “If you suffer the English among you, you are dead men.” It also says those who joined the uprising complained that British officers treated them no better than slaves or dogs.

parties.name: Britain, under General Jeffery Amherst, with the garrisons of its forts, the colonists and Sir William Johnson, who handled relations with the Native peoples
parties.said: The article says Amherst believed that, with France out of the picture, the Indians would have to accept British rule and could offer no serious resistance, and that he saw the giving of presents, a French custom, as little more than bribery. In 1765 General Gage wrote, it says, that he was determined to have “none our enemy” among the Indian peoples.

causes.note: Resentment of British army policy after the French and Indian War: in 1761 Amherst cut the presents given to chiefs and restricted the sale of powder and shot, and officers made little effort to hide their contempt. The article cites Dowd (2002), who argues that the army’s presence, attitude and policies mattered more than colonial expansion.

The article says a religious awakening swept through Indian settlements in the early 1760s, fed by discontent with the British, food shortages and epidemic disease, and that Neolin joined Christian ideas with traditional beliefs. The article on Neolin calls his message a direct inspiration for the war; how far it moved the many peoples who joined is not measured in the sources read.

Land: the Shawnees and Lenape of the Ohio country had been pushed out by colonists, which the article says drew them into the war. It also cites Dowd (2002), who argues that most of those involved were not immediately threatened by settlement and that historians have put too much weight on colonial expansion.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article says the total loss of life is unknown. It gives about 400 British soldiers killed in battle (its infobox says about 450) and perhaps 50 more captured and put to death, an estimate of 2,000 settlers killed or captured and about 4,000 who fled, and at least 200 Native warriors killed in battle, with Native losses mostly unrecorded.

outcome.note: Hostilities largely ended after British expeditions in 1764, followed by talks. Pontiac made a treaty with William Johnson at Fort Ontario on 25 July 1766; the article says no lands were ceded, no prisoners returned and no hostages taken, and that scholars now usually see the war as a military stalemate.

after.note: The Crown issued the Royal Proclamation on 7 October 1763, drawing a boundary between the colonies and Indian land west of the Appalachians. The article says it has been called a Native American “Bill of Rights” and still informs relations between Canada and the First Nations, while many colonists and land speculators felt it denied them the fruits of victory, a resentment it names among the things that led to the American Revolution.

entries.label: The Haitian Revolution
entries.summary: From 1791 enslaved people of the French colony of Saint-Domingue rise against slavery and colonial rule, in a war that draws in Britain and Spain and ends on 1 January 1804 with the independence of Haiti. The articles report that a Vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman, led by the priest Dutty Boukman, gave the signal for the rising, and that Vodou, a mixture of African religions and Catholicism, was practised by many who took part.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Haitian Revolution
sources.note: a very long article; its opening, the background, the rising of 1791, the aftermath and the casualties were read, and none of the historians it names was opened

parties.name: The enslaved people and free people of colour of Saint-Domingue, with leaders including Dutty Boukman, Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines
parties.said: The article reports that the signal for the rising was given by Dutty Boukman, a high priest of Vodou, and Cécile Fatiman at a religious ceremony at Bois Caïman, and that Dessalines declared independence at Gonaïves on 1 January 1804. It quotes the reply of his men at the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot, “We shall die for liberty!”. The sources read do not say how the Bois Caïman ceremony is evidenced.

parties.name: France, under the monarchy, the Republic and Napoleon, with the colony’s planters
parties.said: The article says the planters had long feared a revolt and were well armed, and that white militias struck back in September 1791. It says France declared slavery abolished in the course of the war, and that after Napoleon’s expedition of 1802 Black cultivators revolted again when it became apparent that the French intended to re-establish slavery, as they had nearly done on Guadeloupe.

parties.name: Britain and Spain, who entered the war after 1793
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Britain’s expedition cost its treasury four million pounds and about 100,000 men dead, wounded or disabled, mostly by yellow fever, before it withdrew.

causes.note: The article places the rising in the crisis that followed the French Revolution: free people of colour pressed for citizenship, Vincent Ogé’s revolt of 1790 and a decree of May 1791 followed, and clashes with slave owners destabilised the colony.

The article says the enslaved developed a religion mixing Catholicism and West African religions, which it says implicitly rejected their status as slaves; that the Maroon leader François Mackandal, a Vodou priest, drew on African traditions to unite runaway bands; and that the signal for 1791 came at a Vodou ceremony. The Vodou article says many Vodouists took part in the revolution. How far religion shaped its course is not measured in the sources read.

Slavery was the base of the colony’s sugar and coffee economy, which the article calls the richest of the French colonies. It says the enslaved outnumbered the other groups ten to one and that a high death rate led the planters to import people from Africa continually.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives 200,000 dead among the enslaved Afro-Haitians, 25,000 among white colonists, 57,000 to 75,000 French dead (37,000 killed in action) and 100,000 British dead or wounded, mostly by yellow fever, without saying who counted them.

outcome.note: Dessalines declared the colony independent on 1 January 1804 and renamed it Haiti. The article says France did not officially recognise the independence of Haiti until 1825.

after.note: The article calls it one of the only known slave rebellions to found a state free from slavery, though not from forced labour, says it reshaped debates over slavery and sparked revolts in nearby colonies, and cites the historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot’s remark that its history has been “silenced” beside that of the French Revolution. The Vodou article says Vodou has faced much criticism through its history.

entries.label: The jihad of Usman dan Fodio and the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate
entries.summary: Usman dan Fodio, an Islamic scholar exiled from the Hausa kingdom of Gobir, leads his followers in a war against Gobir and other Hausa kingdoms. It ends with the capture of Gobir in 1808 and the founding of the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in nineteenth-century Africa.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jihad of Usman dan Fodio
sources.note: dan Fodio’s own writings were not opened

parties.name: Usman dan Fodio and his followers
parties.also: His followers named him Amir al-Mu’minin, “Commander of the Faithful”
parties.said: The article says his preaching stressed the duty of Muslim rulers to promote Islam and to rule justly, and criticised corruption, hypocrisy, the oppression of fellow Muslims and the tolerance of beliefs and practices in conflict with Islam. In 1804 his followers declared him Amir al-Mu’minin and renounced their allegiance to Gobir.

parties.name: The kings of Gobir, Nafata and then Yunfa, and the other Hausa kingdoms
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that Nafata restricted the preaching of dan Fodio’s followers, that Yunfa, his former pupil, exiled him from Gobir, and that on 21 February 1804 Yunfa declared war on him and threatened punishment for anyone who joined him.

causes.note: Dan Fodio’s call for rulers to govern as Muslims, and the restrictions placed on his preaching and on his followers, are named as the lead-up to the war.
The article says Hausa rulers enforced harsh conscription and taxation, and that Fulani communities felt especially wronged by Hausa taxation and control of land.
Fulani herders and settled Hausa farmers competed for resources; war disrupted society and led to the enslavement of war captives.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded: the sources read give no figure for the dead.

outcome.note: Dan Fodio’s forces took one Hausa kingdom after another, captured Gobir in 1808 and executed Yunfa. The Sokoto Caliphate was founded, at first headed by dan Fodio himself.

after.note: By 1837 the Caliphate had, the article says, a population of 10 to 20 million, the largest in West Africa; it was dissolved when the British, French and Germans conquered the area in 1903. The success inspired similar jihads elsewhere in West Africa.

entries.label: Tecumseh’s War and Tenskwatawa’s revival
entries.summary: From a religious revival led by the Shawnee prophet Tenskwatawa, which called on Native peoples to reject European ways and cede no more land, his brother Tecumseh builds a confederacy against the United States. Governor Harrison’s army meets Tenskwatawa’s followers at Tippecanoe in 1811, and the war merges into the War of 1812 until Tecumseh’s death in 1813.

parties.name: Tecumseh’s confederacy and Tenskwatawa, known as “the Prophet”, with Britain from 1812
parties.said: The article says Tenskwatawa urged Native people to reject European American ways, such as liquor, European-style clothing and firearms, and called on the tribes to give up no more land to the United States; it says Tecumseh’s confederacy was built on the foundation of his younger brother’s religious appeal, and that Tenskwatawa’s teaching became more militant as it spread.

parties.name: The United States: Governor William Henry Harrison of Indiana Territory and the government
parties.said: The article says Harrison’s stated goal was to force Tenskwatawa’s followers to accept peace, though he acknowledged he would make a pre-emptive attack if they refused, and that he had orders from the Secretary of War to use force to disperse the Indians at Prophetstown. After Tippecanoe, it says, many Americans blamed the British, and Andrew Jackson claimed that the Indians were “excited by secret British agents”.

causes.note: A nativist religious revival from 1805 led by Tenskwatawa, begun with a witch-hunt among the Lenape after the death of their chief Buckongahelas, in which, the article says, several suspected witches were killed; it drew followers from many nations and threatened the influence of chiefs who cooperated with the United States.

The refusal to cede more land to the United States and Tecumseh’s aim of Native independence from outside dominance; the war is viewed by some historians as the last of a long struggle for control of the Great Lakes region.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives two totals for the two sides over the whole war, 913 to 1,059 and 3,501 to 3,505, including wounded, captured and missing, so they are not a count of the dead alone; the sections read give no figure for those killed at Tippecanoe.

outcome.note: Harrison’s army defeated Tenskwatawa’s warriors at Tippecanoe on 7 November 1811 and burned Prophetstown; Tecumseh died fighting in the Battle of the Thames in 1813, and his confederacy broke up.

after.note: The article says Harrison and many later historians called Tippecanoe a deathblow to the confederacy, though Tecumseh began to rebuild it, and that the battle cost Tenskwatawa prestige. Harrison later became President of the United States; Canadians remember Tecumseh as a defender of Canada.

entries.label: The 1838 Mormon War in Missouri and Executive Order 44
entries.summary: In the summer and autumn of 1838 unrest in northern Missouri between members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints and their neighbours, vigilantes and the state militia ends in an order by Governor Lilburn Boggs on 27 October that the Mormons be driven from the state. About ten thousand Mormons leave for Illinois. Missouri formally rescinded the order in 1976.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Missouri Executive Order 44
sources.note: it quotes the order and its rescission of 1976; the text itself was not opened

parties.name: The Latter Day Saints (Mormons) of northern Missouri
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The second article says that in 1831 Jackson County was designated as the place of Zion, a sacred place where Mormons believed they would gather before the Second Coming of Jesus Christ; the first records that the Mormons retaliated against the vigilantes’ attacks in Daviess County.

parties.name: Anti-Mormon vigilantes, the Missouri militia and Governor Lilburn Boggs
parties.also: The order is called the Mormon Extermination Order
parties.said: Executive Order 44 says, as the article quotes it, that the Mormons had shown “open and avowed defiance of the law” and “made war upon the people of Missouri”, and that “the Mormons must be treated as enemies, and must be exterminated or driven from the State if necessary for the public peace”. Boggs later said, the article reports, that he had meant only to subdue them without bloodshed; two historians say the word then covered expulsion.

causes.note: The second article names the religious and cultural differences between the Mormons and their non-Mormon neighbours, and the Mormons’ gathering at a place they held sacred, as the root of the tension.
The second article also names economic competition and fears of cultural displacement as parts of the tension.

Disputes over voting and political strength as the Mormon population grew, which flared in the Election Day fighting at Gallatin on 6 August 1838, with state militia refusing to protect the town of De Witt.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the first article’s infobox gives 21 Mormons killed, 17 of them at Haun’s Mill, and one on the other side, with about 10,000 Mormons and about 100 others displaced. Whether anyone was killed because of the order itself between 27 October and 1 November is debated; the second article says most scholars find too little evidence that militiamen invoked it.

outcome.note: The order of 27 October 1838, issued after the Battle of Crooked River, was carried out by the state militia; the Mormons surrendered on 1 November and were expelled from the state.

after.note: The article says the Mormons fled to Illinois. Governor Kit Bond rescinded the order on 25 June 1976, 137 years after it was signed, calling it unconstitutional, at a conference of the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints.

entries.label: The Caste War of Yucatán and the Talking Cross

places.name: Chan Santa Cruz, now Felipe Carrillo Puerto

entries.summary: From 1847 the Maya of the Yucatán peninsula revolt against the Yucatecan government, in a war that begins over land and debt labour. From 1850 a “Talking Cross” at Chan Santa Cruz, believed to carry messages from God to the Maya, becomes the religious and political centre of the Maya of the southeast, who keep their own state for decades. The main article dates the war to 1915, with minor clashes until 1933, and puts the toll in the hundreds of thousands.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Caste War of Yucatán
sources.note: it names the historians behind it; none was opened

parties.name: The Maya of the southeast, called the Cruzoob, the people of the Cross, with leaders such as Cecilio Chi and Jacinto Pat
parties.said: The article says that in 1850 the Maya of the southeast were inspired to continue the struggle by the apparition of the “Talking Cross”, believed to be a way in which God communicated with the Maya, which dictated that the war continue. It quotes a letter of Cecilio Chi of 1849 saying that Governor Santiago Méndez had come to “put every Indian, big and little, to death”, and that the Maya had answered in kind.

parties.name: The Yucatecan government, descended from the Hispanic population, and later the Mexican state
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Catholic Church, generally allied with the stronger classes, had a leading role where military organisation was strongest, and that the Yucatán government sold Maya prisoners into slavery during the war, so that the peninsula became a platform for the Cuban slave trade.

causes.note: The article says that from the late eighteenth century the growth of henequen and sugar cane drew investment onto Maya customary lands, that laws passed after 1821 encouraged it, and that by the 1840s land loss had forced much of the Maya peasantry into indebted labour on haciendas.

The Talking Cross made Chan Santa Cruz the religious and political centre of the Maya resistance from 1850, and the article says the Cruzob broke with traditional Catholicism, a break that the Ixcanha Maya, about a thousand people, refused. The article on Chan Santa Cruz calls the movement a reappearance of Maya religion in a partly syncretic form. The sources read tie religion to the war’s continuation rather than to its outbreak in 1847.

The article on Chan Santa Cruz says the Maya leadership saw an opening when the Yucatecan elite declared independence and began fighting over resources. Britain recognised the Maya state as de facto independent from the late 1850s to 1893 because of its trade with British Honduras.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives about 314,000 dead on the rebel side and 50,000 military, 364,000 in all, without saying who counted them, and says that the population of the Yucatán was halved through war, disease or migration.

outcome.note: The article’s infobox gives a Maya victory to 1883, with the state of Chan Santa Cruz established, and a Mexican victory from 1884 to 1915, when Mexico retook the peninsula. The Mexican army occupied Chan Santa Cruz in 1901, and the article on it says General Francisco May signed a formal peace treaty with the government of Mexico in 1935.

after.note: The article on Chan Santa Cruz says the shrines of the Talking Cross remain part of local culture and that in 2002 the Mexican government lifted a stigma that had attached to indigenous priests under civil and Church law, recognising the Church of the Talking Cross as a legitimate religion, with a plaque at a shrine in Carrillo Puerto.

entries.label: The Taiping Rebellion
entries.summary: Hong Xiuquan, who had come to believe he was the younger brother of Jesus, leads a movement that sets up the “Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace” at Nanjing and fights the Qing government for fourteen years. It ends with the fall of Nanjing in 1864. Estimates of the dead range from twenty million to a hundred million, most from famine and plague. Some historians prefer the name Taiping Civil War.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Taiping Rebellion
sources.note: it reports the historians it names; none was opened

parties.name: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom, under Hong Xiuquan, who took the title Heavenly King
parties.said: The article says that after a series of visions and a reading of Christian pamphlets Hong came to believe that his celestial father was God the Father and his elder brother Jesus Christ, and that he was directed to rid the world of demons, among them the Qing government and Confucian teachings. The article on him says he presented his teaching as a restoration of the ancient Chinese faith in Shangdi.

parties.name: The Qing dynasty, ruled by Manchus, with provincial armies and later foreign-led forces
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the Qing government had recently been defeated in the First Opium War, was weak in the southern regions, and that Britain and France intervened in a limited way against the rebellion after the Taiping refused to agree not to attack Shanghai.

causes.note: Hong’s visions and the Christian pamphlets he read gave the movement its creed, which the article calls a fusion of Christianity, Taoism, Confucianism and indigenous millenarianism. The article says the kingdom replaced Confucianism, Buddhism and Chinese folk religion with its own faith, burned Buddhist libraries and Confucian books and destroyed idols; missionaries who had welcomed the movement later doubted it, and one wrote of seeing no sign of Christianity near Nanjing.

The article says anti-Manchu feeling was strongest among the Hakka of the south, that the government, commanded by Manchus, had become increasingly corrupt, and that the Taiping aimed at the political overthrow of the Qing and a general change in the workings of the state.

The article names famines, natural disasters and defeat in the First Opium War, heavy taxes and rising rents, a population that nearly doubled between 1766 and 1833 on the same cultivated land, and the strain of the illegal import of opium.

casualties.unit: dead, civilians and soldiers, most of them from plague and famine
casualties.basis: Deaths during almost fourteen years of the rebellion; there was no reliable census, so the article calls every estimate speculative.
casualties.note: The article’s opening gives 20 to 30 million (5 to 10 per cent of the population) and 73 to 100 million (about a quarter); its section on the toll says the most widely cited sources give 20 to 30 million and that some analysts claim as many as 100 million.

outcome.note: Hong died in June 1864 and Nanjing fell a month later, ending the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom; the article says the fighting did not stop at once and the last Taiping army was destroyed in August 1871. It says both sides killed civilians on a large scale: Taiping soldiers killed many Manchus, and the Qing killed many civilians in Nanjing.

after.note: The article says the war cost the Qing dynasty heavily in economic and political stability, that thirty million people fled the conquered regions, and that fighting spilled into Vietnam, where Taiping remnants became the Yellow Flag and Black Flag armies. It calls the rebellion widely considered the most important event in nineteenth-century Chinese history.

entries.label: The Xhosa cattle-killing movement, 1856–1858

places.name: The mouth of the Gxarha River, on the Wild Coast

entries.summary: In April 1856 a young Xhosa woman, Nongqawuse, reports that spirits of ancestors have told her that the Xhosa must kill their cattle and destroy their crops, after which the dead would arise and the settlers would be swept into the sea. Many obey, the promised day passes, and by 1858 about forty thousand are said to have starved. Historians read it as a millenarian response to cattle disease and the loss of land, and the colonial government’s part in it is debated.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nongqawuse
sources.note: a short article

sources.title: Wikipedia: History of the Cape Colony from 1806 to 1870
sources.note: the section on the cattle-killing, which cites J. B. Peires’s account; the book was not opened

parties.name: Nongqawuse, her uncle Mhlakaza and the Xhosa who obeyed, among them the Gcaleka chief Sarhili
parties.said: The article says Nongqawuse claimed that the spirits of two ancestors told her the dead would arise, that all living cattle must be killed because they had been reared by contaminated hands, that cultivation must cease, and that people must abandon witchcraft, incest and adultery; in return the spirits would sweep all the European settlers into the sea.

parties.name: The Xhosa who did not believe, called the amagogotya, “the stingy ones”
parties.said: The article says a small minority refused to kill their cattle and neglect their crops, and that Nongqawuse used their refusal to explain why the prophecies failed over the fifteen months from April 1856 to June 1857.

parties.name: The Cape colonial government under Governor Sir George Grey, and the settlers
parties.said: The article on the Cape Colony says Grey ordered the settlers not to help the Xhosa unless they entered labour contracts, and that he and his administration believed in a “Chief’s Plot”, in which the chiefs had deliberately starved their people into desperation so as to recruit them for war on the settlers. It says this account was used to justify the confiscation of land, and that Peires stresses Grey’s part in encouraging the movement and profiting from its failure.

causes.note: The prophecy, with its promise that the dead would rise and the settlers be swept away, and its call to give up witchcraft, incest and adultery, is described in the article as a millenarian belief. It says that when the first predicted day, 18 February 1857, passed, Chief Sarhili announced a new day eight days later, and that this failed as well.

The article on the Cape Colony says lung sickness spread through the Xhosa cattle from 1854, after infected animals imported from the Netherlands in 1853, and caused widespread cattle deaths before the prophecy; the other article says many herds were suffering from it.

The article says historians see the movement as a millenarian response both to the cattle disease and to the stress of the continuing loss of Xhosa territory and autonomy; it quotes Peires that it broke “the dogged resistance to colonial expansion which the Xhosa had sustained for nearly eighty bitter years”. The “Chief’s Plot” account of the colonial administration is the opposing reading.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the articles give about 40,000 people starved to death by early 1858 and over 400,000 cattle killed, a fall in the population of British Kaffraria from 105,000 to under 27,000, and another 50,000 Xhosa who left to look for food and work in the Cape Colony.

outcome.note: The promised day passed without the dead rising, and the practices ended by early 1858. The followers, the article says, first blamed those who had not obeyed and then turned against Nongqawuse.

after.note: The article on the Cape Colony says Governor Grey’s administration confiscated land from several chiefdoms, imprisoned chiefs and set up labour contracts, as Peires emphasises, and that over two hundred farms of about 1,500 acres each were created for settlers. Nongqawuse was handed to a British officer, later lived on a farm in the Alexandria district and died in 1898; the valley where she said she met the spirits is still called the Valley of Nongqawuse.

entries.label: The Reform War in Mexico (the War of the Three Years)
entries.summary: From 1857 to 1861 Mexican liberals and conservatives fight a civil war over a constitution that cuts the powers and property of the Catholic Church. The Church had threatened excommunication for officials who swore to the constitution. The liberals win on the battlefield, and guerrillas then remain active in the countryside.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Reform War
sources.note: it reports the historians it names; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Constitution of 1857
sources.note: the text of the constitution was not opened

parties.name: The Liberals, who held the constitutional presidency under Benito Juárez
parties.said: The article says the liberal program, written into laws that went into the Constitution of 1857, aimed to limit the executive and the political, economic and cultural power of the Catholic Church: the sale of church property, the separation of church and state, the loss of army privileges and secular public education. On 4 December 1860, as the war turned, Juárez signed the Law for the Liberty of Religious Worship.

parties.name: The Conservatives, led by General Félix Zuloaga and later General Miguel Miramón
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says that Zuloaga’s Plan of Tacubaya of 17 December 1857 nullified the constitution, that conservatives and the Catholic Church were intensely opposed to its anti-clerical provisions, and that the Church decreed excommunication for anyone who took the oath to it.

causes.note: The constitution ended Catholicism as the official religion, set up secular public education, removed the legal privileges (fueros) of clergy and army, and forced the sale of church property. The Church decreed excommunication for those who took the oath to it, and the article says many Catholics in government lost their jobs rather than swear.

A fight over a federal constitution that limited the executive and the army. President Comonfort first agreed to the Plan of Tacubaya and then resigned on 11 January 1858; Juárez held the constitutional presidency, and the conservatives formed a rival government in the capital.

The Lerdo Law of 1856 forced the sale of most of the Church’s rural property, and also of the communal lands of indigenous peoples. On 12 July 1859 the liberal government nationalised church property, and the article says its sale gave the liberal war effort new funds.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives 8,713 casualties for the liberals, 11,355 for the conservatives and 70,000 in total, without saying whether these are dead or all casualties or how they were counted.

outcome.note: The liberals won: the conservative forces surrendered on 22 December 1860 and Juárez returned to Mexico City on 11 January 1861.

after.note: The article says guerrillas stayed active in the countryside and some joined the French intervention that set up the Second Mexican Empire, whose emperor, it says, ratified the Reform Laws; the liberal government fought on until the empire fell in 1867. It says the war left the nation’s infrastructure and finances in ruins.

entries.label: The Mahdist War in Sudan
entries.summary: In 1881 Muhammad Ahmad, a Sufi preacher, proclaims himself the Mahdi and leads a war against Egyptian rule in Sudan. His followers take Khartoum in 1885 and found a state that lasts until Anglo-Egyptian forces defeat it at Omdurman in 1898; the last organised resistance ends in 1899.

parties.name: Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself the Mahdi, and his followers, the Ansar
parties.also: Later led by the Khalifa Abdullahi; called Mahdists in English
parties.said: The articles say he preached renewal of the faith and the liberation of the land, claimed on 29 June 1881 to be the Mahdi, appointed by a prophetic assembly (hadra) in the Sufi tradition, and framed the Mahdiyya as a return to the early days of Islam. To the governor’s friendly letter he replied by telegram: “He who does not believe in me will be purified by the sword.”

parties.name: The Egyptian administration of Sudan, and later Britain with Egypt
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that the governor Rauf Pasha believed the Mahdi would be satisfied with a government pension and sent him a friendly letter, and that in August 1881 he sent two companies of infantry to arrest him, who were destroyed at Aba Island.

causes.note: The article lists among the forces seen as causes Muslim revivalist anger at the Egyptians’ lax religious standards and at their appointing non-Muslims such as the Christian Charles Gordon to high posts, and Sudanese Sufi resistance to the Islam of Egyptian officialdom.
Sudanese anger at foreign Egyptian rule, which was weakened when Egypt’s debts brought in foreign financial control and the forced abdication of its ruler in 1879.
Heavy taxation, forced labour and coercion under Turco-Egyptian rule, and the Egyptian abolition of the slave trade, a main source of income in Sudan.

casualties.unit: fall in Sudan’s population during Mahdist rule, from all causes
casualties.basis: A loss of more than half of Sudan’s people over the period of Mahdist rule, from fighting, famine, disease and flight together; it is not a count of those killed in battle.
casualties.note: The article attributes the estimate to Sir Reginald Wingate and says some contemporary academics consider these numbers exaggerated.

outcome.note: Anglo-Egyptian forces reconquered Sudan in 1898 and the Mahdist state collapsed after its defeat at Omdurman; the last organised resistance ended in 1899.

after.note: Sudan became Anglo-Egyptian Sudan (1899–1956), under de facto British control. The Mahdi’s tomb was destroyed in 1898 so that it would not become a rallying point; it was later rebuilt, and one of his descendants, Sadiq al-Mahdi, twice served as prime minister of Sudan.

entries.label: Religious conflict at the court of Buganda, 1885–1892
entries.summary: Between 1885 and 1892 the court of the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, is the scene of a three-way struggle among Catholic, Anglican and Muslim followers. The king, Mwanga II, has converts to Christianity executed in 1885 and 1886, factions of the three faiths depose and restore kings in civil wars from 1888, and in 1892 fighting between Catholics and Protestants ends in a treaty that gives each its own area. The article says the reasons for the executions are still heavily debated.

sources.title: Wikipedia: the article on the converts executed in Buganda in 1885–1887
sources.note: the article’s own title uses the name by which the Catholic and Anglican churches honour them; it quotes the historians Behrend, Ward, Oliver and others, none of whom was opened

parties.name: Kabaka Mwanga II and the older chiefs of his court
parties.said: The article says the French missionary Lourdel, who was a witness, held that the main cause of the executions was Mwanga’s feeling of being despised by the literate Christians who claimed a superior knowledge of religion, with the refusal of the court pages to meet the king’s sexual demands as a secondary cause. The article on Mwanga says his father had balanced Catholics, Protestants and Muslims against each other, and that Mwanga saw the missionaries as the greatest threat to his rule.

parties.name: The Christian converts at the court, Catholic and Anglican, among them pages and chiefs
parties.said: The article says twenty-two converts to Catholicism were burned alive at Namugongo in 1886, that some who gave up their faith were spared, and that the converts, at least the Catholics, had been taught that they risked death for their faith. It records that Matthias Gayinga rejected the sexual demands of a friend of the king and was punished but not killed, and that Anatole Kirrigwajjo declined a high post that he could hold, he said, only at the peril of his soul.

parties.name: The Muslim party at court, whose faith came with Arab traders from Zanzibar
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says that in October 1888 the Muslims seized power, expelled the Christian leaders, and deposed and killed the king Kiweewa when he refused to be circumcised, putting Kalema in his place; they were beaten in February 1890 and withdrew to Bunyoro.

causes.note: The article quotes Heike Behrend: “The reasons behind the persecution are still heavily debated.” It sets out views that the king resented literate Christians (Lourdel), that the converts were seen as rebels and tools of foreign imperialism (Ward), that the refusal of the pages was the immediate pretext (Kiewet-Hemphill, Thoonen), and Roland Oliver’s objection that resentment of Christianity does not explain why chiefs and women among the converts were not attacked.

A three-way struggle for political influence at court among the Anglican, Catholic and Muslim parties, during the Scramble for Africa. The article says the killing of the Anglican bishop James Hannington on the king’s orders in October 1885 may have been meant to tell the British that he did not want them to make inroads, and that the killing of young converts also served the older chiefs, who were jealous of their rise.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article names 22 Catholic and 23 Anglican converts as executed between 31 January 1885 and 27 January 1887, and gives no figure for the dead of the civil wars of 1888 to 1892.

outcome.note: After fighting at Mengo in January 1892, in which the company’s agent Lugard supported the Protestants and Mwanga and the Catholics had to flee, a treaty of 30 March 1892 assigned separate areas to the Protestants (the largest), the Catholics and, a small one, the Muslims, and Mwanga nominally became a Protestant.

after.note: The article says the Church Missionary Society used the deaths to win public support in Britain for acquiring Uganda, that Buganda became a British protectorate in 1894, and that Mwanga declared war on Britain in 1897, was defeated, and was exiled to the Seychelles, where he was received into the Anglican Church. It says the Catholic Church beatified the twenty-two Catholic converts in 1920 and canonised them in 1964.

entries.label: The Ghost Dance and the killings at Wounded Knee Creek
entries.summary: In 1890 the Ghost Dance, a Native American religious movement founded on the teaching of the Paiute prophet Wovoka, spreads among the Lakota at a time of lost land, hunger and cut rations. On 29 December, during an attempt to disarm Spotted Elk’s band at Wounded Knee Creek, soldiers of the 7th Cavalry and the Lakota fight, and many Lakota, most of them women and children, are killed.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Wounded Knee, the article on the events of 29 December 1890

parties.name: The Lakota who took up the Ghost Dance, among them Spotted Elk’s band of Miniconjou
parties.said: The first article says Wovoka taught that the white settlers would disappear from Native lands, the ancestors would lead the people to good hunting grounds, the buffalo would return, and the dead would come back, all through the slow, silent performance of the dance; by 1890 nearly a third of the Lakota had taken it up. It says the dance was not a break with Lakota faith but a way to revive it, and that Kicking Bear taught that the dance shirts would turn bullets, which the article says he misunderstood.

parties.name: The United States government and the Army, among them the 7th Cavalry
parties.said: The second article quotes the government’s aim in breaking up the Great Sioux Reservation in 1890: to “break up tribal relationships” and “conform Indians to the white man’s ways, peaceably if they will, or forcibly if they must”. It says Army officers put Spotted Elk, who was on its list of ‘trouble-making’ Indians, under watch and tried to collect the weapons of his band.

causes.note: The spread of the Ghost Dance among the Lakota: the second article says it was not only a religious movement but a response to the gradual loss of the Native way of life, and that it found its place within the largely non-doctrinal framework of Lakota religion.

The great bison herds had been hunted almost out of existence, treaty promises were not kept, farming failed on the reduced reservations, and in 1890 rations were cut by half, leaving the Lakota at risk of starvation.

In February 1890 the government broke the Great Sioux Reservation into five smaller ones, against a treaty, to make room for white homesteaders, with a policy of assimilation by schooling in English and Christianity.

casualties.unit: Lakota killed at Wounded Knee Creek on 29 December 1890
casualties.basis: Lakota men, women and children killed in the fighting and its aftermath at the camp, apart from those who died later of wounds.
casualties.note: The first article’s opening gives 250 to 300 Lakota killed and 51 wounded, and 25 soldiers killed and 39 wounded, six of whom died later; its infobox gives 90 killed and 4 wounded, and 200 civilians killed and 46 wounded. The second article says 200 to 300 Lakota were killed, most of them women and children, and that many of the 25 soldiers killed died from their own side’s fire.

outcome.note: The fighting came when a Lakota man refused to give up his rifle and a weapon went off, after which an officer gave the order to fire and the Army used rifles and rapid-fire Hotchkiss guns; Kicking Bear surrendered his weapon to General Nelson Miles afterwards, ending the Pine Ridge Campaign.

after.note: The first article says nineteen soldiers received the Medal of Honor for Wounded Knee, and thirty-one for the campaign as a whole; it has sections on the commemoration of the Lakota dead.

entries.label: The War of Canudos
entries.summary: A religious community led by the preacher Antônio Conselheiro settles at Canudos in the backlands of Bahia and is attacked by four military expeditions of the young Brazilian Republic, which sees it as a monarchist threat. The settlement is destroyed in October 1897. Historians differ widely on how many died.

sources.title: Wikipedia: War of Canudos
sources.note: it reports Euclides da Cunha, Peter Robb and the other historians named; none was opened

parties.name: Antônio Conselheiro and the people of Canudos, who called their settlement Belo Monte
parties.also: Called the Conselheiristas; the press called them monarchists
parties.said: The article says Conselheiro claimed to be a prophet and predicted the return of the Portuguese king Sebastian, held that it was the monarch’s God-given right to rule, and preached an ultra-conservative doctrine that implicitly criticised the behaviour of many priests. The settlement was supported by farming and the leather trade, and the poor were kept by donations.

parties.name: The Brazilian Republic: the federal army and the government of Bahia
parties.said: The article says the press branded the Conselheiristas monarchists, that rumours spread that they planned to “depose the new Republican government” and “restore the monarchy”, and that the authorities saw the settlement as a threat to the Republic. Walnice Nogueira Galvão, it adds, holds that the peasants had no connection with real monarchists.

causes.note: Conselheiro’s preaching and prophecy drew thousands to Canudos, and, the article says, the Church hierarchy saw him as a threat to its authority and popularity.
The young Republic feared a monarchist restoration; Galvão holds that the fear was unfounded and that the war consolidated the republican government.
Poverty, repeated drought, and, for the people of the sertão, a Republic that brought them “only an increase in taxes”; local landowners were hostile to Conselheiro’s following.

casualties.basis: Those who died in the four expeditions and the final destruction of Canudos, residents and attackers together.
casualties.note: The article gives Joel Singer’s 5,000 as the lowest estimate, Robert Levine’s about 15,000 between, and Euclides da Cunha’s about 30,000 (25,000 residents and 5,000 attackers, 1902) as the highest. Peter Robb notes that da Cunha saw only the aftermath.

outcome.note: The fourth expedition destroyed Canudos in October 1897; Conselheiro had probably died of dysentery on 22 September, and only about 150 survivors remained.

after.note: Galvão writes that the war consolidated the republican government and ended the fear of a monarchist restoration, and that the military made a practice of tying up prisoners and beheading them; the article adds that public opinion later turned against the conduct of the war.

entries.label: The Boxer Uprising in North China
entries.summary: From 1899 to 1901 villagers in North China, in a society called the Righteous and Harmonious Fists and known in English as Boxers, attack missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreign property, and in 1900 the Qing court backs them against an eight-nation foreign force. The force relieves the besieged legations in Beijing and occupies the region for more than a year, and the war ends with the Boxer Protocol of 1901. Historians dispute whether to call it a rebellion, an uprising, a movement or a war.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Boxer Rebellion
sources.note: it reports the historians and eyewitnesses it names, and says some eyewitness accounts have recently been questioned; none was opened

parties.name: The Boxers, the Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, and from June 1900 the Qing court under the Empress Dowager Cixi
parties.said: The article gives the Boxers’ slogan as “Support the Qing government and destroy the foreigners”, and quotes the historian Joseph Esherick that “foreign” meant the foreign religion, Christianity, and its Chinese converts as much as the foreigners themselves. It says the imperial edict of 21 June 1900 told the army to join the Boxers, a de facto declaration of war, and that officials in the southern provinces ignored it.

parties.name: The Eight-Nation Alliance of American, Austro-Hungarian, British, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Russian troops, with the foreign legations, missionaries and Chinese Christians
parties.said: The article on the alliance says its stated aim was to relieve the legations besieged in Beijing, that neither side issued a formal declaration of war, and that the later stages developed into a punitive colonial expedition that looted Beijing and North China for more than a year. The other article says the allies argued China had broken rules of war that they themselves ignored.

causes.note: The article calls missionary activity a major source of discontent in the north. The treaties of 1860 let missionaries preach anywhere in China and buy land for churches, and it says there was strong public indignation when Chinese temples were replaced by Catholic churches, seen as built against feng shui; some linked the drought to church placement and to Christians not worshipping local deities.

Anti-imperialist feeling in the scramble for concessions after the First Sino-Japanese War, including the German occupation of Jiaozhou Bay after the Juye Incident of 1897, when two missionaries were killed. The article says the Qing government shifted to support the Boxers after it refused to concede in the Sanmen Bay affair, and the other article says the attack on the Taku Forts in June 1900 pushed it further.

Drought followed by floods in Shandong in 1897 and 1898, imported foreign cotton that hurt the local cotton economy, a falling traffic on the Grand Canal, and the destruction of burial sites for German railways and telegraph lines.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s infobox gives 100,000 deaths in all, including 32,000 Chinese Christians and 200 Western missionaries in northern China. A section on the killing of Christians estimates 136 Protestant missionaries, 53 of their children, 47 Catholic priests and nuns, 30,000 Chinese Catholics, 2,000 Chinese Protestants and 200 to 400 Russian Orthodox Christians killed, and says Yuan Shikai’s forces killed tens of thousands in the campaign against the Boxers.

outcome.note: The Qing court signed the Boxer Protocol on 7 September 1901. It ordered the execution of ten high-ranking officials and set an indemnity of 450,000,000 taels of silver, to be paid by 1940; the article says that with interest it came to 982,238,150 taels and that China paid 668,661,220 taels between 1901 and 1939.

after.note: The article says that in punitive expeditions from September 1900 to March 1901 European and American forces carried out public beheadings of suspected Boxer sympathisers, looting, the destruction of religious buildings and the burning of religious texts, and widespread rape, and that British and American observers criticised German, Russian and Japanese troops most. It adds that part of the American share of the indemnity went to educate Chinese students in the United States, and that the China Inland Mission’s Hudson Taylor refused compensation for its losses.

entries.label: The Maji Maji Rebellion in German East Africa

places.name: The Matumbi Hills, in Kilwa district

entries.summary: From July 1905 to 1907 Africans of German East Africa, in what is now Tanzania, rise against German colonial rule, which had imposed taxes, forced labour and a cotton quota on villages. A spirit medium, Kinjikitile Ngwale, gave followers water mixed with castor oil and millet, called maji, said to turn German bullets to water. Historians differ on how far religion, rather than grievance over colonial policy, drove the rising.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Maji Maji Rebellion
sources.note: it reports the historians it names (Iliffe, Haustein, Sunseri and others); none was opened

parties.name: The Maji Maji insurgents: the Matumbi, Ngindo, Yao, Ngoni and other peoples, following the spirit medium Kinjikitile Ngwale, called Bokero, and later leaders
parties.said: The article says Kinjikitile, who practised a folk Islam with animist elements, claimed to be possessed by a snake spirit, Hongo, and told his followers that their ancestors had commanded a rebellion; German anthropologists recorded that he gave them war medicine that would turn German bullets into water. After a defeat in October 1905 the Ngoni threw away their bottles of it, crying “The maji is a lie!”

parties.name: The German colonial government of German East Africa, under Governor Gustav Adolf von Götzen
parties.said: The article says Götzen set up an inquiry after the rebellion whose members divided between those who saw an irrational movement spawned by sorcerers and headmen using maji, and those who stressed the burdens of German administration, and that his circle fostered the image of a superstitious movement. It quotes John Iliffe that Götzen’s 1909 history of the rebellion makes no reference to the cotton scheme he had started.

causes.note: The article says Germany levied head taxes from 1898 and relied on forced labour, and that in 1902 Götzen ordered villages to grow cotton for export on a quota, though cotton’s need for water made it impossible to grow in most of the country; forest and wildlife protection laws added hardship, as wild pigs damaged crops, and drought threatened the region in 1905.

The insurgents turned to war medicine as a unifying force. The article says later historians challenge the view of a single movement and see a series of revolts for many reasons, religion among them; on Islam it quotes Jörg Haustein’s conclusion that the claim that Islam was a factor is not warranted by the sources, and it quotes John Iliffe, who sees a movement that began in peasant grievances and was sanctified and extended by prophetic religion.

Opposition to the colonial government’s agricultural and labour policies and to its violently repressive methods. The article says Tanzanian nationalists later used the rebellion as an example of unity against foreign rule, a view that other historians have challenged.

casualties.unit: dead of famine, disease and violence
casualties.basis: Deaths during the rebellion and the famine that followed it, overwhelmingly from famine.
casualties.note: The first article gives 75,000 to 300,000, the second says over 100,000 or 200,000 to 300,000. It says the famine that followed, the Great Hunger, was caused in large part by the scorched-earth methods used to put down the rising, which scholars have described as “genocidal”. German-side losses are given as 15 Germans, 73 African soldiers (askari) and 316 auxiliaries (ruga ruga).

outcome.note: The article’s infobox gives a German victory, with the fighting ending in 1907. It says the war was followed by the famine and that, afterwards, the imperial government made administrative reforms under Governor Albrecht von Rechenberg.

after.note: The article says the rebellion became a focal point in the history of the region, that Tanzanian nationalists later claimed it as a first stirring of national unity, and the article on Kinjikitile says he, hanged for treason on 4 August 1905, is regarded by present-day Tanzanians as a proto-national hero.

entries.label: The Contestado War in southern Brazil

places.name: Irani, on the disputed border of Paraná and Santa Catarina

entries.summary: From 1912 to 1916 settlers and poor farmers in the Contestado, a disputed border region of southern Brazil, many of them followers of a healer called the “holy monk”, fight state police and the federal army in a war that begins over land. The rebels came to believe they were fighting a holy war for a heavenly monarchy, and the sources also tie the war to their poverty. Between ten and twenty thousand people are estimated to have died.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Contestado War
sources.note: it reports General Estillac’s own report; none of the historians it names was opened

sources.title: Portuguese Wikipedia: Guerra do Contestado
sources.note: in Portuguese; some of its passages carry the tag “needs sources”, and none of those was used

parties.name: The caboclos, settlers and small farmers of the Contestado, followers of the monk José Maria and then of leaders such as Adeodato
parties.said: The English article says José Maria declared the Republic of Brazil “the devil’s law”, set up a community with its own government and a guard of twelve men, and that his followers founded villages, each with a patron saint, in hope of a “heavenly monarchy”. The Portuguese article says they believed he would rise again with an “enchanted army” to help bring the republic down.

parties.name: The federal government of Brazil, the police and troops of Paraná and Santa Catarina, and the landowners and their armed men
parties.said: The English article quotes the report of General Estillac after the assault on Santa Maria on 5 April 1915: “everything was destroyed”, with an estimated 5,000 houses razed and over 600 irregulars killed, and the mission “entrusted to the Army is now accomplished”. The Portuguese article says the federal government saw signs of an insurrection in the movement and sent troops to put it down.

causes.note: Land: the Portuguese article says a strip of land was cleared for a railway built by an American company, which drove out settlers and ruined small timber growers, and that when the work finished many railway workers were left without work. The English article calls the war a guerrilla war for land between settlers and landowners, backed by the state’s police and army.

Both articles say the rebels believed they were fighting a holy war, which the Portuguese article says heightened their spirits for the fight; the English article adds that the war also reflected dissatisfaction with their material situation. How far the war was one of religion, and how far of land and poverty, is not settled in the sources read.

The region was contested by Paraná, Santa Catarina and Argentina, which gave the war its name, and José Maria’s preaching was monarchist and opposed to the republic founded in 1889. A fight at Irani on 22 October 1912, in which the Portuguese article says eleven of his followers, including José Maria, and ten soldiers died, is named as the start of the war.

casualties.unit: dead, in combat, of hunger and of epidemics, civilians included
casualties.basis: Deaths in combat, of hunger and of epidemics in a district of about 40,000 people.
casualties.note: Both articles give 10,000 to 20,000, without saying who counted. The English infobox gives 5,000 to 8,000 dead, wounded or missing among the rebels and 800 to 1,000 on the government side, and the Portuguese opening says about 8,000 of the rebels died.

outcome.note: General Setembrino de Carvalho, the articles say, avoided direct battle, surrounded the rebel strongholds and cut off food; the last of the villages was destroyed in December 1915, and the war ended with the arrest of Adeodato in August 1916. In October 1916 the governors of the two states signed an agreement on their boundary; the two articles give it different days.

after.note: Adeodato was sentenced to 30 years in prison and killed in 1923 by the jail warden in what the English article calls an alleged escape attempt. The Portuguese article lists later events: a popular rising in the Paraná part of the contested area in 1917, final approval of the boundary agreement in August 1917, and a revolt of caboclos against land surveys in 1921.

entries.label: The Cristero War
entries.summary: A rural Catholic uprising in west-central Mexico against the government of President Calles, who enforced the anticlerical articles of the 1917 Constitution through the Calles Law of 1926. It ended in 1929 in an agreement brokered by the United States ambassador; resistance and repression went on for years. Estimates of the dead differ widely.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Cristero War
sources.note: it cites the journal and the historians behind its figures; none was opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Calles Law
sources.note: the text of the law was not opened

parties.name: The Mexican government under President Plutarco Elías Calles, and then President Emilio Portes Gil
parties.said: The article says Calles’s administration believed the Church was challenging its revolutionary programme and its legal basis, and resolved to enforce the Constitution’s secularist articles strictly. The Law for Reforming the Penal Code, signed in June 1926, set penalties for priests and others who broke Article 130: a fine of 500 pesos for wearing clerical dress in public, and up to five years in prison for a priest who criticised the government. Calles also backed a national Mexican Catholic Apostolic Church in 1925, which accepted the Constitution.

parties.name: The Cristeros, with the National League for the Defense of Religious Liberty and Catholic supporters
parties.also: Named for the cry of Cristo Rey, Christ the King
parties.said: The article says the rising was a response to the enforcement of Article 130 through the Calles Law, and that the Church hierarchy tacitly supported it; it records that on 3 August 1926 about 400 armed Catholics shut themselves in a church in Guadalajara and exchanged fire with federal troops until their ammunition ran out. The Calles Law article says the Church saw the law as a trap meant to bend the Church to the state.

causes.note: The Constitution of 1917 and the Calles Law restricted the Church and its clergy, and the rising was a response to their enforcement; the article says Calles sought to limit the Church’s power and to suppress popular religious practice.
A struggle between church and state that the article traces back to the War of Reform in the nineteenth century, sharpened by the Mexican Revolution and by Calles’s strict enforcement.

The article says the rebellion has been read both as a major episode in the struggle between church and state and as the last major peasant uprising in Mexico after the military phase of the Revolution.

casualties.basis: The lower figure counts the dead of the war itself: about 56,882 federal soldiers, about 30,000 Cristeros and some others; the higher is an estimate that includes civilians.
casualties.note: The article’s text gives “some 90,000”; its infobox gives 56,882 federal dead, 30,000 to 50,000 Cristero dead and an estimated 250,000 including civilians, from a journal it cites without naming who counted. It adds that after the 1929 truce the government executed some 500 Cristero leaders and 5,000 other Cristeros.

outcome.note: Ended on 21 June 1929 by the arreglos, an agreement between the government and Church representatives mediated by the American ambassador Dwight Morrow: the government granted amnesty to Cristeros who laid down their arms and the Church withdrew its support for the fighters. The Calles Law stayed on the books, though the federal government made no organised attempt to enforce it.

after.note: The article says the government often did not keep the terms of the truce, that at least 40 priests were killed between 1926 and 1934, that 4,500 priests had served before the rising and only 334 were licensed in 1934, and that many Cristeros fled to the United States. President Cárdenas and Congress condemned the military persecution of the Cristeros in 1935, and bans on the Church’s anticlerical laws were no longer enforced under President Ávila Camacho from 1940.

entries.label: The arreglos that ended the Cristero War
entries.summary: On 21 June 1929 the Mexican government and representatives of the Catholic Church, with the American ambassador Dwight Morrow as mediator, reach the arreglos that end the Cristero War: the government gives amnesty to those who lay down their arms and the Church withdraws its support for the fighters.

parties.name: The Mexican government under President Emilio Portes Gil
parties.said: The article says the government made some concessions and granted amnesty to Cristero combatants who laid down their arms, and that, as Portes Gil had promised, the Calles Law remained on the books while the federal government made no organised attempt to enforce it.

parties.name: Representatives of the Mexican Catholic Church
parties.said: The article says the Church withdrew its support for the Cristero fighters. The Calles Law article says the Church had seen that law as a trap meant to bend the Church to the state.

parties.name: The United States ambassador Dwight W. Morrow, as mediator
parties.said: No statement of his is quoted in the sources read; the article says he brokered the negotiations between the Calles government and the Church.

causes.note: The Calles Law and the constitutional articles on the Church, which the rising had been fought against.
The government and the Church each had reasons to end the fighting; the article names the American ambassador’s mediation as decisive in bringing them to terms.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the war it ended are given in the entry for the Cristero War.

outcome.note: Amnesty for Cristeros who laid down their arms, and the Church’s withdrawal of support; the Calles Law was left in force but not organisedly enforced by the federal government.

after.note: The article says the government often did not keep the terms: it executed some 500 Cristero leaders and 5,000 other Cristeros, and bans on the Church’s anticlerical laws were no longer enforced anywhere in Mexico only under President Ávila Camacho from 1940.

entries.label: The Partition of India (1947)
entries.summary: In August 1947 British India is divided into two states, India and Pakistan, on lines drawn between districts with mostly Muslim and mostly non-Muslim (Hindu and Sikh) populations. Millions of people cross the new borders, and there is large-scale violence between Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs. Estimates of the dead differ widely. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Partition of India
sources.note: it reports Yasmin Khan and the other historians named; none was opened

parties.name: The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, which demanded a separate Pakistan
parties.said: The article reports that in July 1946 Jinnah said that if Muslims were not granted a separate Pakistan they would take “direct action”, and that he announced 16 August 1946 as Direct Action Day, warning Congress: “We do not want war. If you want war we accept your offer unhesitatingly. We will either have a divided India or a destroyed India.” The two-nation theory, as the article describes it, held that Indian Hindus and Muslims were two distinct nations, because religion produced cultural and social differences.

parties.name: The Indian National Congress, and Hindu and Sikh organisations and leaders
parties.said: No statement of the Congress is quoted in the sources read. The article records that the Hindu nationalist Vinayak Savarkar set out an early form of two-nation thinking in 1923 and that the Arya Samaj leader Lala Lajpat Rai wrote in 1924 for a “clear partition of India into a Muslim India and a non-Muslim India”, after riots against Hindus in Kohat.

parties.name: The British government and the last viceroy, Lord Mountbatten
parties.said: The article says Mountbatten was told to avoid partition and preserve a united India, but that the tense communal situation led him to conclude that partition had become necessary for a quicker transfer of power; the partition was set out in the Indian Independence Act 1947.

causes.note: The demand for Pakistan rested, in the article’s account, on the claim that Hindus and Muslims were separate nations because of religion; the article also records Hindu-Muslim violence before the partition, as in the Calcutta killings of August 1946, in which about 4,000 died by official accounts.
The end of British rule and the division of powers: the partition was set out in the Indian Independence Act 1947, with the princely states left to join India or Pakistan or stay independent.

casualties.unit: deaths in the violence of the partition
casualties.basis: People killed in the communal violence before, during and after the partition; the article says the number is disputed and that it displaced between 12 and 20 million people along religious lines.
casualties.note: The article’s infobox gives 200,000 to 2 million; the sources read do not say who proposed each end.

outcome.note: The Indian Independence Act 1947 divided British India into the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan, which came into being at midnight on 14–15 August 1947, with Bengal and the Punjab divided by district according to non-Muslim or Muslim majorities.

after.note: A pact signed at New Delhi on 8 April 1950 by the prime ministers of India and Pakistan confirmed minority rights, let refugees return to dispose of their property, and set up minority commissions; more than a million refugees moved from East Pakistan to West Bengal after the partition.

entries.label: La Violencia in Colombia

places.name: Santa Rosa de Osos, seat of a diocese named in the sources

entries.summary: From 1948 to 1958 a civil conflict between the Conservative and Liberal parties, mostly fought in the countryside, kills at least two hundred thousand people in Colombia. It is held to begin with the assassination of the Liberal candidate Jorge Eliécer Gaitán on 9 April 1948. Reports that Catholic Church authorities backed the Conservatives, and anticlerical attacks on priests and churches, are part of the record. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: La Violencia
sources.note: it says documented evidence from these years is rare and fragmentary, and it reports two books of the early 1950s; neither was opened

parties.name: The Conservative Party, the government, the army and police, and Conservative-supporting paramilitary groups
