parties.said: The article says that in one account local police and political leaders encouraged Conservative peasants to seize the lands of Liberal peasants after the Conservatives returned to power in 1946. It says Conservative politicians and churchmen had taken from Europe what it calls a Judeo-Masonic conspiracy theory, portraying the Liberal Party as part of an international anti-Christian plot, which moved some Conservatives to try to eliminate the Liberals among them.

parties.name: The Liberal Party and the Liberal- and Communist-aligned guerrilla and paramilitary groups
parties.said: The article says that after Gaitán’s death a conspiracy theory circulated on the left that leading Conservatives, militant priests, Nazis and Falangists were plotting to take over the country, and that it gave radical Liberals a reason for violence, among it attacks on churches, convents and monasteries in which priests were killed by militants looking for arms; it says no serviceable weapons were found.

parties.name: The Catholic Church authorities, among them Bishop Miguel Ángel Builes of Santa Rosa de Osos
parties.said: The article says that press reports at the time said the Church authorities supported the Conservative Party, and that several priests, among them Bishop Builes, were accused of encouraging the murder of the opposition during mass, which it calls unproven, with no formal charges and no official statement from the Holy See or the bishops. It says a priest’s book of 1950 recounted such events and that its author was prosecuted for libel by the Conservative Party.

causes.note: The conflict was between the Conservative and Liberal parties and is held to begin with the assassination of Gaitán on 9 April 1948 and the Bogotazo rioting that followed. The article says an alternative historiography places the cause in the Conservatives’ return to power after the election of 1946.

The article says the majority of the population was Catholic, that reports of Church support for the Conservatives are unproven, that anticlerical attacks took place, and that both sides held conspiracy theories with a religious colour; how far religion drove the conflict is not measured in the sources read.

Land: the article says seizures of the agricultural lands of Liberal peasants provoked peasant-to-peasant violence throughout Colombia, and that the conflict caused millions of people to abandon their homes and property.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article says La Violencia is estimated to have killed at least 200,000 people, almost one in fifty Colombians, and that the Bogotazo rioting of 9 April 1948 left about 5,000 casualties. Its infobox gives 2,900 soldiers and 1,800 police dead from 1948 to 1957, 3,000 to 5,000 Conservative paramilitaries dead and 15,000 rebels dead.

outcome.note: Most armed groups demobilised under an amnesty declared by General Rojas Pinilla after he took power in June 1953. After his fall in May 1957 the Liberal and Conservative parties made a series of pacts, accepted by referendum on 1 December 1957, creating a National Front of 16 years in which the presidency alternated between the parties. In 1958 President Lleras Camargo created a commission on the causes of La Violencia, headed by Bishop Germán Guzmán Campos.

after.note: The article says the end of La Violencia was not the end of all violence in Colombia: a communist guerrilla movement began in 1959, and the article on the National Front says the FARC began in 1964 and the ELN in 1965. It says the National Front reduced the polarisation of party members, and that by 1970 the share of people identifying with either party had fallen by 70 per cent.

entries.label: The Liaquat–Nehru Pact on minorities (1950)
entries.summary: On 8 April 1950 the prime ministers of India and Pakistan, Jawaharlal Nehru and Liaquat Ali Khan, sign a pact after six days of talks to guarantee the rights of minorities in both countries after the Partition and to avert another war. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Liaquat–Nehru Pact
sources.note: a short article; the text of the pact was not opened

parties.name: Jawaharlal Nehru, prime minister of India
parties.said: No statement of his is quoted in the sources read. The article records what the pact provided for: refugees allowed to return to dispose of their property, abducted women and looted property to be returned, forced conversions not recognised, and minority rights confirmed.

parties.name: Liaquat Ali Khan, prime minister of Pakistan
parties.said: No statement of his is quoted in the sources read. The article says the pact, which he signed with Nehru, was the outcome of six days of talks sought to guarantee the rights of minorities in both countries and to avert another war between them.

causes.note: The pact dealt with the position of religious minorities in each country, with the return of abducted women, and with forced conversions, which it declared unrecognised.
Its stated aims were the protection of minority rights and the avoidance of another war between India and Pakistan.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the violence of the Partition are given in its own entry, with the disputed range.

outcome.note: A bilateral treaty signed at New Delhi on 8 April 1950; it also brought in a visa system for refugees, restricted free passage across the border and set up minority commissions in both countries.

after.note: The article says more than one million refugees migrated from East Pakistan, now Bangladesh, to West Bengal in India, and the other article describes displacement of between 12 and 20 million people at the Partition.

entries.label: The Nigerian Civil War (the Biafran War)
entries.summary: In 1967 the Eastern Region of Nigeria, mostly Igbo and mostly Christian, declares itself the independent Republic of Biafra after military coups and the killing of many Igbo in the Muslim-majority north in 1966. The federal government fights to bring it back; the war ends in January 1970 with Biafra’s surrender, after a famine. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Nigerian Civil War
sources.note: it reports Gowon, Azikiwe, the scholars named and the relief organisations; none was opened

parties.name: The federal government of Nigeria, under General Yakubu Gowon
parties.said: On the war’s end Gowon said, the article reports: “The tragic chapter of violence is just ended. We are at the dawn of national reconciliation.” Critics of the view that the war was aimed at the Igbo as a people, the article says, hold that Nigeria was fighting to keep control of Biafra and its people rather than to expel or destroy them.

parties.name: The Republic of Biafra, under Lieutenant Colonel Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu
parties.said: The article says that after the killings and the flight of Igbo from the north, the leaders of the Eastern Region concluded that the federal government could not or would not protect the Igbo, and that an independent Biafra, declared on 30 May 1967, was the only way to secure them. It records that Biafra complained to a Paris-based group of international lawyers, which concluded that the federal government’s actions amounted to the crime of destroying a people.

causes.note: The article says the conflict came from political, ethnic, cultural and religious tensions, between the north, whose Hausa-Fulani people were ruled by a Muslim hierarchy, and the Igbo of the east, who overwhelmingly became Christian; it notes that world Christian organisations took up the Biafran cause, aware that the Biafrans were Christian and the northern rulers of the federal government Muslim. It names ethnicity and political power first.
The military coups and counter-coup of 1966, and the killing of an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 Igbo in the north that year, which sent more than a million Igbo to the east and led the east to secede.
The article says competition for political and economic power increased the tensions, and has a section on the fight for control of the oil-producing areas.

casualties.unit: dead, mostly Biafran civilians, most of them from starvation
casualties.basis: People who died in the war and in the famine caused by the blockade of the Eastern Region, with 45,000 to 100,000 of them combatants killed.
casualties.note: The article’s infobox gives 500,000 to 3 million Biafran civilians and says modern experts put the toll between 500,000 and one million from famine and fighting; it does not say who gave the three million. Whether the war and the killings of 1966 amount to the deliberate destruction of the Igbo people is argued: Herbert Ekwe-Ekwe and other academics say they do; critics accept that starvation policies were pursued deliberately but dispute the intent.

outcome.note: Federal forces launched a final offensive in December 1969 and January 1970; Ojukwu went into exile, and his deputy signed the surrender at Lagos on 14 January 1970, ending the secession.

after.note: Gowon spoke of national reconciliation; the other article has a section on later Igbo and Biafran nationalism. The article records that relief reached Biafra by an airlift organised by volunteer and church bodies.

entries.label: The Troubles in Northern Ireland
entries.summary: From the late 1960s to 1998, Northern Ireland is divided by a conflict between unionists and loyalists, mostly Protestants, who want it to stay in the United Kingdom, and nationalists and republicans, mostly Catholics, who want a united Ireland. Paramilitary groups on both sides and the British state take part. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 is usually taken as its end. Whether religion was a cause or only a marker of the two communities is argued.

sources.title: Wikipedia: The Troubles
sources.note: it reports the books and studies it names; none was opened

sources.title: Malcolm Sutton, An Index of Deaths from the Conflict in Ireland (revised extracts: introduction and statistical summary), CAIN, Ulster University
sources.note: a compiled index naming each death; the author is a private researcher whose figures CAIN publishes by permission

parties.name: Unionists and loyalists, mostly Ulster Protestants, with loyalist paramilitary groups
parties.said: The article says they wanted Northern Ireland to remain in the United Kingdom, and that loyalists opposed the civil rights campaign in the belief that it was a front for republican activity. It records that on 21 May 1966 the Ulster Volunteer Force issued a statement declaring “war” against the IRA and anyone helping it.

parties.name: Nationalists and republicans, mostly Irish Catholics, with republican paramilitary groups
parties.said: The article says they wanted Northern Ireland to join a united Ireland, and that a non-violent civil rights campaign, which included the Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, sought an end to discrimination against the Catholic and nationalist minority. Republican paramilitary groups, among them the Provisional IRA and the INLA, carried on guerrilla and bombing campaigns.

parties.name: The British state: the British Army and the Royal Ulster Constabulary, with Irish security forces
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that the government tried to suppress the civil rights protests, that the police were criticised for sectarianism and for their handling of the protests, and that British troops were sent in after the riots of August 1969, in what became the army’s longest operation.

causes.note: The constitutional status of Northern Ireland, whether to stay in the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland, was the stated aim of each side and the matter on which the Good Friday Agreement of 1998 rests.

The article calls it an ethno-nationalist conflict with a strong ethnic and sectarian dimension, between communities divided by religion, and says that despite the division between Protestants and Catholics it was not a religious war.

casualties.unit: people killed as a result of the conflict
casualties.basis: Two compilations that name each person: Sutton’s index in CAIN counts 3,532 deaths from 1969 to 2001; the book Lost Lives, in its 2006 edition, counts 3,720 from 1966 to 2006.
casualties.note: Sutton’s index attributes 2,058 of its deaths to republican paramilitary groups, 1,027 to loyalist groups, 371 to British forces (366) and the Irish Republic’s forces (5), and leaves 76 not attributed; for most years it gives the counts by group. The article gives a third breakdown of 3,466 deaths, of them 3,218 in Northern Ireland, 125 in Great Britain, 105 in the Republic of Ireland and 18 elsewhere in Europe, and says 107,000 people were estimated to have been physically injured.

outcome.note: The Good Friday Agreement of 10 April 1998 is usually taken as the end of the conflict. The article lists, as the results, a military stalemate, the Agreement and the St Andrews Agreement of 2006, the withdrawal of British forces from Operation Banner and the disarmament of paramilitary groups, and continuing sporadic violence.

after.note: The article says some walls built to separate the communities remain, and that some researchers see the legacy of the Troubles as still shaping life in Northern Ireland more than twenty years after the Agreement, with inequality and division between Catholics and Protestants continuing.

entries.label: The Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 in Sudan
entries.summary: In 1972 the government of Sudan and the Southern Sudan Liberation Movement sign an agreement at Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, that ends the First Sudanese Civil War and gives the south regional autonomy. Talks had gone through the All Africa Conference of Churches and the World Council of Churches, and the negotiations were moderated by the first body’s Secretary General. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Addis Ababa Agreement (1972)
sources.note: a short article; the text of the agreement was not opened

parties.name: The government of Sudan under President Gaafar Nimeiry, with a delegation led by Abel Alier
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the war says that before it the northern elite held two common explanations: that it was left over from southern grievances against British rule, or that it was an attempt by southern insurgents to challenge the government.

parties.name: The Southern Sudan Liberation Movement, with a delegation led by Ezboni Mondiri
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the war says southerners saw the war as bound to come: after independence the southern elite had little power in Khartoum, and southerners were treated as a minority both ethnic and religious.

parties.name: The mediators: the All Africa Conference of Churches and the World Council of Churches, with Burgess Carr moderating, and Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as observer
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says discussions in 1971 went through the two church bodies and that Carr, then Secretary General of the All Africa Conference of Churches, moderated the talks at Addis Ababa; the article on the war says Haile Selassie observed the agreement.

causes.note: What it settled: the south gained a degree of autonomy as the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region, with its own legislative and executive bodies and no longer divided into three regions; Anya Nya soldiers were to join the army and police, and the south could not have its own military. The accords were written into the constitution of Sudan.

The article on the war says southerners were a religious as well as an ethnic minority in the state, and that the northern ruling class tied the conflict to the south’s embrace of Christianity and modernity. The article on the agreement records the church bodies’ part as go-betweens.

The article says the war had grown costly in lives and resources for the northern government and the southern population, and that later unrest in the south came from resource infringements and marginalisation by the north.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article on the First Sudanese Civil War (1955 to 1972) gives 500,000 to one million dead, only one in five of them armed combatants, with hundreds of thousands more driven from their homes.

outcome.note: The agreement ended the First Sudanese Civil War, which the article dates from 18 August 1955 to 27 March 1972, and created the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region with a regional assembly and executive council.

after.note: The article says a decade of relative peace followed but the tensions behind the war were not removed. In 1983 President Nimeiry declared all Sudan an Islamic state under Sharia law, including the non-Islamic majority southern region, and the autonomous region was abolished on 5 June 1983, which ended the agreement and began the Second Sudanese Civil War.

entries.label: The Lebanese Civil War
entries.summary: From 1975 to 1990 a many-sided war is fought in Lebanon, first between Christian militias and Palestinian factions allied with Muslim, leftist and pan-Arab groups, and then among shifting alliances, with Syria, Israel and other states taking part. It grows out of tensions in Lebanon’s system of power-sharing among its religious communities. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Lebanese Civil War
sources.note: it reports the historians it names; none was opened

parties.name: The Lebanese Front, made up of nationalist Maronite and other Christian militias, with the South Lebanon Army
parties.said: The article says the Lebanese Front consisted of nationalist Maronites who were against Palestinian militancy in Lebanon, and that although the militias began by trying to be politically oriented, non-sectarian forces, in the long run almost all of them openly identified with one community. No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read.

parties.name: The Lebanese National Movement and the Palestine Liberation Organization, with allied Muslim, leftist and pan-Arab groups
parties.said: The article says the Lebanese National Movement consisted of pro-Palestinian leftists, and that it was replaced after the Israeli invasion of 1982 by the Lebanese National Resistance Front. No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read.

parties.name: Outside states: Syria, Israel and, the article says, Iran, with international peacekeeping forces
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records the Syrian intervention of 1976, Israeli invasions in 1978 and 1982 and the deployment of a multinational force and of the United Nations Interim Force.

causes.note: The article says the war arose from long-standing political and sectarian tensions within Lebanon’s confessional system, in which offices and seats are shared among the religious communities.
Demographic change, the presence of armed Palestinian groups after the Arab–Israeli conflict, regional rivalries and the Cold War, which the article names beside the sectarian tensions.

The article notes that much of the fighting was between sectarian and ideological coalitions but that significant violence also took place within single communities, so that how far the war was one of religion, of ideology or of outside powers is not settled in the sources read.

conflict.casualty_note: Not recorded as a range: the article’s opening gives an estimated 120,000 deaths and nearly one million people displaced, without saying who counted them.

outcome.note: The Taif Agreement of 1989 was designed to end the war; the infobox dates the end of the fighting to 13 October 1990.

after.note: The Taif Agreement adjusted the share of Christians and Muslims in Parliament to equal numbers and moved powers from the Maronite president to the Sunni prime minister; the article says Syria, which the agreement told to withdraw within two years, kept forces in Lebanon until 2005.

entries.label: The Second Sudanese Civil War
entries.summary: From 1983 to 2005 the government of Sudan in Khartoum fights the Sudan People’s Liberation Army, which began in the south, in a war that spread to the Nuba Mountains and the Blue Nile. It ends with the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of 2005, and South Sudan becomes independent in 2011. Whether the war was mainly about religion, resources or governance is argued; this entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Second Sudanese Civil War
sources.note: it reports Douglas Johnson and the other sources it names; none was opened

parties.name: The government of Sudan in Khartoum, under President Gaafar Nimeiry and later governments
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says that in 1983 Nimeiry declared all of Sudan an Islamic state, ending the Southern Sudan Autonomous Region, and that after 1985 he gave public assurances that the rights of non-Muslims would be respected, which southerners and other non-Muslims remained suspicious of.

parties.name: The Sudan People’s Liberation Army and Movement, led by John Garang
parties.said: The article says the SPLA, founded in 1983, identified itself as a movement for all oppressed Sudanese citizens and at first campaigned for a united Sudan, criticising government policies for leading to national “disintegration”; it aimed to re-establish an autonomous southern Sudan.

causes.note: Some sources, the article says, describe the conflict as ethnoreligious: the pursuit by the Arab Muslim central government, in 1983, of Sharia law for non-Muslim southerners led to violence and then civil war. The historian Douglas Johnson points instead to exploitative governance as the root cause.

The article says the war was partly about natural resources: oil fields lie between north and south, and the first violations of the 1972 agreement came when Nimeiry tried to take control of the oil fields on the border; the south also has the better water and land.

A long pattern in which central governments have tried to dominate the peoples of the periphery, with allegations of marginalisation; the article says violation of the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972, which gave the south autonomy, led to the second war.

casualties.unit: dead, mostly civilians, from fighting, starvation and drought
casualties.basis: People who died as a result of the war from 1983 to 2005, in the main civilians, many from hunger and drought as well as from fighting.
casualties.note: The article’s text says roughly two million died, and its infobox gives one to two million; it says four million people in southern Sudan were displaced at least once, and does not say who counted.

outcome.note: The Comprehensive Peace Agreement, signed on 9 January 2005 at Nairobi, ended the war: the south had autonomy for six years, to be followed by a referendum on independence, and oil revenues were to be shared equally during that time.

after.note: A referendum was held from 9 to 15 January 2011, in which 98.83% voted for independence, and South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011, six years after the war ended.

entries.label: The Taif Agreement (the National Reconciliation Accord)
entries.summary: Signed in October 1989 in Taif, Saudi Arabia, by the surviving members of Lebanon’s 1972 parliament, the agreement is meant to end the Lebanese Civil War. It shares seats in Parliament equally between Christians and Muslims and shifts powers from the Maronite president to the Sunni prime minister. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Taif Agreement
sources.note: the text of the agreement was not opened

parties.name: The surviving members of Lebanon’s 1972 parliament, with Speaker Hussein El-Husseini
parties.said: The agreement’s official purpose, as the article gives it, was to provide “the basis for the ending of the civil war and the return to political normalcy in Lebanon”. It sets as its principle “mutual coexistence” among Lebanon’s different sects and their “proper political representation” as the aim of electoral laws after the war.

parties.name: The mediators: Saudi Arabia, with the United States taking a discreet part and Syria exerting influence behind the scenes
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the agreement came into effect with the active mediation of Saudi Arabia, and was confirmed only after the anti-Saddam Hussein alliance had formed.

causes.note: The sharing of power among the religious communities: before Taif the Sunni prime minister was appointed by and answerable to the Maronite president; after it he was answerable to Parliament, and seats were to be shared equally between Christians and Muslims.

The ending of the war, the disarmament of militias, the reassertion of the government’s authority in the south, and special relations with Syria with a timetable for its withdrawal; the article says Hezbollah was allowed to stay armed as a “resistance force”, which the Swedish academic Magnus Ranstorp ascribes in part to its leverage as holder of Western hostages.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the war it ended are given in the entry for the Lebanese Civil War.

outcome.note: The agreement was signed on 22 October 1989 and ratified by the Lebanese parliament on 5 November. Its constitutional amendments, in force from September 1990, cut the ratio of Christians to Muslims in Parliament from 6 to 5 to 1 to 1 and lengthened the Speaker’s term from one year to four.

after.note: The article says the agreement set two years for the end of the Syrian presence, and that Syria did not withdraw its forces until 2005; it also says it is argued that Taif turned Lebanon towards the Arab world, especially Syria.

entries.label: The Algerian Civil War (the “Black Decade”)
entries.summary: In January 1992 the Algerian army cancels an electoral process that the Islamic Salvation Front was expected to win, and a war follows between the government and several Islamist armed groups that lasts until 2002. Algerians call it the Black Decade. Who was responsible for some attacks on civilians is disputed, and the toll is estimated at anywhere from about forty-four thousand to two hundred thousand. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Algerian Civil War
sources.note: it reports the researchers and human rights bodies it names; none was opened

parties.name: The Algerian government and army, with the National Liberation Front (FLN)
parties.said: The article records that the army cancelled the electoral process on 11 January 1992, forcing President Bendjedid to resign, and that the Islamic Salvation Front was officially dissolved on 4 March. It reports President Bouteflika as saying in 1999 that 100,000 people had died by then, and in 2005 that about 150,000 had been killed.

parties.name: The Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) and its supporters, with the armed groups that grew out of the movement
parties.said: The article says the FIS co-leader Ali Benhadj declared in 1990 that he intended “to ban France from Algeria intellectually and ideologically”, and that from prison he issued a fatwa blessing the Islamic Armed Movement, a group that favoured a long guerrilla jihad against the state. It says the first act of jihad against the government came on 28 November 1991, before the election.

parties.name: The Armed Islamic Group (GIA), from 1993
parties.said: The article says the GIA took a hard line against both the government and the FIS, affirming that “political pluralism is equivalent to sedition”, and that its leader Antar Zouabri claimed the attacks on the villages of Rais and Bentalha as an “offering to God”, declaring that all who were not with it were apostates. It says the group’s responsibility for those attacks is disputed.

causes.note: The FIS, an Islamist party, won the local elections of 1990 and the first round of the parliamentary elections in December 1991. The article says armed groups then declared jihad on the government, that the FIS leadership was at best divided on the desirability of democracy, and that its local administrations were praised by many while alarming the educated French-speaking class.

The army cancelled the electoral process on 11 January 1992 after the FIS had won 188 seats to the FLN’s 16 in the first round; the article says thousands of FIS members were arrested, 5,000 by the army’s account and 40,000 according to Gilles Kepel. The Sant’Egidio article calls the cancellation a coup, as does the article on the war in its headings.

How far the war was a fight over religion, over political power or over the interests of the army and the security services is argued. The article says the suspicion that the state controlled parts of the GIA is rejected by many researchers and regarded as plausible by others, and it lists what kept Algeria from becoming an Islamic state: the army rank and file, veterans of the War of Independence and the secular middle class.

casualties.unit: dead and disappeared, civilians, insurgents and government forces together
casualties.basis: Deaths and disappearances in the fighting between 1992 and 2002.
casualties.note: The low end is a 2008 study the article cites, about 26,000 killed and 18,000 disappeared and presumed dead; the high end is Fouad Ajami’s argument that the toll could reach 200,000 and that it is in the government’s interest to play it down. The 100,000 and 150,000 of President Bouteflika’s speeches lie between, and the article says the commonly cited figures are not broken down by side and may be too high. It says over 70 journalists and over 100 foreigners were killed.

outcome.note: The article’s infobox gives a government victory and dates the end of the war to 8 February 2002. It says that by 1996 and 1997 the Islamist resistance had lost popular support, that one armed group, the Islamic Salvation Army, declared a unilateral truce, and that an amnesty referendum in 2005 on the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation passed with 97 per cent of the vote on a turnout of 80 per cent.

after.note: The article says the charter gave immunity from prosecution to surrendered fighters and to army personnel, which human rights bodies and families of the disappeared opposed, and that a state of emergency stayed in force until February 2011. It also says the war left the public with a deep fear of instability and that Algeria was one of the few Arab states not to take part in the Arab Spring.

entries.label: The Bosnian War
entries.summary: After Bosnia and Herzegovina votes for independence from Yugoslavia in 1992, war breaks out among the government, whose people are mostly Bosniaks, who are mostly Muslim, and the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat leaderships, whose people are mostly Orthodox and Catholic, with Serbia and Croatia in support. It ends with the Dayton Agreement in 1995. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bosnian War
sources.note: it reports the demographic studies of the Research and Documentation Center, Sarajevo and the Hague tribunal; neither was opened

parties.name: The government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose people are mostly Bosniaks
parties.said: The article says Bosnia and Herzegovina passed a referendum for independence on 29 February 1992, in a country that was 44% mainly Muslim Bosniaks, 32.5% Orthodox Serbs and 17% Catholic Croats, and that it was internationally recognised in April 1992.

parties.name: The Bosnian Serb leadership and the Republika Srpska, led and supplied from Serbia
parties.said: The article says the Bosnian Serb political representatives boycotted the referendum and rejected its result, and that, in anticipation of it, their leadership proclaimed a “Republic of the Serb People” of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

parties.name: The Bosnian Croat leadership and Herzeg-Bosnia, led and supplied from Croatia
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that a Croat–Bosniak war broke out in 1993 and that the Washington Agreement of 1994 ended it.

causes.note: The breakup of Yugoslavia after the secession of Slovenia and Croatia in 1991 and the referendum on Bosnian independence of February 1992, which the Bosnian Serb representatives rejected.

The article names the three main groups by religion as well as by ethnicity, Muslim Bosniaks, Orthodox Serbs and Catholic Croats, and sets the war within the breakup of Yugoslavia; it does not name religion itself as a cause, and how far the war was one of religion, ethnicity or state power is argued.

casualties.unit: people killed or missing in the war
casualties.basis: A demographic reconstruction for the Hague tribunal in 2010 gave a minimum of 89,186 and a probable 104,732 deaths, counting battle and mass violence but not non-violent rises in deaths; it excludes deaths from hunger or illness.
casualties.note: The Research and Documentation Center in Sarajevo recorded 101,040 dead or missing in its final report of 2012, of whom 61.4% were Bosniaks, 24.7% Serbs and 8.3% Croats, with 38,239 civilians; the article calls it the most authoritative account. Estimates of 200,000 and more were cited in 1994 and later revised downward.

outcome.note: The war ended when the Dayton Agreement was initialled on 21 November 1995, after a military stalemate.

after.note: NATO-led forces were deployed to oversee the peace and a High Representative to oversee its civil side. The article on Dayton says the agreement has been praised for lasting peace and criticised for a complex political system and for entrenching the results of forced displacement.

entries.label: The Chapultepec Peace Accords in El Salvador
entries.summary: On 16 January 1992 the Salvadoran government and the guerrilla coalition FMLN sign the Chapultepec Peace Accords in Mexico City, ending a civil war that began in 1979 and killed, by the United Nations’ report, more than seventy-five thousand people. Earlier rounds of talks, from 1984 to 1987, had been mediated by Archbishop Arturo Rivera y Damas, and the final talks had observers from the Catholic Church and the United Nations. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Chapultepec Peace Accords
sources.note: the text of the accords was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Salvadoran Civil War
sources.note: a very long article; its opening, background and the sections on the early years were read, and the United Nations report it cites was not opened

parties.name: The Salvadoran government, under Presidents José Napoleón Duarte and later Alfredo Cristiani
parties.said: The article on the war says the government was backed by the United States, which held that its aid was justified because the insurgents were backed by the Soviet Union. The accords article records that Cristiani called for a dialogue meeting in September 1989 and that the two sides then asked the United Nations Secretary-General to mediate.

parties.name: The FMLN, a coalition of left-wing guerrilla groups, with leaders such as Guillermo Ungo
parties.said: The article on the war says the FMLN was backed by Cuba, Nicaragua and the Soviet Union. The accords article says it launched a general offensive on 11 November 1989 to demonstrate its military strength, and that its armed wing was to be dissolved and become a political party.

parties.name: The mediators: Archbishop Arturo Rivera y Damas for the Catholic Church in 1984 to 1987, then the United Nations’ Álvaro de Soto, with observers from the Church at the final talks
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says Rivera y Damas acted as a mediator in rounds of talks at La Palma and Ayagualo in 1984, at Sesori in 1986 and in San Salvador in 1987, and that the final negotiations had observers from the Roman Catholic Church and the United Nations, with de Soto, the Secretary-General’s special representative, as mediator.

causes.note: The accords covered five areas: changes to the armed forces and demobilisation of the FMLN, a new National Civil Police in place of the National Guard, changes to the judicial system and the defence of human rights, changes to the electoral system, and measures in the economic and social fields.

The Church’s part was as mediator and observer. The article on the war has a section on the assassination of Archbishop Óscar Romero, who had written to President Carter in February 1980 to ask him to suspend US military aid, and reports the killing of four American Catholic church women in December 1980; how far these events shaped the settlement is not measured in the sources read.
The article says that after ten years of war more than a million people had been displaced out of a population of 5,389,000, and that 40 per cent of the homes of the displaced had been destroyed.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the war it ended is given in the article on the Salvadoran Civil War as having killed more than 75,000 people between 1979 and 1992, by a United Nations report, with about 8,000 disappeared; the accords article says anywhere from 70,000 to 80,000.

outcome.note: The accords were signed on 16 January 1992 at Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City. A ceasefire of nine months took effect on 1 February 1992 and, the article says, was never broken, and a United Nations mission supervised compliance for three years.

after.note: The article on the war says the army was restructured, the National Guard and Treasury Police dissolved and the FMLN’s armed wing turned into a political party. It says a 1993 amnesty law hindered accountability for wartime killings, and that in 2016 the Supreme Court of Justice ruled the law unconstitutional.

entries.label: The Rome General Peace Accords in Mozambique
entries.summary: In October 1992 the government of Mozambique and the rebel movement RENAMO sign a peace treaty in Rome that ends a civil war begun in 1977. The talks were brokered by two members of the Community of Sant’Egidio, a bishop and an Italian government representative. The article on the war gives its causes as local strife and Cold War politics. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Rome General Peace Accords
sources.note: a short article; the text of the accords was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mozambican Civil War
sources.note: it reports the Gersony Report and the scholars it names; none was opened

parties.name: The government of Mozambique under President Joaquim Chissano, with FRELIMO, its delegation led by Armando Guebuza
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the war says FRELIMO was a ruling Marxist party that attempted to establish a socialist one-party state.

parties.name: RENAMO, led by Afonso Dhlakama
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article on the war says RENAMO opposed FRELIMO’s attempts to establish a socialist one-party state and had the backing of the governments of Rhodesia and South Africa; the accords article records that RENAMO declared on 21 October 2013 that it was annulling the accord after a government attack on its base.

parties.name: The mediators: Andrea Riccardi and Matteo Zuppi of the Community of Sant’Egidio, Bishop Jaime Gonçalves, and Mario Raffaelli for the Italian government
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says talks began in July 1990 and were brokered by this team of four; the article on the war adds that the Mozambican Church Council and the Italian government mediated and that the United Nations supported the negotiations.

causes.note: The accords ended the war: RENAMO units were to be demobilised or merged into the armed forces, and a United Nations force arrived to oversee a two-year transition to democracy, with elections on 27 and 28 October 1994. The article on the war says the war ended after the Soviet Union and South Africa stopped supporting FRELIMO and RENAMO respectively.

The mediation came from church-linked people and bodies: two members of the Community of Sant’Egidio, a bishop and the Mozambican Church Council. The sources read do not say what part each played beyond bringing the two sides to talk.

The article on the war says the war destroyed much rural infrastructure, including hospitals, rail lines, roads and schools, left the government economically devastated and caused famine, which it names among the reasons the government sought an end to the fighting.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the article on the war gives over one million Mozambicans killed in the fighting or by starvation, with five million displaced across the region. It reports that both sides were accused of abuses against civilians and that scholars it names differ on how the abuses were shared between them.

outcome.note: The General Peace Accords were signed in Rome on 4 October 1992 by President Chissano and the RENAMO leader Afonso Dhlakama; the article on the war says they took effect on 15 October 1992.

after.note: A United Nations force oversaw the transition and the elections of October 1994. The article on the war says tensions between RENAMO and FRELIMO flared again between 2013 and 2018, and that RENAMO then resumed its insurgency on a smaller scale.

entries.label: The Dayton Agreement (1995)

places.name: Paris, where it was signed on 14 December 1995

entries.summary: The General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, initialled at Dayton, Ohio, on 21 November 1995 and signed in Paris on 14 December, ends the Bosnian War. Bosnia and Herzegovina stays one state made of two parts, Republika Srpska and the Federation. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Dayton Agreement
sources.note: the text of the agreement was not opened

parties.name: The warring parties: the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat leaderships, with Serbia and Croatia
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the parties agreed to peace and to a single sovereign state of two parts, the largely Serb-populated Republika Srpska and the mainly Croat and Bosniak Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

parties.name: Those who judged it afterwards
parties.said: The article reports that Charles-Philippe David calls Dayton “the most impressive example of conflict resolution”, while Patrice McMahon and Jon Western write that, “as successful as Dayton was at ending the violence, it also sowed the seeds of instability by creating a decentralized political system that undermined the state’s authority”.

causes.note: The agreement’s stated purpose was peace and stability in Bosnia and Herzegovina and regional balance; it fixed the structure of government, the boundary between the two entities and a rotating state presidency.

It adopted power-sharing among the country’s three main groups, named in the other article by religion as well as ethnicity; critics, the article says, hold that it entrenched the results of forced displacement.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the Bosnian War are given in its entry, as a range with its basis.

outcome.note: Bosnia and Herzegovina remained a single state with a central government, a rotating presidency, a central bank and a constitutional court, made of the Federation and Republika Srpska; a NATO-led force, a High Representative and the OSCE were charged with implementing it.

after.note: The article says the agreement is praised for establishing lasting peace and criticised for a complex system of government; it calls it a “construction of necessity”, aimed at freezing the military confrontation.

entries.label: The Sant’Egidio Platform on peace in Algeria
entries.summary: On 13 January 1995 most of the main Algerian opposition parties, among them the Islamic Salvation Front, the National Liberation Front and the Socialist Forces Front, meet in Rome under the auspices of the Community of Sant’Egidio and issue a joint platform for ending the civil war. The government rejected it, and the armed groups either dismissed it or answered with ultimatums. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Sant’Egidio platform
sources.note: a short article; the text of the platform was not opened

parties.name: The opposition parties that signed: the FIS (Rabah Kebir and Anwar Haddam), the FLN (Abdelhamid Mehri), the FFS (Hocine Aït Ahmed), the Workers Party, the Islamic Renaissance Movement and others
parties.said: The article says that in a joint statement they rejected violence to achieve political goals and called for respect for human rights and democracy. Their platform demanded new parliamentary elections, the repeal of the dissolution of the FIS, independent investigations of human rights abuses since the army cancelled the elections, and the withdrawal of the army from politics.

parties.name: The Algerian government, under President Liamine Zeroual
parties.said: The article says Zeroual categorically rejected the platform, denouncing it as a threat to national sovereignty because it invited foreign intervention into Algeria’s internal affairs.

parties.name: The armed Islamist groups: the Islamic Salvation Army and the Armed Islamic Group
parties.said: The article says the Islamic Salvation Army called the platform a diversion, and the Armed Islamic Group presented three ultimatums: the punishment of secularist generals, a ban on the communist and atheist parties, and the release of Islamist leaders from prison.

parties.name: The Community of Sant’Egidio, which hosted the talks in Rome
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article calls it the Catholic Community of Sant’Egidio and says it had played an important part in the Rome General Peace Accords of 1992 that ended the civil war in Mozambique.

causes.note: The platform set out a way out of the war through new elections, an end to the army’s role in politics and a renewed commitment to the constitution. The article says the FIS, FLN and FFS together had won 80 per cent of the votes in the 1991 election, which it calls significant.

The talks were hosted by a Catholic community, and the article says the presence of the FIS and its commitment to a peaceful transfer of power were significant. It says the platform was meant as a model of democratic governance and political reconciliation, and that the armed wings of the Islamists were already dissatisfied with it when it was signed.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement was proposed, not reached: the war it addressed is given in the entry for the Algerian Civil War, with its estimated toll.

outcome.note: The platform was never put into effect: the article says it lacked the endorsement of the armed Islamists and was rejected by the President.

after.note: The war went on until about 2002. The article on the war records that later peace measures came from the government: a 1999 amnesty law and, in 2005, the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, which French newspapers criticised for the conditions of its campaign.

entries.label: The South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission
entries.summary: In 1996, after the end of apartheid, South Africa’s government sets up a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu. It takes statements from people who say they suffered gross human rights violations and lets those who testify apply for amnesty. Whether it achieved reconciliation, and whether granting amnesty was just, are still argued. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Truth and Reconciliation Commission (South Africa)
sources.note: it reports the surveys and critics it names; the commission’s own report was not opened

sources.title: Wikipedia: Desmond Tutu
sources.note: a very long article; its opening and its section on the commission were read

parties.name: The Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, with Alex Boraine as deputy
parties.said: The article on Tutu says he proposed a threefold approach: confession, with those responsible fully disclosing their activities; forgiveness, in the form of a legal amnesty; and restitution, with those responsible making amends. It says he advocated restorative justice “in the spirit of ubuntu”, opened meetings with prayers and often referred to Christian teachings, which frustrated some who saw too many religious elements in an expressly secular body.

parties.name: The people who gave statements about their experiences, and their families
parties.said: The article says the commission invited witnesses identified as “victims of gross human rights violations” to give statements and chose some for public hearings. A 1998 survey it cites of several hundred such people found that most felt the commission had failed to achieve reconciliation between black and white communities, that justice was a prerequisite for reconciliation, and that the commission had been weighted in favour of those responsible. The article on Tutu says he singled out those who expressed forgiveness.

parties.name: Former leaders and officials who appeared, or did not, before the commission
parties.said: The article says former State President P. W. Botha defied a subpoena, calling the commission a “circus”, and that former President F. W. de Klerk appeared and repeated his apology for the suffering caused by apartheid but, local reports noted, did not accept that his party’s policies had given the security forces a “licence to kill”.

causes.note: The article on Tutu says the post-apartheid government had to decide how to respond to abuses by the state and by anti-apartheid activists, the National Party wanting a comprehensive amnesty and the ANC trials of former state figures. The commission was set up under the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act of 1995, and the article says the first coalition government chose forgiveness over prosecution and reparation over retaliation.

Tutu, an Anglican archbishop, drew on the African idea of ubuntu, which the article describes as a spiritual awareness of our interconnectedness as a human family, and on Christian teaching. Some saw too many religious elements in a secular body; the article says opinions differ on the effectiveness of the restorative approach compared with retributive justice, and a survey of three ethnic groups found all thought it effective in bringing out the truth, to varying degrees.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement of a kind, a commission and not a treaty: the article says the commission found about 7,000 political deaths under apartheid between 1948 and 1989, 73 of them in detention, and more than 19,050 people who were “victims of gross human rights violations”, with 2,975 more identified through amnesty applications.

outcome.note: The first hearing was held in April 1996, and the hearings were televised. Of 7,111 amnesty applications, the article says 5,392 were refused and 849 granted. The Institute for Justice and Reconciliation was set up in 2000 as the commission’s successor.

after.note: The article says many black South Africans were angered at amnesty for abuses by the apartheid government, and the family of Steve Biko brought a legal action calling the commission unconstitutional. Over 300 cases of gross violations remained unresolved when it closed and were handed to the National Prosecuting Authority. Critics cited argue that its mandate left out systemic wrongs such as forced removals and pass arrests; the BBC called criticism of the amnesty a basic misunderstanding of the mandate, which critics dispute.

entries.label: The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement
entries.summary: On 10 April 1998 the British and Irish governments and most of Northern Ireland’s political parties sign an agreement that ends most of the violence of the Troubles. It restores self-government on a power-sharing basis, accepts that Northern Ireland’s status changes only by the consent of its people, and commits all to human rights and equality. Voters in both parts of Ireland approve it on 22 May.

sources.title: The Agreement reached in the multi-party negotiations, 1998, in the CAIN web service, Ulster University
sources.note: the text of the Agreement; only its Declaration of Support was read closely

parties.name: The British and Irish governments and most of Northern Ireland’s political parties
parties.said: The Declaration of Support says the participants “believe that the agreement we have negotiated offers a truly historic opportunity for a new beginning”, that “the tragedies of the past have left a deep and profoundly regrettable legacy of suffering”, and that they “firmly dedicate ourselves to the achievement of reconciliation, tolerance, and mutual trust, and to the protection and vindication of the human rights of all”.

parties.name: The people of Northern Ireland and of the Republic of Ireland, who voted on it
parties.said: In the referendums of 22 May 1998 the article says turnout in Northern Ireland was 81%, with 71% in favour, and in the Republic 56%, with 94% in favour; of those who voted in Northern Ireland, almost all Catholics voted for the Agreement, compared with 57% of Protestants.

causes.note: The Agreement dealt with sovereignty, governance, discrimination, military and paramilitary groups, justice and policing. It records that the majority of the people of Northern Ireland wished to remain in the United Kingdom, and that a substantial section of them and the majority on the island wished for a united Ireland.
The Agreement affirms “the mutual respect, the civil rights and the religious liberties of everyone in the community”; the article counts the support of the two communities separately in the vote.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the conflict it ended are given in the entry for the Troubles.

outcome.note: The Agreement, signed on 10 April 1998, restored self-government on the basis of power-sharing, accepted the principle of consent, committed to civil and political rights and cultural parity of esteem, and provided for police reform, the disarmament of paramilitary groups, the early release of paramilitary prisoners and demilitarisation. It also created institutions between Northern Ireland and Ireland and between Ireland and the United Kingdom.

after.note: Power was devolved to the new Assembly on 2 December 1999. The article says the fragility of cross-community support for parts of the Agreement helps to explain later difficulties in keeping the power-sharing executive going, and that many of its rights provisions, including a Bill of Rights for Northern Ireland, have yet to be fully carried out.

entries.label: The Comprehensive Peace Agreement in Sudan
entries.summary: On 9 January 2005 the government of Sudan and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement sign the Comprehensive Peace Agreement, also called the Naivasha Agreement, which ends the second civil war, shares oil revenue, sets up power-sharing and promises the south a referendum on independence after six years. This entry is within living memory, and each statement is labelled.

parties.name: The Government of Sudan
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article says the agreement was meant to end the war, to develop democratic governance across the country and to share oil revenues.

parties.name: The Sudan People’s Liberation Movement
parties.said: No statement of theirs is quoted in the sources read. The article records that the agreement set a timetable for a referendum on southern independence and that the south would have autonomy for six years before it.

parties.name: The mediators: the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, with the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway
parties.said: The article says the peace process was encouraged by the Authority and by this “troika” of donor countries.

causes.note: Self-government for the south, power-sharing, the arrangement of armed forces and a referendum on secession; the article lists protocols on principles of government, power-sharing, wealth-sharing and the contested areas of Abyei, Southern Kordofan and the Blue Nile.
Oil income was to be shared evenly between north and south, and jobs were split by agreed ratios.

Some sources describe the war as one over the imposition of Sharia law on non-Muslim southerners; none of the protocols the article lists is on religion, and the article does not say how the agreement dealt with it.

conflict.casualty_note: A settlement, not a conflict: the dead of the war it ended are given in the entry for the Second Sudanese Civil War.

outcome.note: The agreement of 9 January 2005 gave the south autonomy for six years, then a referendum; if it had gone for unity the two armies were to merge into a force of 39,000; oil income was shared evenly; jobs in the central administration were split 70 to 30 in the government’s favour.

after.note: The southern referendum of 9 to 15 January 2011 gave 98.83% for independence, and South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011.
